Report 20: users restored in Feb 2021 came back and raised their ratings (23 five-star reviews carry the revocation theme as amended reviews); a 20 Oct 2020 launch failure fixed next day drew praise for the speed. Report 23: 12 edited reviews, several visible upgrades after a developer fix; sync-migration recoveries within weeks; reviewers upgraded on learning a backup path existed. Report 24: a 2018–19 billing crisis was fixed in one month and the mean snapped back from 2.884 to 4.206 for four years; refunds that land turn 1★ into 4★ edits. Report 25: a Turkish localisation request made eight times in Jan–Jun 2026 was answered on 27 Jul 2026 ('Türkçe dil desteği sonundaaa! 🌟') — the clearest shipped-fix-visible-in-reviews event in the corpus. Report 26: a visible 2024 engineering turnaround — crashes 3.37% → 0.13%, the 'music can't be turned off' bug 2.88% → 0.00%, mean 4.339 → 4.675 — with the substantive-only mean rising too; a reviewer thanked the team for adding a calendar; Russian localisation criticised in 2023 was praised by 2025. Report 27: requested features ship on a 6–18 month lag — per-weekday flexibility (Jul 2025 → Mar 2026), reordering (Sept 2024 → Aug 2025), goal end date and archiving (Dec 2025 → on the listing by Sep 2026); the crash was fixed within about four months and the mean recovered to 4.829. Report 28: a 1★ upgraded to 5★ after one support e-mail ('The devs pay attention. 5 stars now'); bugs collapsed from 11.3% (2023) to 0.7% (2025) after a genuine stabilisation. Report 29: the calendar bug fell ~8× between 2025H2 and 2026H1 and the mean rose 4.39 → 4.66; habit editing missing in 2024 was added by May 2025 — but 'a fix ships, and the reviews it caused remain on the store page forever'. Report 30 (counter-evidence): the developer's response to the cap complaint — one more free habit — did not change the rate or the ratings. Report 31: the original solo developer shipped a wished-for feature two days later, replied to a crash e-mail and fixed it 'ASAP', restored a purchase 'within minutes' — support praise 18 (mean 4.78), 11 in E1; after the sale, public developer replies began only in 2024 with split outcomes (restored within days vs a promised refund never issued, 'they sneakily changed their developer response') and support-unresponsive stayed at 20.8% in E5. Report 33: fast fixes after a review earn thanks and rating rises ('thank you for responding right after my review'; a 1★ raised to 4★ after a fix); a public roadmap and feature voting; the Jan 2018 purchase wave fixed in two weeks and the Sep 2025 launch crash in 1–3 days; 'An update improved it' 112 (mean 4.78). Report 34: 52 developer-praise reviews (mean 4.96), 31 naming 'Kevin'; replies turned ratings up ('Updated to 4 stars - thank you devs for the response!'); weekly habits and a reviewer's suggestion built on request; an in-app 'in progress' roadmap list ('this informing and communicative attitude was a huge plus'); the share fell 13.2% (E1) → 5.2% (E5). Report 41: eleven requested capabilities shipped inside the corpus with requesters returning to confirm (notes, Watch, % widget — review edited twice, Shortcuts in the same month, CSV export, vacation mode, heat maps, mood, custom day start 'It was not available at that time, but it is now', Czech / Italian / Traditional Chinese); a support reply 'within hours. Twice' closed a lifetime sale. Report 42: reviewers notice fixes — 'Thanks for the update, it helped remove the lag. I'll bring my subscription back'; 'how much the app has improved in that time! Progress details, results info, charts' — vs 'they just reply the same thing to everyone'. Report 43: at least four verified cases of shipping what reviewers asked — Apple Watch (12 requests, none after it shipped), drag-to-reorder (7 asks, shipped Nov 2025), the timer music fix that turned a 2★ into 5★, and a feature 'added a few days later' (Jan 2026); three of the top four feature gaps have since closed. Report 46: each shipped request stops and a praise theme starts — widgets (Sep 2020), Watch (Mar 2021), journal / calendar (Dec 2023), folders (Aug 2025), no-account use (2024), Turkish and Chinese UI; personal support praised by 53 ('reach out to Joan and received a response in less than 30 minutes'; 'Joan helped me add my previous habit data from a different app'), eight ratings raised after contact. Report 47: 12 reviews (mean 4.42), 10 since 2024, acknowledge a fix — photo multi-select within a week of the request ('まさか本当に意見を取り入れてくださるとは'), late-night gap, Sunday week start, hiding non-scheduled days; stagnant-development complaints 3 ('1年以上更新がないのも残念', 2023). Report 48: 103 praise shipped updates and the public feature-voting board (4.80); 55 confirm a specific fix (4.78); Australia has the highest dev-listens rate anywhere (6.45%); several reviewers raise their rating in place after contact. Report 49: an official Discord with an active developer (17, 4.65) and visible responsiveness (19, 4.74) both rise across eras; an Indonesian reviewer abandoned over rigidity, wrote in, returned months later to find customisation built — 'THIS APP HAS BEEN IMPROVED A LOT'; 8 more noticed. Report 50: 'the developer implemented what I asked and more - he pretty much filled all the gaps I identified'; 'crowdsourcing feature ideas from the community(!!!)'; 'reorder habits without scheduling (*this was updated very soon, thank you)'; requests moved from 'does it exist' (widgets, Watch, to-dos) to 'does it go deep enough' within ~18 months. Report 53: VoiceOver unlabeled buttons reported Dec 2021 and a fix confirmed Mar 2022; an icon suggestion implemented within days. Report 54: 'I know from Reddit that you aren't spending much time on this app anymore, but please fix this small necessary thing! I would pay for the premium version again in a heartbeat!' (4★). Report 55: a reviewer raised their rating when version 1.4.11 fixed the crash, after 'nearly nine months of complaints'. Report 56: 'It didn't have options for reminders & shuffling the order of your habits, but it does now! -Even more happy with it' — visible shipping raised a verdict; 13 of 67 thank the developer by name. Report 57: seven of the ten largest early complaints were fixed (streaks, backup, Watch, custom widget restored after complaints, widget tap, keyboard, past-date, accidental purchase) — 'Recent update is a godsend. They fixed an issue with the widgets and this app is back to being one of my top 3 apps'. Report 59 (Tappsk): PR_DEV 1,244 (8.20%, 4.96★, rising to 10.0% of the latest era) — reviewers thank the developer by name, praise fast Telegram replies ('Поддержка решила вопрос очень быстро'; 'j'ai réussi à joindre le support par Télégram qui a été d'une grande aide'; 'поддержка подарила мне подписку навсегда другой аккаунт'), and a fixed bug earns a 'P.S. Все исправлено, спасибо'; the report says keep the developer's visible presence. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): zero customer-support mentions in 45 reviews — nobody reports contacting the developer, including the three whose app broke after paying; failed purchasers asked for a fix, not a refund. Report 65 (Rabit): a first-run block (12 of 26 reviews in 16–31 Jul 2021, mean 1.42) was fixed within days and reviewers came back — 'CORRIGIRAM O BUG — OBRIGADAAAA! Amei!' (DEV_FIX 3, mean 5.00) — 'the corpus's proof that fast fixes are visibly rewarded'; the Apr–Nov 2022 crash wave (13 of 67, eight payers) was not visibly fixed and one reviewer could not open the app for seven months. Report 67 (Habio): MKT_REVIEW_MISLEAD 74 (3.61%) cite other reviews, mostly as a warning to would-be buyers — 'the first several top-rated reviews were all previous users warning others not to pay'.

title: Cross-sell an app family on brand trust
statement: Under-used monetization asset. Report 23: Streaks is sold in a bundle with Streaks Workout and HealthFace. Report 24 (counter-evidence): a nine-app family (Clarify, Shape, Elixir, Lumière, Lune, Ambiance, Sphere, Mind, Enchant), each its own download and subscription, is experienced as advertising inside a paid product and as a billing trap; Clarify, the ADHD sister app, is named almost only inside billing complaints (mean 1.637). Cross-sell on brand trust works only while the trust and the billing are clean. Report 28: cross-promotion from the sibling app Study Bunny drove launch (31.8% of 2021 reviews, a beta-forgiving cohort with zero 1★) and still drives a tenth of reviews, but fell to 3.8% by 2026 — the app now acquires on its own store presence, so the rating and the ad policy are commercially decisive; users ask for single sign-on and a shared bunny across the family. Report 31 (counter-evidence): the Growth Bundle cross-sell became the only upgrade path and a post-purchase 'gift' upsell that broke entitlements — 36 bundle complaints (mean 2.03). Report 36: a 5-app 'Not Boring' membership — SUITE+ 34 (mean 4.41; 'I purchased the S2 for the weather app, but Habits is really the star for me'; 4 of 34 payers bought for the suite) vs SUITE- 9 (mean 3.22; 'Theoretically it includes 3 other apps, but this is the only good one … the calculator app … lags'): the weakest app in the bundle drags the perceived value of the price. Report 52: a studio family (布谷布谷, 须臾, 青子记账, 千结) with common cross-purchasers (USER_CROSSAPP 230, 4.57, payer lift ×3.49). Report 53: WaterMinder buyers arrive happy, but 2023–25 reviewers link the developer to the 'Done' app's degraded lifetime upgrades and call the whole portfolio a scam — 'I will be regretfully avoiding this developer because their pricing policies'.

title: Goodwill conversion — a generous free tier and 'support the devs'
statement: Small, pure-margin, mean 4.69. Report 5: the dominant purchase path was years of free use followed by upgrading to scale it or to say thanks. Report 20: a large share of pre-2021 purchases were donations — 'I'll definitely choose the highest one because this developer deserves the best'; 'I bought the paid function not because I needed it, but as a thank you.' Report 26: 'bought premium right away just to support the developers'; 45 call the free tier generous (mean 4.49). Report 28: 'I've spent money on this app SOLELY to support the developer because I can't thank him enough'; 'the actual habit tracking is FREE' praised by 13. Report 31: 'supporting a small team' was an E1 purchase trigger ('there is a small team behind so I was happy to pay'; 'happy to support the designers'). Report 33: supporting a small team was a purchase trigger ('I can see this team cares'); 48 call the free tier sufficient (mean 4.85); Vietnamese reviewers take pride in a Vietnamese-built app. Report 34: supporting a solo developer is a named purchase motive ('I paid the app to support solo developer'); 13 of 51 payers praise the developer. Report 36: patronage 5 of 34 payers (14.7%) — 'l'idée de payer 15€ par an pour féliciter, soutenir et remercier le travail d'une équipe indépendante'; proof-first 6 of 34 (17.6%) — 'Have been having it for free until today and decided to purchase'. Report 41: 'Just bought the premium to support the developer i don't even need the features tbh'; decisions made in 20 minutes to a few days on a 3-habit free tier. Report 43: 'I purchased the premium version because I want to support the excellent privacy and pricing policies!'; 'you wouldn't do your job for free. Don't expect programmers to work for free either'; 'I wanna donate the developer'. Report 46: 'I paid the subscription fee because it's a great app with a developer who obviously cares' (ADHD); 'I bought it to support the developer' — 13 (mean 4.92), 12 of them before July 2023; three free users state their condition ('If it helps me build three habits, I'll come back and pay!'). Report 47: gratitude that the app is free 25 (4.24%, mean 4.68 — 'この手のアプリはタスク増やすと課金が必要だけど…'); willing to pay 14 (mean 4.57), 9 before 2022, mostly to remove banners — the 'I'd pay to remove ads' user of 2019–23 became either a subscriber or a leaver after 2024 (ad-removal requests 2.6% → 0%). Report 48: 'free is enough' 248 (5.63%, 4.82) — the load-bearing praise of the freemium era; 38 payers describe months or years of free use before paying 'to support the developers'; pay-to-support-dev 7–9 at 5.00 — 'sustained free use first, then payment as endorsement'. Report 50: free tier praised by 12 (4.92) and price-positive 16 (4.81) — 14 five-stars volunteer the fair price unprompted; 'Has everything that u need and even more for free'; the documented purchase path runs through sustained free use first (a month; six months; 'Once [the habits are] internalised I'll be delighted to pay for more options'). Report 52: supporting an indie developer is a named purchase trigger (DEV_TRUST ∩ paid 52 at 4.98; bought 'so the app can keep running'). Report 54: 4 bought to support the developer, all 5★ — 'make a high quality product, offer it for free without junky ads, and without high pressure sales tactics. Let the app speak for itself'. Report 56: a fully free app with no commercial surface — 0 of 67 mention paying — and exactly one unprompted request to donate ('Eager next for notification and donation options'), backed by 13 (19.40%) who thank the developer; the only monetisation path the corpus supports is voluntary (D3). Report 57: 'you made a good app, so I bought Premium'; 'the purchase option is one-time rather than subscription, so I intend to pay soon as a gesture of thanks'. Report 58: willingness to pay is patronage-shaped, not access-shaped — 'I wish and hope and pray it will continue to be free and to those who can, please support the developers! <3' (PH); 'The framing that works is support the creator, not unlock the feature'. Report 59 (Tappsk): PR_FREE 493 (3.25%, 4.91★ — 'no limit on the to-do list in the free version'), PR_NO_ADS 127, and buying 'чтобы поддержать разработчиков' (to support the developers) / 'чтобы отблагодарить разработчиков' (to thank the developers) as stated purchase triggers; the report says keep a free tier genuinely usable for tasks. Report 65 (Rabit): 'Rabit's free tier was not a cost — it was the acquisition engine and the review engine' (48 reviews at 4.88); 'no ridiculous paywalls. everything you need is free'. Report 67 (Habio): the non-seeded 5★ reviews are mostly free-era — 'Let's you have as many habits you want for free'; 'This app doesn't ask for payments which I really love'.

title: Weight English-speaking rich markets; volume ≠ revenue
statement: Purchase-signal density is 8.5× higher in the US than China; BR/MX/ES/FR volume is localisation-blocked. Report 16 (contested): the price backlash was STRONGER in high-spend markets — a value-comparison effect ('not worth it at any price', measured against Streaks, Notion, Procreate) — while the rest of the world's complaint was language. Report 20: revocation and delivery grievances were concentrated in the high-spend storefronts (us, gb, de, ca, au, fr: revocation 19.3% vs 8.1% in ru/ua; widget 7×) — the damage landed on the revenue-generating cohort; Russia's higher mean reflected when its users arrived and what they bought, not a better product. Report 23 (counter-evidence): in a paid-up-front app the high-spend and high-volume storefront groups are statistically indistinguishable (4.22 vs 4.22) and only marginally better than the rest of the world (4.12) — what varies by country is which complaint dominates, not how much. Report 24 (counter-evidence): the rich English-language storefronts were the worst — US/UK/CA/AU/NZ/IE (62.87% of the corpus) all above the corpus billing rate and all collapsing to 2.1–2.6 in 2024–26, while Latin America and the Gulf held 4.12–4.59; what varies by country is the funnel, not the product. Report 25 (third corpus in a row): high-spend and high-volume storefront groups are indistinguishable (3.74 vs 3.73) and only marginally above the tail (3.62); monetisation friction is identical (22.5% vs 23.0%) — the paywall objection is global, not a low-income-market phenomenon; what differs is the mix (rich markets praise the price and buy lifetime; the rest hit the launch blocker and billing). Report 26 (the reverse pattern): the high-spend markets (us, gb, de, fr, ca, au = 40.84%) rate lowest (4.489 vs 4.626) and complain most about the paywall (15.3% vs 8.7%; cap 6.2% vs 2.2%) — the free-tier design is costing most where the money is; Russia (19.18%, mean 4.697, 85.3% 5★) and Brazil (4.663) are the happiest markets. Report 27: high-spend markets (92, mean 4.641) and the rest (46, 4.652) are indistinguishable; free-praise appears in 12 of 23 storefronts with no income split — the anti-paywall stance is category-wide. Report 28: the high-spend group (us, cn, jp, gb, de, fr, kr, ca, au, tw = 67.1%) rates lower (3.956 vs 4.181) with ad complaints 5.5pp higher and paywall friction 2.5× higher; GB complains about ads more than the US yet rates higher ('I love this, please fix the ads'); the US carries 71% of payers and the most precise criticism. Report 29 (fourth corpus): high-spend markets rate 0.27 lower and report bugs 3.5× more while praising zero cost at the same rate (48.0% vs 44.0%) — the appeal of free is uniform across income bands; India (mean 4.895, zero bug reports) is not comparable as satisfaction because its reviews are shorter and post-fix, but its dark-mode rate is the strongest country-level feature signal. Report 30 (fifth corpus): the high-spend group (US, GB, FR, DE, JP, KR — 58 reviews) is 67% templated and yields 8 substantive reviews at mean 3.50 vs a 4.79 headline; volume and signal are inversely related — the long tail (36 reviews, 69% substantive) carries the real signal: 47.2% monetisation complaints at mean 3.19. Report 31: high-spend storefronts (78.0%) and the rest of world are almost identical on sentiment (2.34 vs 2.42) but high-spend reports the money story (1.9× cap, 1.4× friction, 1.9× support-unresponsive) and the rest of world the crash wave and language (3.3× localisation); the tail of 71 small storefronts rates better (2.58) than the 9 core ones (2.30) — the more reviewers engaged with paying, the worse the rating. Report 33: high-spend storefronts rate lower (3.60 vs 3.93; ≈3.70 without China) and differ in what money buys — 1.6× payers, 3× Premium not granted, 2.3× billing integrity — with price objection identical (5.2%); the 81-storefront tail rates higher and pays less (3.89 vs 3.71). Report 34: the US (265) is the comparison-shopping market — competitors named 2×, payers 9.06% vs 5.65%, price praise 2× — with less wall friction but 9 of the 14 explicit churn reviews; non-US users hit the cap (6.07% vs 3.77%) and the English-only UI more. Report 36: US 252 (4.095) is the outcome market (outcomes 15.08% vs 6.94%) and reports confusion 3.4× more (onboarding 4.76% vs 1.39%); non-US reviews are feature-request-shaped (unmet 25.69% vs 11.90%) and ask for sync 4× more (9.72% vs 2.38%); the monetisation problem is identical across both. Report 41: high-spend markets self-report paying 2.4× more (9.59% vs 4.00%) and hit the cap 2.3× less; subscription objections are 9 of 10 inside high-spend markets; the UK is the best market (zero cap complaints, 12.5% payers), Canada the most price-sensitive yet most-converting (17.6% objections, 13.7% payers). Report 42: a $39.99–$59.99 app almost absent from high-spend markets (63 of 206; Germany, Australia, China zero) and rated worst there once bursts are removed (2.587); its review base moved to Brazil and Russia, and 20 long-tail storefronts show 46.9% cap complaints with one payer — 'an uncontrolled A/B test of paywall-first onboarding with no trial' (mean 2.906). Report 43: a 64% US corpus where the high-spend group (79.15%) is indistinguishable from the rest (4.006 vs 4.045) and every language request comes from outside it; non-US reviewers self-report paying more (10.04% vs 6.11%, weak) and criticise the dated design more (4.37% vs 1.47%). Report 46: the least US-concentrated corpus (33.43%); the payer rate is twice as high in high-spend markets (5.61% vs 2.85%) and highest in the US (6.04%) while the cap objection is identical everywhere; every regional-price complaint is outside the group; Germany loves the product and disputes the model most (price 2.4×, anti-subscription 3.8×), Russia calls the price fair on an apparently lower tier, China wants a buyout and fears the app will vanish (跑路), India negotiates for 4–7 free habits, Turkey is the clearest regional-price market. Report 47: Japan 369 (62.65%, mean 3.54 — where the full arc plays out) and Korea 92 (15.62%, 4.33 — a requesting market: crash 14%, widget and back-dating over-indexed, praise 4.33) are the only eligible storefronts; the high-spend group is 86.93% of the corpus; Korean reviews fell from 32 (2020) to 1 (2025) — the report's E5 is a Korea re-engagement around the widget and back-dating. Report 48: high-spend markets (US, JP, GB, DE, CA, AU, FR, KR, CN; 77.81%) hold 82.6% of identified payers, complain about price and the model more and about the cap less; the UK is the most paid-engaged storefront (6.51% payers vs 3.91%); Japan (18) and Korea (24) are nearly absent — a distribution gap, not a sentiment one; Brazil is the highest-rated and least analytical storefront. Report 49: US 47.00% at 2.97 (behaviour change +4.58pp); UK 2.43 is 'transaction-damaged' (payers 13.92%, misleading checkout +7.48pp); Germany rigidity-focused (cannot edit +9.70pp, no trial +8.08pp); Australia AI-critical (10.34%); the paywall grievance varies only 14.7–19.8% across five markets — universal; the praise is American. Report 50: monetisation friction 9.0% in the US vs 17.0% elsewhere and 10.8% in the (effectively English-language) high-spend group vs 20.5%; every 3-habit-cap report is non-US (TR, AU, MX ×3) — 'US-only dashboards would not have surfaced finding 1 at all'; Japan returned zero written reviews. Report 54: a developed-market proxy group (70.73%, mean 4.103) vs rest of world (3.685): price resistance 2.7% vs 8.3%, restore failures 0.8% vs 4.6%, outcome language 16.9% vs 4.6%. Report 58: all four 'please stay free' pleas and 3 of 4 budget self-identifications are outside high-spend storefronts (PH 3) while free praise is flat — test any monetisation in high-spend storefronts first because they have not publicly asked for the model to be preserved. Report 59 (Tappsk): the English-speaking group (us, gb, ca, au, in: 725 reviews) and Latin America (br + mx: 639) describe outcomes at about twice the global rate (20.3% / 21.3% vs 9.6%) with billing at 1.0% / 0.8% vs 3.7% Russian-speaking; Brazil is the growth market of the late corpus (32.1% of its reviews in the latest era, lowest 1–2★ share above 500 reviews); continental Europe carries the highest price objection (10.6%) and SA + TR 13.6%; no market uniquely asks for a desktop. Report 60 (Mindway): the US (101 of 216) is simultaneously the biggest market, the only paying market in evidence (11 of 13 payers) and the angriest (3.56★; 26 of the 38 1★; 10 of 11 billing failures) — 'Americans complain about value; everyone else complains about access'; a definitional high-spend group (178 reviews) rates 0.62 lower, complains about money half again as often and holds every confirmed payer, while the rest-of-world 4.11 mean is 'users who never got far enough in to be disappointed expensively'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): on 11 high-spend reviews (3.455) vs 26 high-volume (2.846), high-spend reviewers ask for capability (sync, statistics, granularity, legibility) and none objects to the price, while high-volume and long-tail reviewers raise access (the cap, paying at all) — 'consistent with the corpus but not established by it'; India is the most product-engaged storefront (both widget-outcome reviews, the streak-integrity request, the purchase trigger and the brand risk) and the one the report says to research. Report 64 (Critique AI): the visible real user base is overwhelmingly American — all but two price defenders and 9 of 11 focus-mode mentions are US. Report 65 (Rabit): the inversion — the high-spend tier supplies 61 written reviews (12.25%) at 3.33 while the high-volume tier supplies 433 (86.95%) at 3.74; Brazil holds 77.2% of public ratings at rank 3, the US ranks 39th.

title: Free trial before purchase
statement: Weak but present complaint. Report 9: no trial in most storefronts drew 52 explicit requests, several saying they would have bought — and a trial offered in the US but not Saudi Arabia was compared in public. Report 23: a paid-up-front app with no trial — 15 (0.21%, mean 2.40) name the absence, it recurs as a stated regret in refund reviews, and accidental one-tap purchases drive Korea's 6.5% refund rate (7× global); counter-evidence: 'There's no trial because it doesn't need one'. Report 28: five reviewers wanted to pay and were stopped by the absence of a trial — 'I wouldn't have purchased until I was sure I liked the app, and it was impossible to like the app when it was a slew of ads'; 'Unlike Study Bunny, there is no $2.00 30-day trial… that's a full STOP sign'; the dominant purchase trigger is ad removal after sustained free use, which the 'unusable' churners never reach; the sibling app's reported $2 / 30-day trial is the proposed experiment. Report 30: 'I paid the anual subscription… It doesn't have a trial version and it wasn't what I was looking for' (1★); 'before buying something you should be able to try it' (1★); one 3★ could not tell whether the app was paid or free — introduce a trial or a reversible first purchase. Report 31: trial reaction is net-negative (56, mean 2.16) and the positive outcomes are first-year discount trials, not free trials ('an almost-free year is more than enough to know whether the €60 is worth it'). Report 33: for most of the corpus there was no trial ('Three habits, and three days, is simply too little'), and purchase intent 'would buy if…' appears in 44. Report 34: no trial (2022, 2024, 2026) vs a 3-day trial (2025) — 7 complaints (mean 3.00): 'I refuse to pay the min. $9 just to find out if I like it'; a 2018 reviewer proposes '21 days of all bells and whistles … Once you hook them on, charge them'. Report 36: TRIAL 7 (mean 2.43) — 'any sort of trial period — even just an hour — before you blow $15'; 'these issues aren't readily apparent from the free version when you only have two habits to look at'. Report 42: 'no trial' is the lowest-mean theme in the corpus (14, 6.80%, mean 1.29); reviewers name the length they wanted (1 day, 3 days, 7 days, a month) and four met the paywall before any use ('Literally two seconds after downloading'); the report distinguishes it from the cap complaint — a trial asks for temporary full product and is strictly cheaper to grant. Report 43 (counter-case): only 4 of 638 asked for a time-limited trial because a full-featured 3-habit free tier served as one ('The free version has all the features but limits the amount of habits… try it out and if it works for you, you can upgrade as I did') — vs 14 in report 42's 3-habit-plus-paid-basics corpus. Report 46: a 7-day trial is the top purchase trigger ('I paid for the full version after the trial because I could see how much it had helped in just a week'; 'Absolutely did not hesitate to purchase after the week trial'; 'used this app for 6 days and fully expected to delete it… I will be subscribing') — yet 32 (mean 1.88) say the 3-habit free tier is too small to evaluate ('I'd have to subscribe before even trying it'; 'try it for 30 days without limitation'). Report 47: 5-day and one-week trials reported; 'trial not disclosed' 2 (both 1★: '試用期間5日、最初から有償アプリと書け、時間を無駄にした'); a six-year user's app crashed the moment the trial payment went through. Report 49 (the natural experiment): 90 asked for a trial; one arrived 24 Jan 2026 card-gated, auto-charging, annual-only, with a forced loop — hard-paywall complaints went 17.24% → 34.96%, 'advertised as free' 2.13% → 6.50%, 11 new 'trial charged immediately' reviews, mean unchanged (2.77 → 2.78) — 'the reputational cost of a paywall plus the reputational cost of a billing surprise'; reviewers propose 'allow the first week to run freely. Get the user on a run, and they'll pay to continue'; the report: no card and a free first week, or no trial and an honest price — 'The half-measure is the worst of the three options.' Report 50: a 7-day trial ('Download, 7day free trial, then u gotta subscribe') with charges landing before it ended and no expiry reminder (see C029, C152). Report 54: no trial — 7 ask for one ('It's kind of expensive to buy the premium to see if I will like it'; 'use the app fully for 2–3 months before spending the twenty'). Report 57: no trial — 'you only get the urge to go paid after actually trying it free'; 'the Premium features don't land for me — a time-limited trial would be fine'. Report 59 (Tappsk): a trial that needs a card is itself a barrier ('полная версия в пробном периоде требует привязки карты', 1★) and the immediate-charge trial is the 1★ engine ([[C109]]). Report 64 (Critique AI): 'at least bring back the free trial' — the one review implying a trial was removed; 10 reviewers found a 3-day trial while 26 say there is none (possibly A/B-varied).

title: Price level — where 'fair' turns into 'too expensive'
statement: Both coexist for one price; split follows market, payment rails and year. Report 20: $39.99/year for a checkbox app was rejected in every market and language for seven years; Spain, which arrived after the conversion and lost nothing, objected to price (16.9%) but not revocation (2.8%) — the grievance follows arrival date, not nationality. Report 23: price objection 123 (1.69%, mean 2.21, 50.4% 1★) with au 5.7%, de 3.8%, ca 3.6% vs us 1.3%; flat across a 2.5× price rise; China's 1★ reviews are almost uniformly '¥25/30 for a reminder'; Germany objected to €3.99 at launch ('99Ct wären OK'). Report 24: price objection 791 (1.82%, mean 2.248) is about magnitude relative to category ($40/quarter, $80–100/month with bundles vs $5–20/yr rivals), opacity and targeting (premium wellness pricing for people with executive dysfunction and low income) — not the existence of a price; a distinct group calls $20/yr worth every penny. Report 25: only ~12 of 55 price objections are about the level ('£25 for a basic box checker'; '$40??? it's a simple app'); ~8 are stated inability to pay (a student, a child); US names the highest figures ($13/mo, $49 lifetime); Argentina (n=40, mean 2.95, friction 40%) is the most hostile storefront. Report 26: price objection 29 (0.76%, mean 2.76) vs 57 defending the price — 2:1 in favour; high-spend markets (de 19.83%, fr 20.37%, au 18.52%, ca 15.60% friction) are where price-defence arguments are also most articulate. Report 28: 16 price objections (1.95%, mean 2.88) at ~$10–15 consumable tiers — 'too expensive for an unproven, ad-saturated experience, sold as an opaque bundle, with no way to try it'; 'not the level of quality that this kind of money gets you with apps like procreate'; students and minors cannot pay ('strict parents and only my mom knows my Apple ID'); the winning position is 'more affordable alternative' to Finch — do not raise the price. Report 30: the price objection (5, mean 1.40) is price ÷ what you get free — 'Es un check list CARÍSIMO'; 'The price is too high for this quality'; 'para ser de pago es demasiado simple' — while three say the price itself is acceptable, two of them rating 1★/2★ for the cap; 'do not cut the price'. Report 31: 'a subscription for a checklist is unjustifiable' ('almost the price of Disney+!'; 'In this economy?'; 'How is this app worth $499.99?') — price objection 379 (7.31%, mean 1.79), 4.1% (E1) → 13.0% (E2); Canada has the highest price objection (11.6%); do not conclude 'lower the price' alone — restore a trustworthy low-commitment path and make it work. Report 33: price objection 203 (5.15%, mean 2.64), highest in Germany (14.7%), Turkey (10.5%) and France (10.4%) — '269 roubles … I pay 400 for Netflix'; '43 euro … for an agenda???'; '€40 … vous vivez où, Monaco?'. Report 34: ~$9/mo, ~$20/yr, ~$40 lifetime — price objection 25 (mean 3.16), many 'great app, too expensive' at 4–5★; €9.99/month called 'completely of the charts'. Report 36: ~$15/£15/€18 a year for Habits alone and ~$30 for the suite (2022–25) rising to $59–70 by 2026; price objection 36 (mean 2.31) and 'not worth it' 21 (mean 2.24, zero 5★). Report 41: lifetime moved €22 (2021) → €28 (2023) → €22–25 / $22.99 (2026) and price objections tracked it (4.2% 2022, 4.6% 2025, 0% 2026); reserve prices named €10, <$5, £3.99. Report 42: $39.99–$59.99/yr (US), ¥6,900 (JP, both reviews 1★), R$79.90 per 12 weeks (BR) vs 500₽ (RU, 'that's nothing'); price objection 18 (mean 1.67, never above 3★) — 'you pay that much for barely any technology'; 'the subscription price is unreal for what the app delivers'. Report 43: at $2.99 the price objection (36, 5.64%, mean 2.31) was almost entirely an objection to being stopped, not to money ('you can easily set timers on your phone for free'; 'I'm a college student so I'm ~broke~'), and it vanished with the cap. Report 46: $12/year (2019) → $4.99/mo or $30/yr (Jan 2020) → $7.49 / $29.99 / $99.99 lifetime (2023); pricing-model union 212 (9.73%, mean 2.92); Canada's CAD $39.99 / $129.99 sharpens it ('Are you out of your mind???'). Report 48: one-time requesters name $10–$20; the lifetime at $79.99–$149.99 is rejected by 28 who accept the model; Canada is the most price-sensitive storefront (9.47%) with praise intact — 'Canadians like the app and resent the deal more than anyone else'. Report 52: a nine-year price ladder ¥6 → ¥12/¥18 → ¥88 lifetime → ¥98, with a Nov 2019 tier rise (¥8→¥12, ¥12→¥18) and price rise complaints 42 (3.19). Report 53: one-time $4.99 → $7.99 → $12–13 → $19.99 (2017–22), then annual only $39.99 / over €40 / AU$99.99; price is Germany's top theme (18.00%, 'why €14?'). Report 55: reviewers name $5–$10 one-time or a $2.99 download as acceptable against ~$19.99/yr (text sub-cut). Report 57: lifetime roughly tripled between 2020–22 and 2024 (₩9,900 → ₩29,000; ¥1,600 → ¥4,500; $13 → $30–35) before a shift to subscription. Report 59 (Tappsk): the monthly at ~300 ₽ is called too high — 'Месячную подписку можно было бы сделать хотя бы 150р, а не 300'; 'Люди куда охотнее отдадут 100р в месяц'; 'Рублей 199-299' — while the lifetime at 449–600 ₽ on sale (list 1,490–2,500 ₽) sells; MON_PRICE 252 (1.66%), distinctive in France (2.16×) and Turkey (4.49×). Report 60 (Mindway): price points $7/week, €8/week, $39.99–40/year, '$60 a year', a $0.99 paid trial; 'a bit expensive for something I could do myself' (payer, 3★); the objection is relative to free substitutes, not to a number ([[C277]]). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): three reviewers volunteer that the price is good ('The price is also very affordable considering the features it offers'; 'the subscription prices are very good'; 'reasonably priced' — and still did not buy, over the sync gap) against two one-line objections ('It's paid'; 'Asked for a payment in simple app like this') — §8.5: do not raise prices and do not cut them. Report 64 (Critique AI): PAY_PRICE 105 (25.06%, mean 1.94) against 11 defenders (2.63%, mean 4.55: '$40 bucks a year is a steal. A human trainer could cost as much as $40 a week!'; 'way cheaper than others'); PAY_PRICE jumped 19.2% → 34.0% in the latest quarter while defect themes stayed flat and defenders rose 0.8% → 8.7% — 'Contested pricing became a topic on the listing itself'; a price rise, a trial withdrawal or an audience widening past willingness-to-pay cannot be separated without pricing history.

title: Paying customers are the highest 1★ risk — every paid feature must work
statement: Paid cohort rates a full point lower; 28% of payers leave 1–2★; confirmed buyers ×6.7 on 1★. Report 10: paid-cohort mean fell 4.40 → 2.96 across 2022–2026 while the corpus mean barely moved; the five highest paid lifts are all billing mechanics, not price. Report 16: 17 confirmed payers rated 1.21 stars below everyone else; five of the seven billing complaints in the corpus came from them. Report 18: 161 confirmed payers rated 0.30 below the corpus with 21.7% at 1★; their rates of entitlement failure (9.94% vs 1.22%), data loss (12.42% vs 6.01%) and billing dispute (14.29% vs 7.03%) were roughly double the global rates, and by the last era 4.36% of all reviews came from someone who had paid and could not use what they bought. Report 19: 64 of 105 reviewers were confirmed payers and 63 of them left 1★; one third said they could not get their money back and just under one third that they could not stop paying. Report 20: 908 reviewers with payment evidence averaged 1.55 against 3.61 for everyone else — 2.06 stars lower; 76.8% of revocation complaints, 62.1% of widget complaints and 65.5% of support complaints came from the ~22% who paid; the damage was also concentrated in the high-spend storefronts (revocation 19.3% vs 8.1% in ru/ua, broken widget 7×). Report 23 (everyone paid): reviewers who discuss the transaction average 3.52 vs 4.27 for the rest — a dissonance signal; 'I bought this for the Watch and it doesn't work' are the highest-value churn events. Report 24: reviewers who discuss the transaction average 2.006 against 4.356 for the rest. Report 25: explicit payers' mean fell 4.23 → 3.16 → 2.68 across eras (n=13/25/19) while the headline fell 0.27; 14% of payers raise a billing dispute, 8.8% lost access to something bought, 8.8% hit a reliability failure; 52 of 302 one-star reviews (17.2%) show paid evidence — failed customers, not non-buyers venting. Report 26: explicit payers (72) rate a full point below the corpus (3.56 vs 4.570), flat across five years; their top problems are losing the purchase (16.7%) and paywall friction after paying (23.6%). Report 28: identifiable payers rate 3.75 vs 4.03 and 41.7% of them report a failed purchase; a 5★ payer still getting ads writes 'Maybe it just needs to sync up'. Report 30: of the six reviewers who reached payment, five had a bad outcome and none describes a satisfactory purchase; the corpus cannot see quiet happy payers. Report 31: explicit payers went from the happiest segment (E1 mean 3.76) to the angriest (E4 1.35) while their share of reviews rose six-fold to 25.0%; 17.2% of 1★ reviews are from people who say they paid; within 625 payers: not granted 48.6% (1.21), support unresponsive 34.2%, still upsold 31.5%, lag 13.3% ($79.99, freezes on the third habit); a share bought only to make the pop-up go away. Report 33: 427 explicit payers (10.84%, mean 3.16) are polarised — 212 rate 4–5★, 172 rate 1–2★; their mood tracks integrity events, not price (E2 3.77 with a stable lifetime app; 2018 2.83 with 25 purchases not applied; E3 2.78 after Habitify X); after paying: reliability 42.6%, integrity 26.7%, support failure 11.9%, regressions 11.5%; nearly one 1★ in five is a payer. Report 34: payers are satisfied (51, mean 4.63) and E5 is their weakest era (4.23) because every low-rating E5 payer reports a broken paid thing — widget, reminders, lifetime entitlement — not price. Report 36: payers are the least satisfied identifiable group — 34 payers average 3.794 (23.5% 1–2★) vs corpus 4.039 and free-tier praisers 4.88 — because paying exposes no sync (9 of 34, 26.5%), entitlements that don't travel, billing edge cases and bugs ('please fix the bugs (paying user)'). Report 41: 5 of 29 1★ (17.2%) are payers whose specific purchase rationale failed — backfill, Mac sync, Watch sync without iCloud, Health sync, refund; 10 of 60 payers report a post-purchase failure. Report 42: payers (29) rate 2.72 vs non-payers 3.20, 44.8% of them 1★, none 4★ — 'no such thing as a mildly satisfied paying customer'; 9 of 29 hit a defect after paying (freezing '5 minutes to mark two tasks', a launch crash, disappearing habits, premium stats miscalculating). Report 43: payers (48, 7.52%) rate 3.58 vs 4.05 and are 1.9× as likely to give 1★; 11 of 48 (22.9%) hit a defect after paying and 10 of 76 one-star reviews are payers — every one a delivery failure (re-buy after reinstall, restore failed, 'Had it for two minutes after I paid for it and it's glitching', won't open with data gone despite iCloud, a lifetime payer with no support reply, the 2025 popup regression). Report 46: payers (97) rate 3.95 vs 4.35, 1.7× as likely to leave 1★ and 2.9× 2★; 21 of 97 (21.6%) hit a defect after paying; every payer at 1★ (12) is a delivery or billing failure, none a design objection. Report 47: 13 identifiable payers (2.21%, 12 JP) average 3.23 vs 3.83; nine of thirteen report a billing, entitlement or reliability problem (ads reappearing, charged twice, crash after paying, the month view showing a week, the AI toggle stuck off, the rating prompt shown to payers); 4★ holds most of the payers — 'one fix from five'. Report 48: 172 payers (3.91%) average 3.92 vs 4.24 — 84 (48.8%) also report a problem (billing 12, refund 8, no support reply 8, crash 9, sync 6); 31 one-star reviews are from payers — 'the most expensive failure mode in the corpus'; 'The paid experience fails at exactly the moments it matters.' Report 49: 106 payers average 1.92 — 97 (91.5%) carry a complaint; reliability 41.5% of payer reviews vs 13.4% of non-payers; login failure 11.32% vs 1.30%; 57 payers at 1★ 'the most serious group in this report'. Report 50 (counter-case): payers are happy — 9 direct at 4.11 (7 at 5★), 13 with probable at 4.23 vs 4.27 for non-payers; both unhappy payers were hurt by billing, not the product; a Premium user who lost data still wrote a 2,020-character defence — 'Every monetization change should be evaluated against whether it risks converting this segment into the angry-payer segment that most competitors have.' Report 52: payers are the most satisfied segment (306 value-reporting payers at 4.92) until something breaks — entitlement broke 80 at 2.62, data loss 33 at 1.73, support silence 52 at 1.92, reliability 286 at 3.04. Report 53: payers went from 143 at 3.44 (2017–22) to 54 at 2.15 (2023–26); paid and reliability failure 82 at 2.46, statistics broken 24 at 2.25, entitlement withdrawn 10 at 1.50. Report 54: confirmed payers average 3.091 against 3.981 and are 3.3× more likely to leave one star (27.3% vs 8.4%); 12 of 31 one-stars are payers — 'the one-star population is, disproportionately, the company's customers'; the payer segment holds nearly all of six failure themes (10 of 12 value gap, 6 of 6 never unlocked, 6 of 7 restore, 5 of 5 refunds) — 'Free users complain about the gate; paying users complain about the goods'. Report 55: payers are the unhappiest group — PAY_BOUGHT 165 at 2.56, 96 (58.2%) at 1–2★, paid mean 4.24 → 2.78 → 1.91 → 1.41 across eras; 41.8% of payers report a data & account continuity failure, 25.5% support silence, 21.8% sync failure; the continuity chain — crash or new phone → reinstall → login fails → data and premium gone → e-mail support → no reply → refund request and 1★; 'Two online reviews that premium customers had posted convinced me not to'. Report 57: 31 of 99 payers (31.31%) report a purchase-side failure, rising 12.9% (2019–21) → 27.3% → 45.7% (2024–26); payers are 12.71% of reviews but 20.8% of one-stars; in 2026 8 of 12 payers report a failure — the rising payer share may be measuring anger, not adoption; refunds rare (2 genuine) because unhappy payers write a 1★ and stay broken. Report 59 (Tappsk): 147 of 1,090 purchasers (13.5%) rate 1–2★; among purchasers BUG_PURCHASE lifts 8.43×, MON_PAID_TWICE 8.89×, SUP_NONE 6.09×, BUG_SYNC 5.71×, NEG_DEV_PROMISE 4.43× — the paid segment concentrates every failure class; 'написано, что поддерживается семейный доступ' (it says Family Sharing is supported) is a paid-twice complaint. Report 60 (Mindway): the extreme case — 13 explicit payers (6.02%), mean 1.38, 11 of 13 at 1★, zero at 5★; 'not one paying reviewer describes getting value for the money… the most consequential single number in the report'; every refund request, cancellation failure and unexpected-charge report in the corpus comes from this segment; five of thirteen say the paid product is a list, not a tracker; the responsible reading — the segment is biased toward the aggrieved — still leaves 'the only payer voices the store shows prospective buyers are 1★'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 5 of 6 self-identified payers report a defect or shortfall — two entitlement failures, two hit by the June build, one lifetime buyer disappointed by the widget; only one paid reviewer is unreservedly happy ('Worth every penny'); notably neither failed purchaser asked for a refund — both asked for a fix. Report 64 (Critique AI): 13 self-stated payers average 1.85 (10 at 1★) against 3.87 for users who got in without stating payment — access more than doubles satisfaction and stating that you paid halves it again; 12 of 13 report a defect or shortfall. Report 65 (Rabit): 49 self-stated payers average 2.061 against 3.677 (27 of 49 at 1★, 3× over-represented), and the 1★ band's top theme is PAY_PAID (29.67%) — 'the one-star band is mostly composed of (a) people who could not get into the app at all and (b) people who paid and could not get what they paid for. Neither group is a pricing problem'; payer complaints peak in 2023, the cap year; only 2 say paid was worth it against 16 who say not. Report 67 (Habio): 35 deliberate buyers (mean 1.23) report the same failures as everyone else plus locked premium; praise among money-left reviewers has a 0.06× lift.

title: Focus timer
statement: Meaningful in the US, emerging globally. Report 23: timed tasks and a built-in Pomodoro exist; the Pomodoro break cycle was reported broken in 2022 and timers desync between devices. Report 24: a deep-work ramp-up ritual and per-habit timers are named by long-tenure users as the reason they renew. Report 25: a built-in timer that keeps counting past the goal is praised at mean 4.60 (15, 1.15%). Report 28: a timer with auto-mark-complete exists; three want it to run in the background / on the lock screen. Report 36: a timer / pomodoro requested by 4 (mean 2.50), one because a screenshot habit was named 'Run 15 minutes'. Report 41: a per-habit timer with Live Activities praised by 27. Report 43: multi-step timed routines (morning routines, workouts, kids, ADHD) with background-music fade and voice prompts are a core differentiator and the mechanic the ADHD segment names most. Report 47: timers / time tracking requested by a payer for study logging (average and total study time). Report 48: a built-in timer requested by 5–6; time-duration HH:MM units by 8. Report 52: a pomodoro / count-up focus timer linked to habits (FOCUS 390, rising to 5.5% of 2026) — accepted but ranked below check-in speed; the app-block list works backwards; a solid-red focus page redesign (Aug 2026) clashed with the calm style. Report 59 (Tappsk): REQ_TIMER 43 (distinctive in Ukraine, 3.00×).

title: Fitness / health tracking use case
statement: Very strong US use case. Report 31: health and medical routines praised by 36 (hip-surgery physio, Ménière's, a 95-day medication streak); life outcomes 113 (34 kg, 15 lb). Report 33: life outcomes 205 (on the way to 100 books; out of depression; quitting smoking; 1,000+ gym days); medical / mental-health use 20 (mean 4.70). Report 47: fitness / diet users 24 (4.07%, mean 4.08) are the largest named audience. Report 48: fitness / weight 95 (2.16%, 4.87) is the largest segment — 80 lbs lost, 31 lbs and 26 inches; behaviour-change claims 267 (4.95) rising to 8.18% of 2022–26. Report 60 (Mindway): 'Makes me hydrated makes me work out in a lot'; 'work out, drink more water, make my bed, do good in school, and tidy up my room' — health routines are the concrete outcomes named. Report 64 (Critique AI): fitness outcomes carry the corpus's highest mean (12, 4.92); requests for a calorie tracker beside the food scanner, Apple Health and Hevy sync, exercise animations and bodyweight / muscle-group tracking; outcomes run 5× higher in volume markets (11.4% vs 2.2%).

title: Parents tracking kids
statement: Distinct use case; ties to profiles. Report 23: tracking a child's chores alongside your own is one reason for more capacity (3 reviews). Report 26: one reviewer bought it for an elderly parent and one for their children; ages 10–21 self-identify. Report 31: family/child use praised by a handful — a parent tracking attention to each child; a 5-year-old's morning list.

title: Check-off sound and haptic
statement: Named as a reason to keep coming back. Report 16: the press-and-hold fill with a haptic reward was the product's most-praised craft ('Pavlovian in a good way'; 'I'm beginning to crave that feeling') — praise fell three-quarters after a redesign replaced the circles with a list. Report 31: musical completion sounds and haptics are free and part of the category-winning basics (82 mentions, mean 3.62); 7 find sounds interrupt audio. Report 36: hold-to-check with haptics, sound and music is the most specific praise (57, 10.56%, mean 4.61) — 'a small dose of dopamine every time you check something off' — 'the hardest for a competitor to copy'; 'the music is absolutely gorgeous, please upload it to Spotify'. Report 43: 'paid for the full version because i really like the happy sound when completing tasks'. Report 46: sounds / stronger completion feedback requested by 5; a December 2022 completion animation was rejected ('please remove the new animation whenever u log a day it's so annoying'; 'Special FX update unnecessary… I'll not renew'). Report 50: vibration cannot be disabled — 'especially for a (supposedly) peace-of-mind application' (1★, KZ). Report 57: the stamp check-in and its sound are the emotional core — stamp satisfaction 19 (4.947: 'there's hardly a reward system more intuitive and efficient than stamps filling up'), sound 5 ('a little thrill in the sound when you check a habit').

title: Use the language users use: Atomic Habits, 75 Hard
statement: Framing seen in US reviews. Report 23: 14 reviews name Atomic Habits (mean 4.79); also Mini Habits, The Power of Habit, Deep Work and The Power of Full Engagement. Report 24: Atomic Habits adjacency is a named purchase trigger. Report 49: 'Solo Leveling' is the language that sells — 38 name the anime as why they love it (4.87, the highest mean above 30), 'I wanted to level up like jinwoo sung and came across this app through an ad'; 15 name Instagram / TikTok.

title: Never ship and walk away
statement: Abandonment is visible to users within a year; the app becomes an OS-release liability for paying users with no recourse, while the store rating quietly rises on survivorship. Report 8: a ~18-month pause let iOS updates break the create flow, widget and launch, and users publicly asked whether the app was abandoned ('Wrapped 2022' still in settings in 2025). Report 14: a solo-developer app broke at each major iOS transition ('Same thing happened with iOS 13 and it took them a while to fix it'), went five years without an update, and the last thing the corpus records is the product and its checkout failing at once. Report 17: a developer who in early 2022 emailed users personally when their feature shipped had gone silent by 2023 — not an absence of ability but its exhaustion; bug reports at each iOS transition then had nobody to fix them. Report 20: across 92 months no significant new capability shipped — the only material changes were the paywall, a widget that never worked and two data-destroying updates; 'ZERO updates, content, features… NOTHING that justifies a yearly subscription fee.' Report 25: a solo developer's fast turnaround (24-hour fixes) thinned across eras (support praise 3.0% → 0.9%) while a launch blocker survived two release cycles. Report 28: 'incentives stop after level three hundred… makes me assume the developers have taken their hands off the wheel'; the listing's last version is ten months stale. Report 31: after a Dec 2020 sale ('sold from Tree Betty to this new owner') the new operator went silent on support and legacy purchases while escalating monetisation — 'ever since the original designer/developer sold it … it's stopped working'. Report 47: stagnant development 3 ('作者好像不更新了', 2020; '評価が高いアプリなのに1年以上更新がないのも残念', 2023). Report 53: positives vanished before negatives peaked — SUP_GOOD none after Mar 2022, REM_GOOD none after May 2024, WATCH_GOOD 4.3% (2022) → 0% (2026) — while iOS releases broke widgets, Watch app and statistics for a year ('No update to fix issues on iOS 18 for about a year'). Report 54: abandonment 0.9% → 1.4% → 5.0% and support-unresponsive 0 → 0.7% → 4.2% across periods; reviewers escalate from inferring neglect ('after apparently a year since the last update') to reporting a closed channel; a six-year request backlog (widget since Oct 2020, long-range stats since Apr 2020); F6: publish any maintenance signal. Report 55: 'No updates have been issued in over half a year and the developers are no longer answering emails' (2016); no iPhone X layout from Nov 2017 to Dec 2020 (BUG_COMPAT 53); 'The last update was 9 months ago, this is unacceptable for a subscription based product' (2025). Report 57: 'people have been asking about iPad and Mac for years and you always say it's planned — is it ever actually happening?' — 6 told 'planned', never shipped. Report 59 (Tappsk): NEG_DEV_PROMISE 88 rising to 1.1% of the latest era, 4.43× among purchasers — 'there were added zero new features'; 'Два года прошу добавить эту простую фичу' (asking for this simple feature for two years, 1★); 'приложение вообще не меняется годами'; REQ_TIME, REQ_BACKFILL, REQ_PHOTO, REQ_STATS and REQ_SHARED never stop; SUP_NONE also peaks in the latest era (0.8%). Report 60 (Mindway): after a two-month acquisition burst the app produced roughly one review a month for 15 months with two four-month silences, and no reviewer in 750 days reports a problem being resolved (is_edited false on all 216) — the 2026 tail is 28.57% paywall complaints and zero benefit claims. Report 65 (Rabit): in-app copy still said 'start your 2024 year strong' in Feb 2025 and the purchase screen still said 2024 in Sep 2026 ('Poderiam verificar o anúncio de compra que está em 2024?'); 'Tinha tudo pra ser do topo de app de hábitos mas não atualiza' (DEV_STALE 5, all 2025–2026); review volume 120 → 106 → 67 → 30 → 12 per year with the mean not recovering — 'attrition, not repair'; F10: 'the clearest public signal that the app is abandoned' is a trivial string.

title: Writes to shared system stores (calendar, health) must be exact and reversible
statement: A paid calendar sync that corrupts the user's calendar is the most severe complaint class in report 2. Report 25: Apple Health values read wrongly — weight interpreted as entry-count, steps off by 568 — in an app whose Health integration is otherwise praised. Report 31: Apple Health counts wrong or doubled in 37 (2.7.1 added a year of steps; sleep 14 h; 26,000 vs 5,000 steps) — de-duplicate imports and show the source value alongside the app's value. Report 33: Health sleep double-counting and data wiped when switching tracking mode — de-duplicate, allow manual override. Report 53: reading, meditation and relaxation timers written to Apple Health as exercise minutes or active calories ('One hour of reading in HabitMinder gave me 60 active minutes'); stand counted while asleep; doubled Health statistics (HK_WRITE 8, HK_BUG 61); F7: stop, or make write-back explicit per habit.

title: Manual reordering, renaming and editing of habits/tasks — free
statement: Trivial, requested for years by 5★ users; best effort-to-goodwill ratio. In report 4 rename/reorder was gated and it was the top complaint among paying users. Report 25: habit/group order resets itself (11, 0.84%) — two long-term users left over it; make reordering a drag gesture. Report 26: reorder habits / per-habit gardens / categories requested by 18 (0.47%). Report 27: habit reordering shipped (between Sept 2024 and Aug 2025) and the order does not stick ('they keep getting jumbled up and going back to the wrong spots'); one user avoids reordering for fear of data loss; another wants grouping by the time a habit is set for. Report 29: 'This could be my perfect habit tracker if I could only reorder the list of tasks… Without it the app is virtually useless' (2★); two of four ask to sort by reminder time, which needs no new data model. Report 31: custom order and forced grouping (22) and an edited habit jumping to the top of the list drew complaints — restore custom ordering and stop moving edited habits. Report 33: custom ordering that sticks requested / broken in 47 (90 routines; broken in v10.7.4–10.7.5 and again in 2026). Report 36: cannot delete or rename a habit easily (10, mean 3.00) and a habit-name character limit (3). Report 43: drag-to-reorder within time windows requested by 7 and shipped Nov 2025 ('The ability to program your day windows and reorder items in time windows is fantastic'); bulk edit across a group 1. Report 46: cannot reorder habits (10, mean 4.10); a limited history view (9). Report 47: reorder / sort habits requested by 6 (all JP, mean 4.33); habit order scrambled by an update in 2022 (5). Report 48: can't edit / delete a log entry 32 (3.22); backfill history praised by 13. Report 50: an August 2026 update removed editing or deleting a single occurrence of a recurring habit ('I love this but I was really disappointed in the update that took away ability to modify time or delete single reoccurring events in a day') — fix F5: a straight revert. Report 54: reorder / drag habits (13, 4.54; 5 payers). Report 55: in 2026 habits cannot be deleted or deactivated. Report 56: reorder requests (4) stopped dead once reordering shipped, because it is visible in the list. Report 57: 27 could not find how to delete or edit a habit though the function exists ('How on earth can you make a habit app and not be able to delete the habits'; 'I got angry and deleted the app'; 'I almost threw my phone') — a user documented it publicly; 'it should be a clear option when viewing the habit detailed view'.

title: Customisable, louder reminder sounds
statement: Asked by happy users; the cheapest 5★ upgrade. Report 20: one reminder per habit with user-written message text — 'small feature, outsized affection' (25 reviews, mean 4.60). Report 65 (Rabit): an audible alarm rather than a silent banner (REQ_SOUND 3, mean 3.00).

title: Skippable, replayable onboarding tour and an in-app help screen — searchable FAQ and per-setting explanations for anything richer than the daily check-in
statement: Hidden gestures (swipe-to-complete, mode toggles) confuse new users; a US-specific 6% complaint in report 2. Report 12: an unskippable narrated intro drew 21 complaints peaking at 16% of 2024 reviews, then fell to one review after a skip control landed — the corpus's clearest fix — while the same intro is praised as a conversion asset. Report 17: a product with its own vocabulary ('what is a sequence? What is a block? What is an activity?') asked for 'a day of experimenting'; users who got through the first day gave 5★, those who didn't quit at 30 minutes — while the paywall demanded payment before that day. Report 18: a five-year vocabulary muddle (습관 vs 루틴 vs 모드) and an onboarding that re-ran on existing and paying accounts with no skip button — a restore-purchase loop returned users to the questionnaire. Report 23: an icon-only first run left new users unable to delete, edit or undo — 63 of 650 1★ reviews; a 66-upvote review asks for plain-language in-app instructions; replace it with a short text-labelled walkthrough covering add / complete / edit / delete / undo / pages. Report 25: confusing/no-guidance 27 (2.06%, mean 2.70); two Brazilian reviewers ask for a tutorial video; comprehension failures worth designing against — how to structure a bad habit ('smoked' or 'didn't smoke'), pinning a weekly habit to a day, stopping a repeat, whether the app is iOS-only. Report 27: a real first-run comprehension cost — four of five confused reviewers got past it and stayed ('a lil hard to figure out at first but now super easy'), the fifth gave 1★; a 30-second skippable explainer is a low-risk fix that does not compromise minimalism. Report 28: 38 onboarding complaints (4.63%, mean 3.24) with one unchanged content for four and a half years — the tutorial teaches the fiction (bunny, mess, carrots) but not how to add, edit or delete a habit ('The tutorial is pointless as they don't show you how to create a task'; 'a steep learning curve with all the unlabeled icons'); 11 more report the add/edit controls genuinely broken and the app cannot tell which it is receiving; the fix is a labelled, skippable tutorial that demonstrates habit CRUD. Report 36: onboarding complaints 16 (mean 1.81, 12 of 16 1–2★), 7.9% of E1 → 1.9% of E5 — 'Is there no manual? Or user guide? I see no way to add new items like a + sign'; 'Is it a game or some kind of something else?' Report 41: onboarding 8 (mean 2.88, lowest non-monetisation) — 'How to use this app🤡 :: Is there a tutorial?'; could not find how to edit a habit; a paying user never started because the skip / miss / stats model was opaque; the report proposes a one-screen 'how this app models habits' card. Report 42: 'Endless screens asking unnecessary questions with no option to skip. I deleted the app after about 15 non-shippable screens, never got to use it'; '~30 questions before I gave up' (both 1★). Report 43: 20 reviews over nine years say there is no tutorial, FAQ or help (see C259). Report 46: onboarding confusion 19 (mean 3.95); the skip-symbol legend is missed at first run and cannot be found again ('I missed the intro and can't find it again'). Report 47: onboarding confusion 9 (mean 2.44) — two could not find back-dating after reading it existed in the update notes, a third the hidden start-date options; today's done / not-done status unclear 5. Report 48: confusing setup 118 (2.68%, 3.11) has sat at 2–3% in E1, E3, E4 and E5 — 'a decade of onboarding friction that no redesign has removed', concentrated on choosing between Habit / Target / Average / Project and on where deletion lives; the existing goal-setting course (credited by 27) could be surfaced at first run. Report 49: onboarding too long 29 (1.55), rising every era to 4.1% — some abandon during the questionnaire before any price is shown. Report 50: onboarding bimodal — confusion 4 (2.75) vs 'The onboarding and habit creation are straight to the point' 3 (5.00). [Merged from C259: Report 43: no guide / tutorial / FAQ / help (9, mean 2.78) plus a learning curve (14, 3.36) — 20 reviews (3.13%) requested continuously from Feb 2017 ('There must be some tips or suggestions in start') to Aug 2026 ('I don't understand nothing') and never addressed: 'There is no help option in settings which makes at least one action I want to take impossible… I can't find instructions for this in the app, on YouTube, or through a Google search'; 'I have had to contact support twice on things that could have explained up front'; 'it took me an hour or so to figure out how to make it work… I'd pay for this if it had some adjustments in usability'. Roughly a tenth of the 29 scheduling-gap reviews ask for capabilities the app already has (custom days, timers, untimed tasks) and land as 1★ / 2★. The same product draws 123 'simple' reviews — daily use is simple, setup is not — so a help screen targets a different surface from the praised simplicity.] Report 52: time-of-day scenes are loved and confusing ('two + buttons'). Report 54: onboarding_confusion 10 (2.71%, 3.70) — the water jar, 'repot' ('Will it restart all my progress?') and where to add a second habit are unexplained. Report 57: onboarding_no_guidance 23 (18 KR, 4 JP) and 65 Korean reviewers (10.74%) asking for help rather than reviewing — an in-app FAQ answering the five most-asked review questions. Report 59 (Tappsk): NEG_ONBOARDING 78 (0.51%, 3.27★) — hidden gestures and an unexplained score make first use confusing even in an app praised for simplicity. Report 60 (Mindway): 'It is overwhelming to set up tasks in the beginning' — a first-run 'pick one of three ready-made days' is the proposed fix (E6); a how-to for bulk-removing unwanted preset tasks is requested by a payer. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'Explain what the options actually do' (PY, 4★) — the cheapest item in the report.

merged_from.title: An in-app help screen — first-run tour, searchable FAQ, per-setting explanations — for any product whose setup is richer than its daily use
merged_from.note: C259 (report 43: no guide, tutorial or FAQ for eleven years) is the help-screen half of the same need C075 covers (hidden gestures and product vocabulary that new users cannot decode); one learnability requirement

title: Never seed the launch rating — templated or bought reviews decay and leave the markets they cover unmeasurable
statement: Users spot it in week one and say so; it contaminates the analytics baseline permanently. Report 16: a reviewer alleged the beta list was asked to 'overcome outdated reviews'; 23 self-identified beta testers were strongly bimodal and the launch rating was spent within six weeks. Report 19: all eight 5★ reviews in a 441-day corpus landed in one nine-day December window, all US, 44–74 characters, morning-UTC, generic register, one containing a homoglyph ('recọmmend') — the report treats them as unable to bear analytical weight and states every positive figure with and without them. Report 30: two dated phrase-bank campaigns seeded 50% of all reviews; when they stopped the rating fell toward 3.0★ and the organic 1★ rate tripled. Report 30: 83 of 166 reviews (50%) came from a five-phrase list in several languages, all 5★, in two dated campaigns; when they stopped the half-year mean fell 4.65 → 3.00, the organic 1★ rate rose 12.5% → 44.4%, and the US and GB storefronts were left commercially unmeasured (the high-spend group yielded 8 substantive reviews at 3.50 against a 4.79 headline). Report 43: 13 US 5★ reviews within 24 minutes on 10 Oct 2016 ('Use!!', 'Best!!', 'Helful'), three days after the first review — lifted 2016's mean 4.45 → 4.58 and the ten-year mean by 0.02; detected by timestamp clustering, not votes. Report 48: 3 reviews claim fake reviews (1.33); no burst or brigading pattern found — the Jan 2015 spike spans 20 storefronts with unrelated texts. Report 49: 27 reviews invert their stars as a signalling channel ('THIS is actually a one star review. I just wanted you to see it'; 'Gunna remove the one Star as soon as I know you got the message'). Report 60 (Mindway): a 45% two-month burst of very short, very positive, mostly non-English reviews with no duplicated authors or bodies — read as a paid acquisition push plus a first-session rating prompt rather than a farm — is disclosed as 'the single most distorting structural fact in the dataset'; the mean it bought decayed to 3.21 within weeks of the push ending. Report 67 (Habio): SUS_SEED 589 (28.72%, mean 4.91, 2024-03-11 → 2025-02-18) — 94.2% on the US storefront, 33.6% Cyrillic author names vs ~1% elsewhere, 3.1% with any helpfulness vote vs 28.3% of other 4–5★, zero mentions of charges or support; a developer reply pasted into a 5★ body, one paragraph split across three accounts in the same hour, six bodies posted twice by different accounts, referral spam, praise aimed at the complaint ('Cancelled my subscription with no issues at all'), praise for frequent updates while the current build dated from 2024-05-15; they supply 545 of 668 praise codes and coincide with a 4.28 US public rating against a non-seeded mean of 1.31; genuine reviewers cite the gap as proof of fraud ('These scammers pay to have their ratings boosted'); §8.7: stop any programme that sources, incentivises or scripts reviews.

merged_from.title: Never seed the launch rating with templated or bought reviews — the rating decays and the markets they cover become unmeasurable
merged_from.note: C244 (report 30: two phrase-bank 5★ campaigns, 50% of the corpus) is the strongest instance of C076, not a separate rule

title: Purchase and signup flow must not leak buyers
statement: People who try to pay and cannot (errors, rejected emails, promos that fail to apply) leave 2–4★ and money on the table. Report 14: two willing buyers in 2020 could not complete the purchase ('When I click upgrade button, it only appears an orange screen and then disappears') — the checkout broke in the app's final months. Report 53: an accidental purchase on first open (kr) and a crash right after paying ₩19,000. Report 55: the purchase button crashed in January 2018 — 'I want to give you money! I want more habits! But you're app crashes whenever I try to upgrade' (PAY_IAP_FAIL 14, 10 that month).

title: Ship the paid feature working before you sell it — the purchase trigger must never be the broken feature
statement: Paid features carry a higher reliability bar; selling broken sync/calendar/stats put payers a full star below free users. Report 20: the widget was by a wide margin the most-named purchase trigger and the feature that most often didn't work — 182 reviews (mean 1.94), 113 from confirmed payers, broken for five years with an in-app FAQ offering 'restart your phone'; even when present it was a Today-view widget while screenshots implied Home Screen. Ship it properly or remove it from the paywall copy and refund on request. Report 23: the Apple Watch is a purchase driver, not a feature — ≥15 reviews name it as the reason to buy and the explicit-bug subset runs at mean 2.57; if you ship a Watch app its reliability budget is your main reliability budget. Report 41: four of ten post-purchase failures bought for one named capability that then failed (backfill, widget ×2, Health sync) — any single-feature failure is a total failure of the purchase. Report 43: 'purchase not delivered' is the most damaging pattern for a one-time product — 4 buyers got nothing ('I paid to upgrade to get the edit function, but no changes happened… Something broken in the backend??'; 'Purchase premium but still getting free trial capabilities'; 'just took my money'), one could not buy, one could not restore. Report 48: the Jan 2015 subscription launch shipped with a broken release — 81 crash-on-launch, 25 data-loss and 20 duplicate-tracker reviews in the same window — and reviewers linked the two: 'they were asked to start paying for an app that had just stopped working'; the 19 Jan – 30 Sep 2015 window averaged 2.06★ with 73.2% 1–2★. Report 53: statistics — a main reason to pay — crashed for paying users from Sep 2024 (STAT_CRASH 28 of 33 since then, 21.7% of all E4 reviews; payer lift 2.95; the 7-day trend view named by 14); a reviewer reset two years of data trying to fix it; F3 'the feature people pay for'. Report 54: the paid tier's named benefit 'Advanced Statistics' is a calendar — 12 value-gap reviews (2.58), 10 payers (22.7% of payers), three quoting the phrase back ('I bought this app bcs it stated advanced statistics for paid version. But I can not call these statistics even basic'); both payers who bought specifically for statistics were disappointed; F4: build it or delete the claim. Report 55: sync and export — the server-dependent parts of the premium bundle — are the two paid features reviewers most often report broken, while 'more habits' costs nothing to deliver.

merged_from.title: Never take a paying user's reason to buy away — the widget sold the upgrade and never worked
merged_from.note: C220 (report 20's widget: the #1 named purchase trigger, non-functional for five years) is the strongest instance of C078, not a separate rule

title: Personal photos as habit icons
statement: Rare, loved, and no competitor in report 2's corpus offers it.

title: Colour themes / dark mode
statement: 'Only green' draws requests; cheap. Report 10: dark mode requested since 2022 as an accessibility need (migraine, light sensitivity). Report 20: dark mode moved from free-ish to paid in the 2021 conversion (89 reviews, mean 2.69) and was a named purchase trigger. Report 24: dark mode requested by 43, 58.1% of them 4–5★ — cheap and asked for by advocates. Report 29: dark mode absent — 15 requests (4.10%, mean 4.67, the highest-satisfaction request group), India 8.77% (2.9× global), 'it's what's missing for 5 stars'. Report 31: dark mode / themes 18; a German visually impaired reviewer: 'no accessibility features, no dark mode, no localisation … unusable'. Report 33: dark mode and themes were Premium in 2019–20; 48 request themes / colours. Report 43: per-habit colours / icons requested by 4 (mean 4.50); dark mode praised. Report 46: dark mode paywalled (2020, June 2024) — the report's #7 fix returns it to the free tier. Report 47: dark mode must keep every control legible — time-picker digits were unreadable in dark mode (2); more colours requested 3 (2019–20), later unlocked by watching a video. Report 48: dark mode requested by 11 (4.64). Report 50: colour coding, app-wide font, text size, dark mode, week-start day and per-habit units praised (customisation 25, 4.80); hex colours, longer habit titles, hide streak count requested. Report 52: dark mode requested (70, weak). Report 54: dark mode requested (5), once for light sensitivity. Report 55: dark mode shipped mid-2020 with 'black writing on the black background' (BUG_DARK 10, 1.90). Report 56: a dark / OLED design praised ('Cool OLED and Minimal Design'); dark mode (Feb) and light mode (Jul) requested five months apart. Report 57: dark mode Premium-gated (US) against a photosensitive user's accessibility need; white text on a white background with Premium themes. Report 59 (Tappsk): REQ_DARK (13) ends in 2021-10, consistent with a dark theme shipping; REQ_THEMES 70, REQ_ICON 20, REQ_FONT 21 continue.

title: Ads in the free tier
statement: A mild negative and a minor purchase reason in report 2; 'no ads' is the best-rated topic in report 1. Report 18: an interstitial ad on every check-off (Oct 2022) drew 17+ protests in weeks and was softened by December; the surviving minimal ads were tolerated. Report 25: six reviewers volunteer 'show me ads instead' of a paywall — ads-as-alternative is requested, not complained about; the app has none. Report 26: three teens independently ask for a rewarded-ad path to extra habits ('I will watch ads all day long if I have to') while 7 reviews (mean 5.00) praise having no ads. Report 27: 12 reviews (8.70%, mean 4.83) praise the absence of ads by name; an ad tier is 'contradicted by evidence'. Report 28 (the strongest counter-evidence in the set): an ad-supported free tier whose interstitial fires on every check-off is 19.98% of reviews at mean 2.73 vs 4.35 for the rest, 52.4% of all 1★, and rose from 3.5% (2021H2) to 39.6% (2024H2) before easing to 16.7%; three reports of non-dismissible ads and one of 'decline the rewarded ad, get a forced ad anyway' are store-guideline risks; an app rated 4+ with 40 reviews from or about children (ages 8–10 self-declared) serves untargeted network ads including AI homework-cheating and Temu wigs; 6 reviewers praise the ads as light and rewarded ads for carrots are accepted — the placement, not the existence, is the damage; the CN storefront (12 reviews, zero ad complaints) may be a natural ad-free control. Report 42: zero mentions of ads; upsell interstitials play the role ('the popups for premium are annoying and difficult to click out of'); one would rather see ads than pay €1.99/month (report 34). Report 47: the corpus is its own before-and-after on ad format — top-and-bottom banners were a mild theme (11, 1.87%, mean 3.55, 2019 – Apr 2024) whose reviewers mostly asked to pay to remove them; a video ad per check-in (May–Dec 2024) averaged 1.46 and generated exits ('1アクションに1回結構な長さのゲーム広告'; '元々入力するのに1分もかからないのに広告も1分じゃ'; 'an ad after every single entry is excessive… worse option than the notes app'); rewarded video for cosmetic colours (2022) was reported neutrally in a 14-vote 5★ — placement on the completion action, not ads as such, is what reviewers punish. Report 48: no ads in any era — 33 praise it, zero complain; two reviewers propose ads instead of the paywall, which the report reads as hostility to the cap rather than endorsement of ads. Report 52: the counter-case at scale — a nine-year Chinese tracker ran splash ads (2019–21, AD_NEG 3.4% / 2.8%) and in-flow ads from June 2025 (35.0% of reviews in six months, the lowest month in nine years); a ¥8 one-time ad-free SKU is accepted by those who find it ('but 8 yuan removes ads forever', 5★) and read as the motive for hostile ads by others; recovered to 5.8% in 2026 with complainants possibly churned. See [[C269]]. Report 64 (Critique AI): with no free tier, 12 (2.86%, mean 1.58) propose an ad-supported way in, one proposes an ad-supported base of a three-tier ladder; a 2★ defends the price as the alternative to 'annoying ads'.

title: Performance must not degrade with habit count
statement: 5+ second taps for the most engaged (paying) users; lag is a churn cause on its own. Report 30: above ~10 habits the list jumps back to the top after every tick and rows cannot be made denser — a defect that only paying users hit; fix it before raising the cap. Report 31: freeze / lag 404 (7.79%, mean 1.62) rising in every era to 26.6% of 2025–26 — '10 seconds for the sound effect, another 20 seconds for the colour to change'; '20-30 seconds per habit'; 'it now takes several seconds to add a single entry … can't cope with too many entries' (iPhone 15 Pro) — set a tap-to-register budget (<100 ms) and test with multi-year histories; some reviewers infer throttling of non-subscribers (untested). Report 42: lag scales with habit count ('the more goals you add the slower it gets'; hit at 15 habits) — 12 reviews (mean 2.58), 9 Brazilian, 4 payers — 'the users most affected are the ones who bought the app to have more than three habits'. Report 53: slowdown with many habits (24-vote jp review); the statistics crash tested against long histories and 20 habits. Report 56: the bottom menu bar blocks the habit list at 9+ habits — the scale 'unlimited habits' invites.

title: Address tracking / privacy visibly
statement: One unrebutted 1★: 'a whole lotta tracking going on by the developer'. Report 13: a 2017 privacy-policy revision drew 11 reviews in a month; location prompts with no stated purpose ('No, you don't need it') and disclosure-to-law-enforcement language made long-time users delete. Report 24: privacy / personal data complaints 138 (mean 1.225, 87.7% 1★) — a long questionnaire and web billing that collects card data before install. Report 27: a no-data-collection privacy label and no account are praised as features (4, mean 5.00); data monetisation is contradicted by the evidence and the listing. Report 29: 'I also appreciate that there's no subscription fees or ads. Am I trading off data privacy for this?' — users of free apps look for the hidden price; the listing's privacy label did not obviously cover the bandwidth-sharing prompt that followed. Report 34: on-device data with no account praised as privacy (7): 'my data isn't stored on a server!'; 'hasn't been larded with privacy-invading trackers'. Report 36: 'Does what it's meant to do while respecting your privacy and not harvesting your data'; 'the developers don't collect your data'. Report 41: 'This app doesn't hoard your data'; privacy / no account 10 reviews, all 5★. Report 43: 'Great data privacy (no data collected)' is enumerated among purchase reasons; 'I want to support the excellent privacy and pricing policies!' Report 46: 'Completely functional without paying! No ads!' (chronic pain); no ads praised by 10 (4.90); no account needed by 2024.
