Report 52: untranslated Chinese UI plus a precise-location request led a US reviewer to title the review 'Malware?? DO NOT INSTALL'; 'still using location after uninstall'; a dead privacy-policy link. Report 53: reviewers who read the privacy policy object to Facebook pixel and Firebase SDKs in a health-adjacent app; unexplained Apple ID prompts on launch (PRIV 7, 1.86); R8: publish and minimise third-party analytics. Report 55: premium required an e-mail account or the purchase was lost; cloud storage of goal data questioned; 'no login needed' praised. Report 56: no data collection named as the primary value by an ES reviewer ('No recopila datos') and corroborated by the listing; adding analytics to learn about churn would contradict it. Report 64 (Critique AI): 'don't put your email in this app' — two German reviewers independently, three months apart; refusal to give card or personal details before seeing the product; a photo demanded before the price; German reviews 28.6% scam and 14.3% privacy (n=14) vs 5.01% / 1.19% globally.

title: Never imply cross-app integration you don't have
statement: Sibling apps raised expectations of integration; the purchases it drove ended in 1★.

title: No rating-prompt or cross-promo spam, especially to payers
statement: Small but consistent complaint.

title: Promos, giveaways and gift codes must work exactly as advertised
statement: Inflate early sentiment; when the promo fails to apply it produces 2–3★ from would-be buyers. Report 5's '1+1' gift code could not be used by the buyer and expired in three months — six years of disputes. Report 9: an advertised 3-month money-back guarantee was not honoured (17 reviews); withdrawing the claim zeroed those complaints and halved refund complaints. Report 26: China App Store shows a ¥38 tier with no in-app purchase path. Report 31: '83–90% off' first-year offers ($8.99–$9.99) checked out at $59.99–$99.99 through 2022–23, and a $19.99 'lifetime' was shown against anchors of $399–CA$499.99 that charged without unlocking. Report 34: the ~29 Jun 2023 free-lifetime giveaway left one reviewer calling it a 'Scam of free life time subscription' (1★) and another asking when the next limited-time free offer comes. Report 42: a promotional R$39.90/year shown, R$99.90 charged at confirm (1★, 'I'm waiting to adjust my rating of the app'). Report 43: a promo-free, ad-free one-time model produced zero unexpected charges, trial traps or chargebacks in 638 reviews. Report 46: a Black Friday €15 price; a December discount honoured after it expired ('Joan still hooked me up with the discounted subscription', 5★). Report 53: a splash screen offering ~90% off the annual plan while the App Store sheet shows the full price, in more than ten currencies ($7.99 → $79.99; €6.99 → €69.99; ¥900 → ¥9,000; 199 → 1,999 TRY) — PAY_PROMO 35 (mean 1.83), Jan 2023 → Feb 2026, 13 with no support reply and 9 asking for refunds; some reviewers did get it, suggesting eligibility rules; the most concentrated trust-destroying pattern in the corpus; F1: show the exact first charge and renewal on the offer screen and never show an offer the viewer can't redeem.

title: Destructive actions on widgets, quick surfaces and running routines need confirmation or undo
statement: An un-undoable reset button on a Home Screen widget destroyed streaks by mis-tap and read as 'a visual cue to break the streak' — a safety issue in a recovery app.

title: Regional pricing
statement: IN, TR, UA, BR, MX, SA reviewers name price as the only blocker; India likes the product and has not yet been asked a price it can accept. Report 23: price objection concentrates in au (5.7%), de (3.8%), ca (3.6%) against us 1.3%; China's number is ¥25–30. Report 25: price-display confusion is a Mexico-specific repeated issue — three reviewers cannot tell pesos from dollars, others name MXN 500, 40, 300, 599 and 299.99 — a pricing-display problem that is cheap to fix; Argentina's hostility (mean 2.95) warrants a look at its pricing display and trial mechanics. Report 33: regional price objections from Vietnam, Turkey (270 TL), Korea ('I'll buy if it's discounted') and Japan (¥19,000 lifetime, 'unfair to base your pricing on [exchange rates] alone'; 「前に比べて値段が爆上がり」) — regionalise lifetime pricing. Report 36: regional pricing complaints from Turkey and a cheaper local rival in India (₹499/yr vs Dayrise). Report 41: purchasing-power-adjusted lifetime tiers proposed for the 63 sub-50 storefronts, where cap complaints are 2.1× the high-volume markets. Report 46: regional price complaints 8 (all non-US — Turkey ₺179 / ₺30 a month, Saudi 109 SAR, Vietnam, Latin America, Israel cannot buy online, Kazakhstan) while Russia calls its price fair; the report's E2 is regional lifetime pricing. Report 48: China's lifetime objection is cost-of-living framed (a lifetime plan near a quarter of a second-hand iPhone); price sensitivity clusters in CA / AU / DE / CN. Report 49: Canada itemises CA$79.99 plus 14.99% Quebec tax; Türkiye objects to dollar-pegged pricing. Report 54: price objections 3.1× more frequent outside developed storefronts; D2: storefront-tiered pricing for CN/TW/PH/TR/BR/CO. Report 57: price objection 8.05% outside Korea vs 0.99% inside, Japan 26.92% — three reviewers on three continents independently propose a cheaper tier of ad removal + groups + backup (~¥2,000), one a monthly plan. Report 59 (Tappsk): the same lifetime unlock is named at 449 ₽ and 2,500 ₽ and at $14 / €4–10 within a year; regional prices could not be established from the corpus. Report 64 (Critique AI): M6 — price for the actual audience: an age- or region-tiered price as an experiment on a teen-heavy creator audience; volume markets ask for free rather than cheaper (20.0% vs 14.3%).

title: No upsell nagging without a 'never ask again' option
statement: Full-screen interstitials, permanent banners and upsells before first value draw complaints even from 5★ users; a subscription launch with nagging cost ~3 points of 1–2★. Report 9: upsell-pressure complaints quintupled (2.16% → 4.84% → 10.23%) as the funnel was tuned harder, becoming the fastest-growing 1★ source. Report 14: the cleanest before/after in the set — rating-and-upsell pop-ups on every launch drew six star-docking reviews in nine weeks ('I docked one star for this'; 'Deleted'), and removing them produced unsolicited 5★ praise ('They removed the pop ups. Nice!!') and a named edge over a rival still 'begging for an upgrade within the first minute'. Report 18: a persistent bottom promo bar and a Dynamic Island discount countdown in 2025–26 were experienced as worse than the 2022 interstitial ads ('Absolutely the worst choice'); upgrade-nag was among the lowest-rated themes (40, mean 2.40★). Report 20: a 'limited time offer' countdown that reset to 60 hours on expiry ran for over four years (Jan 2021 → Mar 2025) beside a full-screen launch interstitial with a low-contrast dismiss — 225 reviews (5.56%, mean 1.80); 'Dark patterns make bad UX!'; 'first the consumer must see the value of the product. And what do you have? Every 2 seconds a subscribe banner.' Report 23: 4 reviews object to ads for the developer's other apps inside a paid app. Report 24: sister-app upsells (308, mean 1.932), referral/share prompts (131) and pop-ups/unskippable steps (182, mean 2.082) inside a paid subscription. Report 25: navigation-blocking upsell sheets — '10 popups in 20 seconds which kills the use'; 'not even my first second on the app 4 ads asking for payment'; a 5-second forced delay on the premium prompt; 'a habit app that starts right away with dark patterns' — 35 reviews (2.67%, mean 1.80); cap the prompt to one dismissible surface per session; a French reviewer notes explosive pop-ups are actively harmful for ADHD users in an app marketed to them. Report 28: forced interstitials on every action ('Ad while you write a habit. Ad while you review habits. Ad while you breathe.') and a rating prompt on open and check-off. Report 31: upsell nag 676 (13.04%, mean 1.72) rising 1.9% (E1) → 22.6% (E4) through a full-screen offer on every launch (2021), a permanent 'Just for you' list cell (2023) and two pop-ups per launch (2024, mean 1.47) — 'the only habit I'm developing is closing the upsell pop up'; a share of E4 purchases were made 'to get rid of the incessant pestering', and when relief did not arrive they produced the angriest reviews; E1 buyers valued 'that they don't prompt you to update every 3 clicks'; cap offers at one dismissible surface per week. Report 34: upgrade nagging 4 (mean 2.00) — 'constantly being nagged to upgrade to premium. I only track one thing'. Report 36: a full-page subscribe screen on every launch — POPUP 24 (mean 2.67), rising to 15.0% of 2026 H2, the only negative theme regularly in 5★ (4 of 24): 'i said no already, please respect that'; 'Can't use the app on my iPhone 13 mini because of a freaking pop up' (5★ titled 'Unusable'); the report calls a once-a-week cap the cheapest change available. Report 42: upsell interstitials 'annoying and difficult to click out of' (3, mean 1.67). Report 43 (counter-case): the in-app upsell is never complained about; the nag is the review prompt. Report 46: the upsell twin of the rating prompt — 'everytiime I try to add a new habit or move between screens the upgrade to premium screen appears and has to be x multiple times' (4, mean 1.50); a paywall on first open for some ('Take a subscription straight away or look at the start screen. That's all'). Report 47: upsell nag 4 (mean 1.25, Jul–Nov 2025) — 'タスクを完了するたびに毎回有料版の導入を進めるページに移るのがうっとうしいから消した' (a paid-version page after every completed task; deleted); the 2024 lesson did not carry over to 2025's upsell screens. Report 48: a full-screen / post-log upgrade prompt introduced around July 2024 drew 6 nag reviews in three months from long-term free users who say it reduced their willingness to pay ('I might even consider paying money for the app. But I darn sure will not… as long as the nag screen is still in place'); one records it being softened and raised their rating — 'the only monetization mechanic in the corpus that users say actively reduced their intent to pay'. Report 53: a 'new year, new me' premium pop-up with a countdown that 'never ends, it just starts over', shown every app open from 2023 (PAY_NAG 42, mean 1.93, 39 of 42 from 2023) — reviewers call the app's own offers 'ads'; M1: once a week at most, never to payers, no resetting countdown. Report 54: upgrade nag including after paying (5, 2.80); 'The paywall is so obtrusive' (GB). Report 55: a full-screen premium pop-up on every launch from July 2020 (PAY_NAG 44, 2.02; still reported Dec 2024) — 'Just ask once and don't make it pop up every time I launch the free app and it gets 5'; M5: one upsell, frequency-capped. See [[C274]]. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_UPSELL 97 (0.64%, 3.33★) — 'Каждый день по 30 раз пихают мне всплывающее окошко «Купите нашу полную версию»' (thirty times a day the buy-our-full-version pop-up); Germany reports it at 2.36×, purchasers at 2.44×. Report 60 (Mindway): 'every 5 seconds it keeps brining up these Hey pay me now Pop Ups… let me do my activities and move on with my life' (1★); 'It keeps saying do you want a free trial for something'; 'it won't allow me make a plan without showing free trial vip' — an upsell that fires inside the task the user came to do; F5: stop firing the upsell inside an in-progress task — 'a description of a broken interaction, not of a pricing disagreement'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'Get one star for annoying me with pop-ups' (PL, 1★) — one review, a full star, 'a setting, not a build'; M5: cut in-session upsell pop-ups or cap their frequency. Report 67 (Habio): NEG_POPUP 19 ('I just wish it was voluntary'); a 2026 dashboard described as 'a mini Time Square Billboard showcase' of upsells.

title: Ask for reviews well — tone converts; cadence and ignoring the OS opt-out backfire
statement: A charming review request produced dozens of reviews; frequent prompts that ignore the iOS opt-out, especially to payers, read as 'scammy'. Cross-promoting the developer's other apps inside the product draws the same complaint (report 2). Cross-promoting the developer's other apps inside the product draws the same complaint (report 2). Report 14: at least three reviews existed only because the app demanded one ('Happy now??'; a body reading 'Review'), polluting the ratings data. Report 20: a review prompt whose decline button read 'let the developers be sad' — 26 reviewers say it is why they wrote (inflating 2019's 5★ count) and two docked stars for the manipulation. Report 23: review-prompt nagging 25 (0.34%, mean 2.72, 40% 1★). Report 24: an in-app review prompt on day 1–3 makes the 5★ band (57.89%, median 105 characters) a first-impression measure — 'they asked me to review it now which I find kind of ridiculous'; the highest-voted reviews are all pre-2024 5★s. Report 25: an onboarding review prompt — 'Why won't it progress without me writing a review?'; 'in the middle of the onboarding questions the app interrupts me to ask me to rate' — pushed ≤25-character reviews from 7.2% to 33.4% of the corpus (150 of 196 5★ in 2026) and median body length from 156 to 53 characters; the all-records mean falls 0.27 while the substantive mean falls 0.73, and 1★ share (16.1% → 26.6%) is the only trustworthy trend line; 43 reviews (mean 4.21) are from people who say they have not used the app yet. A prompt at first launch buys a store rating and costs your own telemetry. Report 26: the app rewards a review with a cosmetic unlock and 13 reviewers say so ('I'm just doing this to get the backgrounds 😋 I haven't even used the app at all'; '(I'm NOT a bot btw)'); ≤25-character reviews rose from 16.5% to 35.0% of the corpus, 83–91% of them 5★; true inflation is unmeasurable and there is App Store policy exposure. Report 27: exactly one reviewer discloses a prompt ('Saw the message and had to rate'), no reward-for-review, and only 12 of 138 reviews are ≤25 characters — the substantive mean (4.594) equals the headline (4.645); a corpus of people who wrote something. Report 28: a rating prompt on open and on check-off shipped in 2026 (5 of 7 complaints are 2026) and already produced a 1★ 'until the rate me notification spam gets fixed'; 134 contentless 5★ records (median 38 chars) suggest the 2026 rating recovery is partly solicited; 'prompting into an ad-frustrated session is actively harvesting negative ratings'. Report 29: a rating prompt fired on the first check-off ('Used the app for 2 minutes then a reminder popped up for me to rate the app. -1 star'; 'so here I am, on day 1') — 39 contentless reviews, all 5★, median 27 characters; the 4.552 mean is partly a prompt-timing artefact that also starves the developer of diagnostic feedback; delay it to day 7 or ~10 completions. Report 30: 83 templated 5★ reviews and a near-absence of 2–3★ (7 of 166) consistent with a prompt routing satisfied users to the store; the public 4.4★ is a decaying artefact. Report 31: no review-prompt inflation — 20 prompt complaints (0.39%) and short reviews ≤7.7% of every era; about 1–2% of 5★ are complaints rated 5 'so people see it'. Report 33: in-app rating prompts 'three in 10 seconds' (Nov 2017 – Jan 2018) made review-nag complaints 3.8% of 2017 before falling to ≤1% every later year; 82 of 88 rating-contradicts-text reviews are 5★ reporting a bug or block; 820 short reviews (20.8%) inflate the positive side. Report 34: a rating prompt during setup ('you want me to rate it before I even finish setting it up'; 'App asks for 5 stars review'); the report recommends prompting after setup and after a 7-day streak. Report 41: 'it asks for a review every day which is needlessly annoying even if you've rated the app' (1★, Aug 2026); 111 of 815 (13.6%) contentless praise at a 69-character median — the signature of prompted reviews. Report 42: a rating prompt inside onboarding — 'Asking for a rating the first time I log in? How could I possibly know. But, since I'm being asked I must give it a one star' — the clearest causal chain to a 1★ in the corpus (2, both 1★). Report 43: the review prompt fires 'every time I open this app', 'every 2 minutes', and to people who already paid ('Paid $3, still kept asking for review. Annoying!') — 4 reviews, mean 2.75, plus a prompt whose Submit stays greyed out; 'a rating-acquisition mechanism actively lowering the rating'. Report 46: the largest self-inflicted problem in a 2,178-review corpus — an in-app rating prompt with no 'don't ask again' (50 complaints, mean 3.22, 10 one-stars; 'App asks me to review 4 times in 10 minutes. I haven't even setup 2 habits yet. Only option is Not now… Think twice before adding dark patterns'; 'you keep asking me for a review? → I'm punishing you'), asked during setup, of subscribers, and across platforms, 'fixed' in June 2023 yet live in August 2026; it capped 11 of 143 three-star ratings; the report's #1 fix: never in the first week, never twice per version, never after a rating or dismissal, never for subscribers. Report 47: rating prompt nag 3 (2023–26, mean 2.33) — a paying user asks it to stop 'せめて課金してる人に対してくらいは' ('at least for people who pay'). Report 48: review-prompt nag 9 (2.22); a prompt existed 2013–15 and ~2021; the prompt-driven share of 379 five-star low-information reviews is unknowable. Report 49: 1★ used as leverage — 'I am enjoying the app and will change the review once they fix it'. Report 50: the review prompt fires during onboarding alongside 'a page of positive reviews less than two minutes after I opened the app' — two 1★ reviews about nothing else ('I don't even star using this app and you ask me for a review'; 'participant reactivity bias plus peer pressure… Absolutely disgusting'); 27 of 142 five-stars ≤ 60 characters — fix F3: move it behind a streak milestone, which also stops inflating the corpus. Report 52: from 2020 a review prompt on the Nth launch ('第500次打开', '第3000次打开') — 40 mentions at 4.50; complaints when it fires before use and when it still insists after the user paid ¥8 to remove ads. Report 53: one jp reviewer nagged to review every time they open the app to log. Report 55: 'You have asked me 4 time within 1 minute to rate your app'; a lock screen and rating dialog that trapped a user (META_PROMPT 9, 2.44); R8: throttle the prompt. Report 58: no review prompt and a 3.30% contentless-praise rate — if a prompt is ever added, gate it behind a real usage milestone so the corpus keeps its value as a discovery instrument. Report 59 (Tappsk): a guilt-trip dismiss button — 'пусть разработчики грустят' (let the developers be sad) — is named in 2.04% of reviews (REV_SOLICITED 309, mean 4.77★, 1.6–2.5% of every era from 2020-01, coinciding with a 10× volume jump); most reviewers quote it fondly ('adorei a estratégia para deixarmos a avaliação'), but 12 of 309 are 1–2★ about the prompt itself ('это манипуляция эмоциями' — emotional manipulation; 'Хватит меня каждую секунду просить оставить отзыв'; 'Saudumme Formulierung') and it feeds distrust of the other reviews (REV_DISTRUST 32: 'начитались купленных отзывов'); the report's experiment: keep the prompt, change the dismiss wording, suppress it after a purchase, a crash or a support ticket. Report 60 (Mindway): a rating prompt fired on first session plus a paid acquisition push produced a 4-month burst — 98 of 216 (45.37%) in 2025-03/04, mean 4.12, 63 at 5★, from 32 storefronts, 52.76% of them content-free — that raised the mean 0.62 stars while adding almost no product evidence; when the push stopped, volume fell from 59 a month to 2 and the mean fell to 3.21, below launch level: 'the burst bought a rating, not a reputation, and it decayed the moment it stopped'; the modal 5★ is nine characters ('Love it') and only 37 of 128 5★ (28.91%) state a reason connected to using the product. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): three of 17 five-star reviews (17.6% of the band) do not endorse the product — 'App doesn't work', a pricing question, a critical entitlement bug — so the public 5★ count overstates satisfaction by roughly that much; seven low-information 5★ ('Good', '👍🏻', 'Excelente') are evenly spread. Report 64 (Critique AI): 11 contradicting reviews, ten at 5★, three explicitly using the star as a message about price ('im only doing 5 star just for you to take the payment subscription away'; 'I only gave 5 stars so you can see this'; 'i'm rating this 5 stars because i support your content bro but just please, please lower that price') — 39.8% of the 5★ band is not a product endorsement.

merged_from.title: No rating-prompt or cross-promo spam, especially to payers
merged_from.note: rating-prompt spam to payers was already the negative half of C094; cross-promo spam folded in

title: Neutral, non-judgemental tone on failure
statement: Reset without shame, no motivational pop-ups, keep history — the differentiation against apps that 'talk'. Report 23: a reminder framed as loss — 'You will lose your streak of X days if you don't do this today' — drew requests in four languages to reframe positively ('pedagogy from the early 20th century'); one string change per locale. Report 24: childish / condescending tone 304 (0.70%, mean 2.701); what paying users value includes that missing a day is not punished. Report 25: 'I clicked, paid £29.99 and I don't even know why. It's a list of aims for the day, I get to see all the things I haven't done and feel bad' — a checklist without a forgiving frame reads as guilt. Report 26: 'accountability and motivation without the shame' — gentleness, no streaks and a calm garden metaphor are the moat (25, mean 4.76; mental-health users 32, mean 4.66). Report 33: guilt copy backfires — 'Let's do better tomorrow, shall we?'; 'Yikes'; a Jan 2026 'Are you sure the day is over?' pop-up on fail/skip with no off switch ('infantilizing … Shipping annoying stuff without an off switch is a churn risk') — 43 reviews on unwanted or guilt notifications (mean 2.33). Report 36: 'As an easily discouraged perfectionist, I LOVE that if you miss a day (or a week) that it doesn't become the app of shame' (20 votes); the motivational text is 'encouraging but never guilt inducing' (13, all 5★). Report 46: 'not ticks to check off but areas that fill with beautiful colours — so I don't feel stressed about not managing something'; 'a triangle in that space… feels like neutral data instead of a personal failing'. Report 47: non-punitive framing praised — 'やったところが色が塗られるので加点方式な感じがして好き' ('what you did gets coloured in, so it feels like scoring points, not losing them'); the report: keep filled colour when a streak breaks, any missed-day marker optional. Report 48: non-punitive framing praised by 39 (0.89%, 4.90). Report 53: reminders phrased as questions — 'instead of stating what I'm supposed to do NOW, it asks questions — Have you walked today?' (REM_GOOD 67, 4.85). Report 55: quirky reminder messages liked by most ('I loved being called a tiger') but pet names drove churn ('Deleted when the reminder called me cutie'); R5: offer a neutral message tone.

title: Privacy and discretion stack
statement: Face ID / passcode lock, no account, discreet app name, alternate icons — zero negative reviews in report 3 and category-critical for recovery users on family phones. Report 33: privacy 23 reviews (mean 1.35) — the in-app help showed other customers' support conversations, e-mails and photos; goal-share URLs readable without login with no off switch; sync requiring Apple ID, Google account and e-mail; third-party analytics — audit support-conversation scoping and make sharing opt-in with unguessable, expiring links. Report 48: 25 reviews object to being forced to create an account and go online for a local tracker — a privacy objection distinct from price, strongest in Germany. Report 49: 20 frame the pre-paywall questionnaire as data collection (1.10) — one demands deletion. Report 52: a passcode lock that an ad dismissal bypasses (2025) — security-relevant despite being a single report. Report 56: no ads, no data collection, no account — 'Dots currently monetizes nothing', itself a differentiator and the credibility that makes a donation ask land.

title: A tip / donate option
statement: People asking to give money with no mechanism to do so. Report 8: in a completely free app, 7 users asked unprompted for a tip jar (all 5★) and 13 more volunteered to pay — mostly one-time, not subscription. Report 27: exactly two reviewers volunteer money unprompted — 'Keep the free app, consider adding a tip jar for users who are thankful'; 'it would be nice to donate to the dev since it's a free app' — both 5★, both framing payment as gratitude, both pairing it with staying free; with 10 developer-gratitude reviews (all 5★) a tip jar is the only monetisation the corpus positively endorses, and Canada is where the evidence says to start. Report 29: 'love to be able to contribute to use it' — a contribution offered in a free app, alongside a lifetime-purchase offer tied to a widget. Report 56: one unprompted donation request in 67 reviews of a fully free app; E1: an unobtrusive tip jar in Settings — no gating, no prompt, no nag — and watch for any negative review mentioning it. Report 58: a voluntary in-app tip is the only payment surface, received warmly ('there are no ads! But you can leave a tip, which is very nice ✨'), zero objections — unlikely to scale alone. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_DONATE_WISH 18 — reviewers buy the lifetime unlock explicitly to support or thank the developer.

title: Time-unit flexibility for counters (hours → years)
statement: What makes day 1 survivable for a quit-habit user; zero 1–2★.

title: Countdown / 'days until' mode
statement: Users want one app for count-up and count-down. Report 23: an end-date / countdown / long-term goal is requested by very happy users (17, 0.23%, mean 4.76, 0% 1★). Report 52: countdown / anniversaries among 'everything else' requests (395). Report 56: a deadline (time-bounded goal) requested once — kept out of scheduling as a different product.

title: Money-saved counter
statement: Standard in quit-smoking apps; named as the one thing missing.

title: Milestones, achievements, celebration
statement: The largest positive-intent request in report 3 (2.21%, six years); shipped Aug 2026. Report 23: the gold-theme completion state — the whole screen turns gold when every task is done — is named by 80 5★ reviews; rewards, badges and milestones requested 136 times by happy users. Report 31: celebration on completion requested by 44 (mean 3.98), while achievements/trophies added in Apr 2023 were unwanted by long-time users. Report 46: the colour saturation itself is the reward — no badges needed; a gentler decay on a miss is asked for by 6 (mean 4.67) but must be tested against the neurodivergent segment. Report 50: badges / achievements requested (1). Report 57: a big confetti pop-up on check-off 'gives me ALL the dopamine' with no penalty for missing. Report 58: an ADHD reviewer asks for 'more of celebration for those who like dopamine hits' while 7 of 8 neurodivergent reviewers praise restraint — make it off-by-default and measure.

title: Inverse / 'good habit' mode for a counter
statement: Recovery users want the number up; chore/ADHD users want it low — one counter, two mental models.

title: Vulnerable users — recovery, mental-health and minors — are a sensitive surface
statement: Alcohol, nicotine, self-harm (incl. minors), drugs, EDs, no-contact; monetisation moves land as 'preying on the vulnerable'; age rating is load-bearing. In report 4: 455 kid/teen reviews who cannot pay, and 89 shame / diet-framing reviews in a 4+ app. Report 24: a product marketed to people with executive dysfunction and low income priced as a premium wellness subscription; diet-culture / eating-disorder trigger complaints (61, mean 2.918); depression/anxiety users are 2.89% of the corpus. Report 26: users describing severe depression, being bedbound, three years clean and wartime anxiety ('This app helped me return to life') — the gentle, non-punitive frame is what serves them; children as young as 10 review the app. Report 28: an app rated 4+ with 40 reviews (4.87%) from or about children — 'I'm ten'; 'im nine'; 'I am a 8 years old' — serves untargeted network ads (AI homework-cheating apps, Temu wigs) and a 'watch an ad to double carrots' prompt; a brand and compliance exposure independent of the rating damage. Report 29: 'You're doing a great service to students who cannot afford to spend on applications' — free access matters to students; 4 student/budget reviews at mean 5.00. Report 31: sobriety, medication and mood-disorder trackers were hit by streak resets, removed quit-to-zero goals and upsells interrupting tracking. Report 49: the acquired audience is young and emotionally timed — 12 minors, 'I saw it on insta at 2am and got the 2am motivation to change my life so now I have a year of this app', buyers 'at the lowest point in life' or in severe depression; mental-health-benefit reviews carry the taxonomy's highest mean (4.94). Report 64 (Critique AI): the creator audience is young — 20 reviews (4.77%, mean 1.90) are minors or argue for them (ages 12–15 self-stated; 'everyone on it seems to be like 12-15 years old'), 13 of 20 in the US; a ~$40/yr annual-upfront plan needs a payment instrument they do not control; a parent bought it for a 12-year-old and asked for a refund; the most-upvoted review (9 votes) asks for an adult tier and a free teen tier; research: what share of installs are under 13 — 'a compliance question as much as a pricing one'. Report 65 (Rabit): medication adherence ('não estou mais esquecendo de tomar meus remédios') and depression ('m'aide à surmonter ma dépression seulement je ne reçois aucunes notifications') — for these users a reminder failure is not an inconvenience. Report 67 (Habio): USE_ACCESS 18 name vulnerability (disability, low income, student, mental-health crisis) and USE_MENTAL 40 — 'Shame on the developers for scamming people, like me, who are trying to work on their mental health' (the most-voted review, 16 votes).

title: Never ship a paywall or feature-removal change silently
statement: Undisclosed changes and 'it was a bug' replies that don't match what users see destroy trust for a year. Report 11: the store description still discloses no paywall at all (0 mentions of premium/subscription/free/unlock) after the retrofit; a grandfathering rule for pre-2026 users is the recommended fix. Report 20: the Feb 2021 restoration was never announced — '4 stars after premium was restored, but not 5 because the devs ignored us for so long and have not acknowledged the issue' — and the March 2025 wipe drew 'no communication whatever about this disaster.' Report 29: the bandwidth-sharing prompt arrived with no announcement; the report's first fix is 'decide and publicly disclose the web-indexing policy'. Report 30: the 2 → 3 cap change shipped without the listing being updated. Report 31: monthly/yearly frequency, streak display, swipe, quit-to-zero, Shortcuts, the tappable widget, 'last done' and day-start time were removed across v2 (Mar 2022) and v3.0 (27 Jan 2023) — feature removal 9.4% of E4, an update blamed for a regression 8.4%; the legacy Premium stopped being recognised in Apr 2023 with no notice. Report 33: Habitify X (~27 Aug 2020) removed time logs, yearly stats, CSV export, swipe, 'N per week', Shortcuts and the Watch app with 'no migration path' — 149 reviews in nine weeks, 42 UPDATE-. Report 36: the Oct 2023 widget gate was read as a bug for months ('the widget app has not been working properly … says that I have to unlock it') and the 2026 cap as 'extremely bugged. I cannot add a second habit'. Report 43: 'pause a habit' vanished in the 2026 update (2★) and 'every 2/3 weeks' schedules silently became weekly after the redesign (4★). Report 46: dark mode 'moved behind a paywall' in a June 2024 update ('Immediate deletion'). Report 47: the May 2024 changes arrived unannounced and the word reviewers use is 改悪 ('made worse', 23 reviews at mean 1.39); the listing still says 'unlimited task registration' while reviewers report a cap of 6 — the report cannot resolve which is current. Report 48: the 2015 conversion was announced as grandfathering prior purchasers and 14 say it was not honoured ('bait and switch', 'SCAM', 'Rent what you've paid for'); the cap reductions of 2018–20 arrived unannounced and were discovered by users deleting a tracker and finding the slot gone (23, mean 2.22). Report 50: the 5 → 3 cap cut reached users without notice — four say they were not told the terms before installing, and the angriest reviews are from people who lost capacity they already had. Report 55: the June 2018 switch from a $4.99 one-time unlock to $19/yr shipped with a release note that said only 'Changes'. Report 57: none of the tier changes was announced — 'there wasn't even an announcement — what's going on?' — F7: an in-app changelog before the next tier change. Report 59 (Tappsk): the January-2021 update capped the free tier at 20 tasks (reviewers also report 10, 3 and '2 habits, 2 recurring'), removed free habits for some ('раньше можно было использовать две, а теперь НИ ОДНОЙ' — before two, now NONE) and simultaneously stopped recognising existing purchases — MON_FREE_CUT 103 (80 in 2021-01→04), BUG_PURCHASE 57 in the era (its peak), any price objection 10.1% of the era (its peak), churn 2.2% (peak), the lowest era mean after launch (4.50★), the second most-voted review in the corpus (94 votes); the developer's reply ('it is 50') did not match the app ('only 20 are available'). Report 65 (Rabit): three model changes in six years each visible in the era means — free 4.49 → optional premium 4.19 → ads + cap 2.98 → notification outage 2.98; the E2 → E3 drop of 1.21 stars coincides exactly with ads plus the cap. Report 67 (Habio): 'I downloaded this app based on the pinned review that stated it had a free version' — the free tier disappeared in 2022 (hard wall 17.74% of that era) while older reviews still said free.

title: Widget variants and customisation as the paid layer
statement: Base single-counter widget free forever; multi-counter widgets, custom art, progress rings, reset-from-widget can be paid — and were report 3's #1 purchase trigger. Report 30 (counter-evidence): a paid widget in a capped tracker lost a user to a competitor with a free widget and is the only named paid feature besides more habits; the report proposes testing widget free vs paid as an acquisition driver. Report 36: once widgets were paid, widget-improvement demand peaked (titles, colours, streak display, interactivity) — 'now that widgets cost money, people want them to do more'. Report 41: widgets are icon-only — 'When you have +10 habits, one habit widget with only icon and no clue to remembering the habit is a pain'; one runs a competitor alongside for text labels (8 requests); widget icons 'Make them bigger and it is 5 stars!'. Report 43: per-habit notification sounds are 'too few' — 'hearing the same sound for every habit… mentally makes me mush all my tasks together'; 'you can't use the notification or ringtone sounds from your iPhone'; a snooze wanted (16, mean 3.94). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): the large heat-map widget is the only named purchase trigger in the corpus ('I bought the paid version of the app (single month), because I wanted to use the larger widget showing the entire heat map and i absolutely love it') and the credited retention mechanism ('Without it I would underestimate the progress and tend to give up… I was able to successfully track and build new habits for the first time with this app'), while a lifetime buyer's only complaint is that it is too basic ('no dark themed widget? Widget so basic? Please step it up, I just paid for lifetime access') and another wants it to surface the next unfinished habit; M3: make the widget the explicit centre of the paid offer; P2: dark theme and a next-unfinished mode — 'highest leverage per unit of work'. Report 65 (Rabit): REQ_WIDGET 43 (8.63%, mean 4.30), first asked days after iOS 14 widgets launched (Jan 2021) and still asked Aug 2025, never shipped, top theme of the 4★ band, twice as hot outside Brazil; four purchases made conditional on it — 'I'll definitely buy the lifetime plus version if you add widgets'; 'If this app had them I would 100% buy the lifetime'.

title: Goals / targets
statement: Tolerated behind the paywall (mean 4.05) and a stated purchase reason. Report 25: a layer of long-term goals sitting above habits is requested by very satisfied users (7, mean 4.71). Report 41: yearly / long-horizon goals requested by 6. Report 48: numeric Target (a number by a date) and Project (milestones, %) trackers with a pace line and projected completion date are what 485 reviewers switched for; goal pacing praised by 56 at 4.97 — see [[C265]]. Report 59 (Tappsk): REQ_GOALS 52 (4.73★).

title: A free trial must be a real trial
statement: It must apply to whichever plan the user picks, and the confirmation must show the exact charge date and amount; a trial that bills at once produced 789 reviews at mean 1.35 in report 4 and must be verified per storefront (Brazil ran 7–11× the global rate). Report 10: 149 users believe they were charged at trial START (mean 1.79) and trial length varied between 2 and 7 days across users. Report 12: a 3-day trial introduced around 2024 shows as subscribed but 'doesn't move past the subscription screen' — the complaint changed shape from 'there is no trial' to 'the trial doesn't work'. Report 13: a trial that cannot start without first authorising a subscription, defaulting to the most expensive annual tier, produced 1,102 auto-charge reviews at mean 1.20 (999 one-star) — the single most damaging mechanic in a 19,850-review corpus; involuntary-charge reviews equalled voluntary-purchase reviews 1:1. Report 18: trials that converted immediately ('in my case there was no free period'; asked for monthly, charged annual; frozen since minute 10, charged a full year) in KR, JP, TW, ID, BR and DE; trial length shrank from 3 weeks to 7 days to 2–3-day variants. Report 19: a 'free trial' that charged (10 of 105) — '$45 for the initial trial', 'free 7 days charged trial' — with the price hidden at decision time and no renewal warning; four non-payers refused precisely because there was no way to try first. Report 24: the 'free trial' charges a 'pay what you can' set-up fee ($1 / $10 / $16.41) on a donation-style screen, classed in the terms as non-refundable — 506 reviews (1.16%, mean 1.136) say the trial was not free and 100 name the fee mechanism (mean 1.110). Report 25: the trial is a net-negative topic (21, mean 2.62, 10 1★) — card required up front, charged inside the window ('it says cost 0 in the trial selector and they charged me 1,500 pesos'), renewal into the wrong plan, and uncertainty about whether cancelling is possible; billing disputes stepped up ~5× after 2024 (0.8% → 3.9%). Report 26: a '3-day free trial' that charges immediately (incl. a lifetime tier charged instantly with no trial disclosed), cancelled before trial end and charged anyway, renewal with no notice — 23 disputes at mean 1.48, the lowest-rated theme in the corpus, and the source of the only accusations of deception ('Scam company. Impossible to cancel and tricks you into renewing'; 'Estafadores'). Report 30: no trial at all, so an annual charge is the first real use. Report 31: a 'free trial' that was actually a paid first year ('told I would be getting one year, 365 days free … now only … a month'), a trial renewing into the most expensive plan, and a trial not visible in iOS subscriptions. Report 33: 2025–26 trials converted to an annual charge unexpectedly ('I signed up for a free trial and somehow got converted to paid'; 'a 7- or 14-day trial, then charged a full year of Pro'). Report 46: two charged on day one of a 7-day trial ('Offerred 7 day trial, but I got charged the same day'); after a trial ends the extra habits are locked, not archivable ('I can't delete them… it falsifies the statistics') — the report's #8: let the user choose which 3 stay and archive the rest. Report 47: no refund requests, but one user cancelled after discovering a half-year plan they did not remember agreeing to ('契約した覚えがないので、もしかしたら無料期間を忘れたのかもしれない。気をつけた方がいいです', 1★, Jan 2026); the fix: a clear notice before a trial converts. Report 48: trial terms 26 (1.65) — charged the full year at the start of a 7-day trial; charged twice after cancelling before the trial ended; refund requests concentrate in 2019+ trial and auto-renew disputes. Report 49: 'I signed up for the 1 week free trial and was immediately charged AU$17.98'; 'immediately charged for one year. It does not show up in your Apple subscriptions and there is no way to cancel your trial!'; cancelled a day early and still charged $50; 'a loop so you can not use the app if you don't accept the free trial'; a 7-day trial only on the annual plan billed €14.99 immediately. Report 50: 'I was charged $30 before my free trial was up'; 'They absolutely DONT SEND THE REMINDER when the trial is about to finish… they charge you automatically the whole year'. Report 53: 7-day trials that several reviewers say billed a full year; M4: charge date and amount on the trial screen and a reminder 24 hours before conversion. Report 55: charged after a trial; a trial that can't be cancelled (PAY_TRIAL 8, 2.12). Report 59 (Tappsk): the 7-day trial that charged immediately or on day six is the largest single source of 1★ reviews across eight years — MON_AUTO_CHARGE 229 (1.51%, mean 1.82★) carries 163 of the 674 1★ (24.2%), co-occurs with MON_TRIAL 111 and MON_REFUND 113; a year's fee (999 ₽ named 73 times) taken at once ('при выборе бесплатной недели сразу списали деньги за год'; '«7 дней бесплатно», а сами втихую списываете на 6 день' — you quietly charge on day 6), charges after deletion ('Списывают деньги, даже если приложение удалено'), peaked 2.9% of 2020 and still 1.2% of 2024–26; the fix list: no charge before day 7, a visible countdown, one-tap cancel inside the app, a confirmation e-mail with the renewal date; a card-required trial is itself a barrier ('полная версия в пробном периоде требует привязки карты'). Report 60 (Mindway): three distinct trial failures from three users — a $0.99 paid trial converting to $39.99 within hours ('with NO EXCEPTIONS OF A REFUND'), a '3 day free trial' that billed a week after cancelling on day two (a 4★ that would otherwise be 5★), and no trial offered at all before purchase ('I'm just out the money now') — 'a flow problem, not three user errors'; F2: audit the trial-to-charge flow end to end. Report 64 (Critique AI): a 3-day trial that requires card details up front, charges the full year on expiry without warning ('it didn't let me know that it was over so it took my money'), cannot be cancelled in-app, and is not reached at all by others — PAY_TRIAL 26 (6.21%, mean 1.58), persistent across 17 months; 3 days cannot test a habit product ('Getting into stuff like this will take at least a month to stick'); M4: 14 days, no card. Report 65 (Rabit): a 7-day trial reported charging the monthly price at once ('isso é propaganda enganosa'), never starting (the subscribe button spins), charging R$199.90 after the app was deleted, and ending free use on day two (PAY_TRIAL_BAD 5); M3: 'the highest-trust-cost surface in the product'. Report 67 (Habio): a $1 / €1 / £1 3-day paid trial (MON_TRIAL_1DOLLAR 148) converting to $40+ plans — MON_TRIAL_CHARGE 173 (8.43%, mean 1.03): 'Factually their 3 days trial for 1,00 Euro is actually a 2 two days trial'; MON_PRICE_MISMATCH 55 charged more than shown; 'they've also never mentioned in their add that the currency is not in AUD'.

title: An obvious 'continue free' path on the paywall — the free/paid boundary must be legible
statement: Users wrote 75 reviews teaching each other where the hidden X was while 1,903 said the app was paid-only; legibility of what is free is a rating decision. Report 24: a real free tier (~3–4 habits, coaching locked) exists behind a small 'X' or 'skip' on the trial splash and is hard to find; 77 reviews (mean 4.442) call it generous once found. Report 34: the wall arrives at habit #3 during setup — 'I added 2, tried to add the third and was prompted to pay'. Report 48: 48 reviews (mean 1.65, rising 0.49% → 2.05% of E5) invested setup effort before meeting an undisclosed 3-tracker wall — 'I lost my time encoding 3 trackers for nothing'; 'Wish i knew before i downloaded and set everything up' — the report's fix #1: disclose the limit on the listing and at first run, 'the cheapest 1★ in the corpus to eliminate… about the surprise, not the price'. Report 49: no 'continue free' path exists at all — 256 say the only free thing is the questionnaire and its result. Report 50: a pop-up 'insisting I pay for premium every time I open the app… it stops me from just being able to use the app' (GB, 1★) — the only report of the paywall obstructing ongoing free use; 'it takes 15 Seconds to ask you for 5,99 every month' (DE). Report 52: 2026 onboarding requires picking 5 habits and choosing a 3-day trial; reviewers ask to skip both and for a visible back control on every paywall screen (M6). Report 54: 'told to upgrade, no way to' (1). Report 59 (Tappsk): paywall surprise 64 at 1.70★ — the lowest-rated monetization code — from users who thought the app was free. Report 64 (Critique AI): with no free tier the 'continue' path is only a dismiss control, and a tenth of the corpus cannot find it — 'you are stuck In the buy screen. You literally can't do anything but just stare at it'.

title: No long quiz before the price; show the price up front
statement: A 10–20 minute quiz followed by a paywall turns a price objection into anger (mean 1.98, 71.9% 1–2★); 'lower the yearly price a bit and show it at the very beginning'. Report 24: a large share of buyers take the questionnaire in a web browser and enter payment details before ever opening the app; onboarding-too-long runs at mean 1.600. Report 42: ~15–30 unskippable setup screens before the price, with a rating prompt inside them (3 reviews, all 1★, never used the app). Report 49 (the strongest case): a 10–20 minute questionnaire plus a pledge before a hard paywall — onboarding-before-price 156 (12.66%, mean 1.15, the lowest of any theme above 20; 140 of 156 at 1★); many do not object to paying, only to the sequence ('they ask for tons of personal stuff before displaying the price wall instead of after'; '30分かけて設定したのに…初めに言って欲しい'), identical in 15+ languages; the never-used cohort (331) grew to 33.1% of the latest era; all 40 'scam' accusations are about this payment experience; the report's fix #1: 'A price shown on the first screen converts a one-star review into a non-download.' Report 60 (Mindway): the sequence ad → onboarding questionnaire → price is what the two ad-sourced reviewers (both 1★) and the scam accusers describe — 'Put the price next to your product in the App Store. Its the only correct way to go about selling a product above board'. Report 64 (Critique AI): PAY_QUIZWALL 23 (5.49%, mean 1.35) — a long survey, a physique photo and an account, then the price: 'why the need to do a survey if it isn't free? couldn't it be mentioned before the survey?'; rose from 3.2% to 8.7% in the latest quarter; M1: disclose the price before the quiz — 'Zero engineering cost, zero revenue cost'. Report 67 (Habio): the quiz doubles as the sales funnel — NEG_ONBOARD_LONG 29 ('so we don't waste our time filling up a bunch of useless data in the first place'), paid on the web before installing.

title: In-app cancellation
statement: Cancel-by-email with no reply converts recoverable disputes into permanent 1★, legal threats and denied refunds. Report 13: in Korea 24.7% of reviews say they cannot cancel and two reviewers published how-to-cancel guides for other users; an in-app 'Manage subscription' link would address a quarter of that storefront's reviews. Report 19: cancellation required email rather than a button, used bold 'stay' and small 'cancel' buttons, ~10 confirmation steps, was split across two subscriptions, and locked the user out of the account mid-flow; 24 of 105 (22.86%) described it and three asked simply for a cancel button inside the app. Report 20: refund requests ignored in Feb 2021 (Apple refunded where the developer would not), 'cannot cancel' reports 2022–2025 with one alleging an FTC-transparency breach, and accidental Touch-ID purchases during onboarding; 125 reviews at mean 1.28. Report 24: cannot find or complete cancellation 1,146 (2.64%, mean 1.115, 0.3% 5★) because the subscription lives on the developer's website; move billing into IAP or surface the web subscription in-app with one-tap cancel. Report 25: two reviewers could not find subscription settings in the app at all — 'I looked for five minutes… Is that even legal?' Report 26: two reviewers could not find any way to unsubscribe; 'well hidden there is a way to contact support… but the button is not enabled'. Report 30: an accidental subscription with no route to a refund (MX, 1★) — the reviewer blames the app even where the flow is Apple's. Report 31: 66 cannot cancel / charged after cancelling (mean 1.39, mostly E4) — no subscription found in iOS Settings; 'cancelled … TWICE and I'm still being charged'; put 'Manage subscription' in the app. Report 33: web-billed (Paddle) subscriptions had no in-app cancel ('payments … through a third party and there's no unsubscribe button'), 13 cannot-cancel reviews at mean 1.62; a deleted account was still charged; cancelling a renewal after a trial ended current access — show renewal date, price and a cancel link for every billing channel, and keep access through the paid period. Report 36: 'Dark pattern: roach motel … Clicking on link In email returns Cannot cancel subscription' (1★). Report 41: 'I would like to unsubscribe and delete the app but there are no means to do that via the app'. Report 42: two cancelled; one could not find how to refund; 'Don't fall for the free-trial trap.. you won't get a refund even if you cancel two minutes after'. Report 43 (counter-case): a one-time purchase produced zero cancellation complaints; the only refund refusal was inside the EU 14-day withdrawal window. Report 46: six cancellations threatened or described, one on the last day of the trial after a developer reply; 'I just cancelled the subscription. That's $29 down the drain'. Report 48: cancellation difficulty 4 (1.25), retained as compliance-adjacent. Report 55: M4 — disclose cap, trial length, annual price and how to cancel inside the app. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_CANCEL_TROUBLE 73 (1.0% of the latest era, its peak) — the subscription is hard to find and cancel, and the direct-card route for Russian users has no cancellation at all because App Store subscription management no longer shows the app ('В Айфоне в подписках вас у меня нет' — you are not in my iPhone subscriptions, 1★); a cancellation that works without the App Store and stops retries after deletion is an immediate fix. Report 60 (Mindway): M_CANCEL_DIFFICULTY 4 (mean 1.00) plus one who cancelled and was charged anyway — 'There is no way to cancel'; 'Please help me unsubscribe'; 'I am getting no help and stopping the subscription'; an AU reviewer still asking how to cancel 14 months after the first report; F1: make cancellation one tap from the main screen and confirm it in writing — 'the cheapest star recovery available' and 'the highest-severity item in the report'. Report 65 (Rabit): 'Comprei por engano e não consigo cancelar, não tem suporte, não tem orientação como faço?' (PAY_CANCEL 3); M4. Report 67 (Habio): MON_CANCEL 361 (17.60%, mean 1.01) and MON_CHARGED_AFTER 351 (17.11%) — an in-app cancellation confirmation screen with no persistent cancelled status, an emailed cancellation link that expires in 20 minutes, 'email not found' when cancelling, deleting the app believed to cancel (CHURN_DELETE 66); §8.1: every subscription visible in app settings with status, next charge date and amount, one-tap cancel with an on-screen and emailed confirmation, an emailed request effective at receipt.

title: One stable, disclosed price — no discount wheels
statement: Users in the same market reported $19.99–$59.99 for the same thing; that inconsistency is what 'scam' language attaches to; a rigged or broken gimmick makes it worse. Report 10: household members quoted $34.99 vs $41.99 on the same day, support could not explain a $19.99–$99.99 range — perceived as discriminatory pricing inside families. Report 18: four to five concurrently live annual prices per storefront produced 'I paid, then it showed me a cheaper price' — charged ₩33,000 and ₩25,000 both, '40% off' banners not honoured, ¥2,900 checkout billed ¥4,150 — and fraud accusations in six languages; Taiwan (2.60★) was almost entirely this; a Dutch user watched the displayed price move 'from over 200 to 68 to 19.90'. Report 20: the app advertised $5.99 / 499₽ / 85%-off and charged $39.99 / 3,150₽ — 28 reports across eight storefronts, Dec 2021 → Apr 2025; below threshold on volume, a consumer-protection exposure by nature. Report 23: a weak cluster (7, 0.10%) says the price shown and the amount debited differed (au, ru, tr, mx) — most likely tax or currency conversion, but a recurring, avoidable trust event. Report 24: annual, quarterly, 'bimonthly', monthly and weekly cycles at overlapping prices ('this page says $59 for a year… it's $40 billed every three months'), different prices on different screens, and a cancel flow that discounts $19.99 → $12.99 → $5 → $2/month; the inconsistency of what users believe they bought is the direct cause of 'charged twice' reports. Report 25: $24.99 shown and $42 charged; €29.99 lifetime followed by two further €6.99 charges; a German purchase sheet showing no price at all; Mexican reviewers unable to tell whether the price is pesos or dollars (four say so in the review) — show the local currency unambiguously and confirm displayed equals charged. Report 30: two yearly SKUs at different prices ($44.99 and $29.99) beside a $59.99 Lifetime produced 'they tell you the plan is for life and it's only for a year'; the monthly option could not be bought ('it charges for a year'). Report 31: reviewers quote 60+ price points across 15 currencies; a 'Christmas' $11.99 → $39.99, perpetual 72-hour countdowns that reset, 83–90% off banners and $399 anchors — and 69 say the advertised price was not the charged price. Report 33: charged more than shown in ~6 cases (¥4,900 → ¥5,150; $39.99 → $48.97; monthly chosen, annual charged). Report 49: a countdown discount that does not apply (an 80% notification resolving to 70%) and 'limited time offers' that tipped purchases (misleading checkout 17). Report 52: price seen as unstable — ¥18 / ¥28 / ¥88 reported in the same months, a ¥12 buyer finding lifetime at ¥98. Report 53: a perpetual 'limited-time' discount offer (2023–26) reads as deception rather than a deal. Report 59 (Tappsk): the discount that sells the lifetime unlock also generates disclosure complaints — 'Kurz nach dem Kauf wurde der Preis durch einen Zufallsgenerator reduziert' (shortly after the purchase the price was reduced by a random generator); the same lifetime named at 449 ₽ and 2,500 ₽ within a year; offers that vanish ('Предложение куда-то исчезло и желание купить пропало') and a buy button that is inactive; the report's fix: one price per region and no re-pricing within days of a purchase — a predictable seasonal sale rather than random rotation reconciles the two findings ([[C003]]). Report 64 (Critique AI): the same year quoted as $40, £40, £24, 40–45€, $39.99, $45, $50, $60, $100, $192, $200 and ₦69,900, plus weekly and monthly SKUs and an exit discount (£2.08/mo advertised, £24/yr charged) — PAY_SCAM 21 (5.01%, mean 1.05). Report 67 (Habio): 13 price points from $0.49 to $79.99 in the US listing, charges above the price shown (55), and currency not disclosed ('never mentioned in their add that the currency is not in AUD').

title: Ads must match the app
statement: Advertised features that are absent create a 'scam' cohort before first open (0.62%, mean 2.42).

title: Content library (workouts, meditation, sleep, journal) as the paid layer
statement: Gives a routine app something to sell beyond the core loop and separates it from 'a fancy Reminders list'. Report 13 (contested): Challenges/Explore content tabs added in 2020 drew 'please let me hide them… I will not pay for an app that is 50% useless content'; nobody in 19,850 reviews asked for content, coaching or AI. Report 24: three narrated coaching pieces a day, multi-week Journeys, meditations, a deep-work ritual, music and soundscapes are what paying users value (coaching praised 6,095, 14.02%, mean 4.483; life-changing 4,468, mean 4.799); repetitive content 103 (mean 2.660); the content must be saveable and replayable. Report 26: background music and nature sounds (559, 14.57%, mean 4.68), daily quotes (58, mean 4.74), themes, backgrounds, seasons, app icons and extra gardens are the content layer — partly free, more paid. Report 46: a free Learn tab (articles, videos, James Clear material) and 7-day e-mail course were praised as 'like a life changing book' by early users (107, mean 4.82) and faded 11.02% → 3.30% as the audience turned mobile; English-only; the report's E6 resurfaces it after day 14. Report 48: a free goal-setting course / handbook is credited by 27–29 reviewers (4.93) and several convert from it — a companion-content funnel rather than a paid layer. Report 67 (Habio): articles, courses and quotes criticised far more than praised (57 vs 12 non-seeded) — 'all the typos and language errors'; a therapist 'would never recommend for a client'; 'essentially charging 1 euro per page'; NEG_SHALLOW 102 'You literally pay to track your own habits'.

title: Mascot / companion character
statement: Small, pure praise in report 4; category norm in pet-style apps. Report 10: the pet is the causal story users tell — 'I will do for the bird what I will not do for myself' — at 70,041-review scale (companion 1,309, cute design 10,074); the same attachment makes data loss feel like bereavement. Report 28: the rabbit is the emotional object — 40 (4.87%, mean 4.15) describe attachment ('I named him Paul'; 'so I dont abandon my rabbit child'), the room-cleaning loop is 'an externalised progress bar with an emotional stake' (60, mean 4.25), 244 (29.72%) describe concrete behaviour change ('made me lose 80 pounds'; 'I take my iron pill just to check it off'); the cute art survives even in 12 of 84 one-star reviews; a bug that made the rabbit drift off-screen when tapped ('I WAS TAPPING ON THE BUNNY AND IT FLEW AWAY') drew 12 reports; users want to pet and feed it (9). Report 49: a character / hero mode with equipment, loot and battles shipped late 2025, cut 'just a checklist' to 1.0% of E4 and immediately generated its own bug theme (5). Report 54: an avocado mascot with facial expressions (9, 4.78 — 'the little avocado characters really motivate me'). Report 60 (Mindway): 'LOVED THE SLIMY MASCOT' (one 5★); the cute / bubbly tone draws one 2★ dissent — n=1 each way.

title: Preset routines / templates / programs
statement: Paywalled in report 4 with little complaint. Report 24: multi-week guided programmes ('Journeys' as a mountain map) and the deep-work ritual are the paid layer and the stated renewal reasons. Report 50: habit templates / suggestions at setup exist; recurring journal templates promised by the listing are still missing ('I hope vote templates are coming as it promises'). Report 60 (Mindway): preset routine packs (self-care, hair care, exercise, chores, hydration) and a self-care guide are the praised entry point (P_CONTENT_PACKS 5, 4.80★: 'having a guide to which to refer'; 'rehberle çok yardım ettiler') and the inferred paid asset — but packs loaded by default are also a clean-up burden ('otherwise you would spend all day deleting tasks', a payer; 'It is overwhelming to set up tasks in the beginning'); E6: a bulk-remove-pack control and a first-run 'pick one of three ready-made days'; custom task creation is limited or gated and is the most-requested capability ('I wish there was a way to personalize or make my own').

title: Redesigns must not regress layout — ship a density / text-size option or an opt-out
statement: A compact-list redesign produced a dated backlash (report 7) while a Liquid Glass refresh drew none (report 8); layout regressions hit neurodivergent users hardest (report 4); a Feb 2024 redesign and continuous UI churn drew a backlash cluster (report 10). Report 23: a list view or density control (45, 0.62%) must be opt-in — 8.9% of that theme's reviews are 1★ precisely because the app changed on them; the v3.0 feature expansion split reviewers the same week. Report 25: complexity is both the top praise and a top complaint (126 vs 27; 65 vs 'too many icons to pick from') — any simplification must be opt-in. Report 27: do not remove features in updates without an opt-out — restore the full-year grid as a selectable view and the 365-dot view as a choice. Report 28: UI bloat / update regression 6 (0.73%, mean 2.50); 'Seems like every update just brings more paywall and more forced advertisements'. Report 30: add a compact list density — rows too large once habit count grows. Report 36: a 2026 layout / scaling regression — font clipped on iPhone SE3, schedule options overflowing on iPhone 13 Plus / iOS 26.2 at first run (an immediate uninstall), an overview 'zoomed in like it was designed for desktop' — 4 of 6 UIBUG records in E5. Report 43: the Oct 2025 redesign split reviewers 4 positive / 7 negative — the negatives are a blocking journal-on-skip modal with no opt-out ('should have option to TURN OFF… the pop up is obscured by my keyboard'), a calendar header 'that takes up too much space', a removed pause button, a scheduling regression and three data losses at the moment the UI changed; the positives are reordering and the restructured routine screen; the report proposes an opt-in theme switch and a one-time 'what changed' screen instead of forced change. Report 48: the 2021 history-logging redesign is the one self-inflicted UX wound (see [[C264]]); 62 call the UI dated but the report advises against redesign for novelty. Report 50: repeated UI redesigns drew three long-term US users in five weeks (Jan–Feb 2025, all churn risk) — 'it's also counter intuitive to create an app about routine and habits and make your users keep adjusting to new layouts'; 'this was perfect as it was when I first downloaded it!… now it's messy' — not repeated in 19 months; 'do not redesign the UI again without a migration path'. Report 52: redesign complaints arrive in release bursts — Oct 2020 widgets (26), Jun 2021 a Success / Pending / Fail sheet on every check-in (29), Sep–Dec 2024 compressed layout (31), Feb–Apr 2026 AI note titles (20), Aug 2026 red focus page (12) — each about losing speed or calm, not a feature; a 5★ reviewer proposes decoupling front-end style from feature iteration; the report's R1: redesigns behind a setting for at least one release. Report 54: §8.5 'Do not redesign' — 128 praise the design and no 1★ criticises it.

title: Sequential routine timer with spoken next step and live finish-time estimate
statement: Report 5's product thesis: removes the need to hold a schedule in working memory and says continuously whether you are still on time; 162 reviewers report they stopped being late. The voice needs an off switch. Report 17: a timeline-first day scheduler that 'queues up duties as the time approaches' was called irreplaceable by nearly a quarter of its reviewers and helped one with time blindness; a paying user proposed backward scheduling from a fixed anchor (work out the latest start for a pre-sleep sequence). Report 18: a per-bundle routine timer (46 reviews, 4.37★) converted — one user set every routine to one minute purely to defeat activation energy 'and then I actually started???'; Japan and the US rated it high-priority and asked for it on the Watch and in the widget, and Japanese users uniquely asked for auto-advancing timers. Report 50: stopwatch and countdown for duration habits; Pomodoro / focus music requested (2).

title: Untimed / checklist mode as a per-routine toggle
statement: A real minority of the ADHD audience finds a mandatory timer anxiety-inducing; the fix is an option per routine, not a separate object.

title: Background battery and thermals
statement: A background timer that drains 30–90% of daily battery and heats the device is report 5's worst non-billing theme (mean 2.94) and loses subscribers who otherwise love the app.

title: Notifications are few and finely user-controllable — per-type settings, escalation opt-in, never spammy and never silently retuned
statement: Some users depend on an un-dismissable alarm, others are driven out by it; a global default serves both badly; removing it broke wake-ups for loyal subscribers. Report 24: all-or-nothing notification settings make users disable everything (744, 1.71%); per-type control is the fix. [Merged from C253: Report 36: notification restraint is praised by 12 (2.22%, mean 4.67) and framed as the reason people switched — 'fine-tuned control over the notifications you receive — probably the #1 reason I've deleted other habit apps was that they spammed me with a billion distracting notifications' (13967987039); a US talking point (3.97% vs 0.69% non-US). More / snoozable reminders are also requested (7) — make any escalation opt-in so the restraint is not lost. Report 43 (counter-case): the nag loop is the differentiator — user-controlled frequency ('as often as you want') is what makes heavy notification acceptable; one review in 638 finds it excessive. Report 46: a daily e-mail at exactly 12 with a new sender address each time (3, mean 1.67, 2020–23) was made switchable ('You can turn them off if you don't like it'). Report 48: notification overload 12 (2.33) against 224 reminder praise — custom text and per-tracker control keep the ratio stable. Report 50: per-habit reminders praised by 10 (4.90); notifications broken on the new Watch app (1).] Report 53: suppress reminders once the habit or its Health goal is met ('it should know based on my steps being tracked that I've met the goal'), several clock times per habit, snooze from the notification (R1); a burst of 10–15 notifications at 8 am ('64 notifications in just a few days'). Report 55: reminders only for undone habits, several per habit (R4).

merged_from.title: Notification restraint — few, finely controllable notifications keep the users that spammy rivals lose
merged_from.note: C253 (reports 36, 43, 46, 48: restraint and fine control are why users switched; heavy nagging is accepted only when the user sets the frequency) is the same decision as C123 (reports 5, 7, 24: escalation must be user-configurable; all-or-nothing settings make users disable everything)

title: Never show ads or upsells to anyone holding an active or historical entitlement — including cross-promotion of sibling apps
statement: Including reward-gated features like streak savers; a 30-second unskippable ad to a payer is the most reliable way to turn an advocate into a 1★. Report 10: a sponsored movie tie-in as the monthly event drew 'I am paying to be advertised to' from multi-year subscribers (mean 3.09, 8× over-represented among payers) after 857 reviews had praised the app for being ad-free. Report 18: 'A pro member should be a pro member regardless of whether they are paying monthly or yearly' — monthly subscribers nagged daily to go annual, and a 'buy the next term' screen that blocked the app entirely. Report 24: in-app advertising of the developer's own sister apps inside paid accounts — 308 reviews, mean 1.932, only 14.6% 4–5★, the lowest satisfied-share of any UX theme ('I'm on the purchased version… I don't want to see adds'); rose 0.11% → 2.03% across eras. Report 28: 'I paid 10$ to remove ads but I still get ads'; a 5★ 'purchased the full version and I am still getting ads' — and even after buying no-ads there is still a prompt to double carrots by watching an ad after every level. Report 31: the promotional banner hid a habit even for paid users (Dec 2020). Report 50: no ads at any tier (5 confirm). [Merged from C248: Report 31: 314 reviews (6.05%, mean 1.57) were upsold after paying — 197 of 625 explicit payers (31.5%) — rising 0.3% (E1) → 12.1% (E4): 'It's not encouraging customer loyalty!!'; mood-disorder tracking interrupted by the offer; a banner in Dec 2020 hid the bottom habit even for paid users. The report's first upsell rule: suppress every offer for any past or present entitlement, and test every-launch vs weekly vs never-for-past-payers on conversion, D30 retention and 1★ rate. Report 33: cross-promotion ads for the developer's other apps (Nirow, Poly) shown to lifetime payers — 'False advertisement – Still get ads with lifetime premium'; a premium user shown notices: 'No. deal with it'; 'I wish the upgrade button would disappear when you buy premium' — 14 + 12 reviews.] Report 52: 40 paying reviewers (including legacy lifetime and ¥8 ad-free buyers) still saw ads — 'I bought lifetime membership before… an ugly ad pops up at every check-in'; F2: verify the entitlement before rendering the first ad. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'never show the lifetime buyer a subscription paywall' is an immediate fix — an app that sells lifetime, annual and monthly SKUs plus a 7-day trial side by side let a subscription charge reach lifetime owners ('купил полную версию на всегда за 1500 тыс, сегодня списалось 999 рублей за подписку' — bought forever for 1,500; today 999 ₽ taken for a subscription); lifetime buyers carry the highest problem lifts among purchasers (MON_PAID_TWICE 8.89×, BUG_PURCHASE 8.43×, SUP_NONE 6.09×) even though the one-time option is praised 93 times against 23 subscription objections. Report 64 (Critique AI): a subscriber reports seeing ads while paying £40/yr (4★) — 'the worst of both models'; F6, verify before acting. Report 65 (Rabit): 'I have ads on a paid subscription- I want a refund'; 'despite buying a premium subscription, I'm still being asked every time I'm in the app to upgrade to premium'.

merged_from.title: Never show an upsell to anyone holding an active or historical entitlement
merged_from.note: C248 (reports 31, 33, 47: upsells and cross-promotion shown to payers and lifetime buyers; a rating prompt shown to payers) and C127 (reports 5, 10, 18, 24, 28, 50: ads, sponsored events and renewal nags shown to subscribers) are one rule: a paying user sees no monetisation interruption

title: Use the lead-user market as the beta cohort
statement: Report 5's home market (Korea) carries the deepest engineering feedback and most detailed feature specs — and uses the review page as a support desk.

title: No default-on social feed in a personal tool
statement: Unwanted by a vocal minority, and a child-safety liability when minors and adults share a feed on a 17+ app. Report 49: social / guild features requested by only 2 — the community lives in Discord. Report 55: a per-habit forum is a support network for most (COMM_GOOD 31, 4.90) but clutter, a one-topic feed and anonymous shaming for some (COMM_NEG 8); R7: topic filters and blocking of shaming replies. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): no review asks for sharing, friends, leaderboards or accountability partners — §8.5: do not chase the 'accountability' positioning with social features.

title: Do not sell in a storefront where the app cannot function
statement: Seven years of 'will not open' from mainland China, with users charged for an app that shows 'no network'. Report 9: in Russia 46% of reviews say the app loads for minutes or only works over a VPN, while 32% of Russian reviewers had paid. Report 33: a mandatory account backend unreachable from mainland China made the app unusable there for eight years — 173 reviews (4.39%; 57.8% of China; 79 of its 101 1★), 18 payers who could not use or restore what they bought (328 RMB lifetime, refunds refused), and an App Store 'Today' feature in Dec 2018 that sent 68 Chinese users into a registration failure ('can't register — and you recommended it on the home page?'); China was lost on reachability, not fit — reviewers praised the design and localisation and asked to pay ('I'd pay 188 RMB lifetime if you fixed the server'). Report 47: registration and login fail from mainland China — 6 of 8 login failures are Chinese ('好像需要vpn'), consistent with a blocked backend; China 32 reviews at mean 4.28 otherwise.

title: Gate on capability, not on quantity
statement: A quantity cap set above the point of core value is noticed, tolerated and does not convert; move the wall to analytics, sync, Watch, widgets, icons, family sharing. See Research Reports/Feature Gating vs Quantity.md. Report 6 contests the 'icons' part: the listing sold Premium on themes and icons and zero of 44 reviewers mentioned them. Report 18: users who paid said the paid tier 'adds nothing, it only removes limits' — 'not so much an amazing paid service as being forced to pay because the basics were cut'; the corpus's own purchase-condition backlog (export, trend statistics, routine modes, timer with time tracking, Watch parity, themes, web/Mac) is entirely additive capability. Report 20: after the conversion the paid layer was colours, dark mode, extended notifications, manual backup and a non-functional widget above a 3-habit cap — the cap sat below the threshold of usefulness and the paid depth did not deliver. Report 24: the free tier gates coaching content (the product's value) at ~3–4 habits; the constraint that makes the product work is pacing, not a paywall. Report 25: gating expanded over time from a habit count to statistics, the calendar view, group creation and — from Nov 2025 — editing the starter habits the onboarding itself created ('You need to get the premium to edit habits, even the ones they start you out with'), which turns a reduced product into a demo; weak by rate (5, mean 1.20), high by consequence. Report 26: the gate sits on quantity (habit count) and on the visible reward (growth stops at 17%) rather than on capability; extra gardens, themes and 'no wither' mode are the paid layer that users accept. Report 28: capping semantics — how important a user is allowed to say something is (1 red / 2 orange priority slots) — reads as the app overruling the user: 'it feels disingenuous to put exercise as low priority just so that i can put washing my face as medium'; 'if I put hygiene as yellow it's just wrong'; if a cap must stay, rename the tiers as labels or let users choose colours; a to-do list that earns nothing while habits do is the same class of gate. Report 30: 'Quer cobrar? Coloque algumas versões na versão pro. Não faz sentido deixar cadastrar 2 habitos' — users themselves ask to monetise depth (widget, sync, themes, history, stats) rather than habit count; a 2★ says the price is fine ('ce n'est pas cher') and still rates 2★ for the cap — the cleanest evidence the cap, not the price, produces low ratings. Report 31: the cap stayed fixed while packaging changed; buyers valued unlimited habits, reminders, charts, groups and export. Report 36 contests the widgets part: reviewers accept paid skins but reject paid widgets and habit caps — skins-only gate mean 2.77 vs widgets 2.64 vs habit cap 2.30 ('Pay for the skins. I am fine with widget restrictions but 59$?'). Report 41: the report's experiment E1 is to move the gate off habit count onto history depth, statistics, widgets, sync or customisation, measuring conversion and the 1–2★ rate together. Report 42: the report proposes moving the wall to history depth, statistics depth or reminder count rather than habit count — statistics already being the top named purchase trigger. Report 43: the report's experiment E3 is to surface the unlimited-habits unlock at a moment of demonstrated value (e.g. a 14-day streak) rather than at a count limit — the historic cap failed because it blocked before value was shown. Report 46: the report's #9 is 3 → 4 free habits — the smallest change that fixes the widget defect and answers the counter-offer without touching the habit-science defence. Report 47: every purchase trigger reviewers name is additive — accumulated value ('プレミアに入ったくらい重宝してます'), study stats, motivation photos, the AI coach, a platform bundle — and none asks to pay to restore something that used to be free; the report's rule: grow premium only through additive value. Report 48: the cap is the dominant mechanical purchase trigger ('I'll probably upgrade to the paid version soon to get more trackers') but a 3-tracker cap on a multi-goal product blocks evaluation — 'You are not allowing a certain group of people try out your app'; multiple reviewers propose the split themselves: pay once for capacity, subscribe for sync / reports. Report 49: 'just a checklist' 38 (1.68) and 'do it yourself instead' 36 (1.36) — a bare checklist reproducible by ChatGPT cannot carry the price; the level-up loop, art and community can. Report 50: 'the entire monetization surface is one number' — no reviewer reports reminders, statistics, journaling, widgets, Health or the Watch app individually gated — 'That clean one-gate model is worth protecting — and §7.2 shows what happens when the one gate moves.' Report 59 (Tappsk): the quantity gate (2 habits, 2 recurring tasks, a few reminders) is the top objection at 697 reviews while the capability gates (iCloud sync, Mac) draw a fraction of that. Report 60 (Mindway): the purest count gate in the ledger — a free tier of roughly 1–3 tasks in a daily routine planner (M_PAYWALL_BLOCK 19, 8.80%, mean 1.63, 13 of 19 at 1★, in six languages: 'I wanted to add third task to do and I can't do it without paying'; 'you need to pay money to just write some freaking habits'; 'quería organizar mi día y no puedo ya que solo por hacer algo me pide pagar'); the cap sits below the app's own minimum viable use — 'a daily routine of two tasks is not a routine, so the free tier cannot demonstrate the thing the paid tier sells' — and it is the only major theme still growing in the 2026 tail (5.33% → 8.66% → 28.57% of period); D1: gate on depth — multiple routines, history, advanced recurrence, the guided content — rather than on count. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): the price is not the problem (three unprompted 'the price is fair' against two one-line objections) — 'packaging (what the free tier contains) and delivery (whether the purchase works) are'; repackage, do not reprice. Report 65 (Rabit): §2.4 — 'Rabit monetises the number of habits. Its behavioural engine — plants, streaks, reminders — is what people love, and it rewards consistency, not volume. So the paywall taxes the axis users do not value while leaving the axis they do value free-but-broken'; a reviewer asks for exactly the inverse ('manter uma versão free com outras funcionalidades pagas mas não bloquear o uso do aplicativo'); M1: raise the cap materially and paywall depth instead of count; the paid tier 'não há grandes diferenças quando paga'.

title: Lead the store listing with what users actually love
statement: Report 6's most-loved feature (the free widget) was one bullet at the bottom of the description and its differentiators (no daily check-in, user-defined day boundary) were not marketed at all — yet they are why people switched.
