Report 23: lead with the streak mechanism and HealthKit automation, not 'to-do list' — the 'just a checklist' 1★ block is an expectation failure; award/editorial traffic (17 reviews naming the Apple Design Award, mean 2.53, the worst channel) arrives expecting 'best app'. Report 24: reviews invoking Apple or Editor's Choice average 1.085 (95.7% 1★) — 'Apple should not feature this'. Report 25: reviewers say the app feels first-party ('went back to check if the app was made by apple') and 37 switched from named competitors — the listing can lead with configurability and Apple-platform depth; measurable outcomes are claimed (45 kg lost in 8 months). Report 26: reviewers convert on the aesthetic within minutes — the listing's visuals and music are doing the selling; the German listing typo 'Gewohnheitstrinker' shows the listing is read closely. Report 27: the origin story in the listing produces 10 all-5★ developer-gratitude reviews; 'From one developer to another — nice piece of work'. Report 28: 'It's a game, not a tracker' (10, mean 2.40 — 'not at all what I was expecting'; 'the only thing I'm tracking is the amount of adds') is a listing and first-run expectation-setting problem costing 2★ reviews with no defect present. Report 31: lead with simplicity, colourful friendly design, build + quit in one list, 'N times per week' and musical sounds — 458 simplicity and 250 design praise reviews prove the brief. Report 41: an app that wins 19.63% of reviews on comparison is under-discovered ('It deserves a way higher ranking and visibility in the search results'; 'I didn't find it the first time'); the listing does not lead with the one-time option, the non-binary ring, full Apple-ecosystem coverage or no ads / no account; outcome stories (10.4% of 2026) are an unused asset. Report 47: why people give 5★ — simplicity 31.8% of the band, the filling grid 18.4%, behaviour change 13.7% ('三日坊主' no longer), design 12.6%, best-of-many 10.5%. Report 48: five-star reviews are simplicity 23.7%, flexible tracker types 13.7%, best of many 13.6%, behaviour change 8.4%; US reviewers talk about outcomes and accountability more than anyone else. Report 50: a Reddit user was acquired by a screenshot of the monthly report ('so pretty'); Instagram-ad and Reddit acquisitions are all 5★. Report 56: the listing leads with the category's language ('simplicity, clarity, and daily consistency') while users say 'actually free, no strings, nothing extra' — E5: rewrite it in the corpus's words; the US over-indexes on outcomes (25.0% vs 9.3%). Report 58: acquisition is founder-dependent and the listing does not claim the ADHD audience that found it; test copy leading with simplicity (the US already leads with simplicity, 50.0% vs 33.8%). Report 60 (Mindway): the marketable asset is concrete habit outcomes in reviewers' own words — 'makes me drink more water'; 'We will drink 4 glasses of water each day'; 'even got me to stretch'; 'This actually helps me with my chores, even though I'm seven'; 'It made me calm'; 'THIS APP MAKES ME FEEL SO MUCH BETTER' — 43 (19.91%) at 4.79★, 'Mindway's value proposition translates' across ten languages, while the listing and the paywall sell task slots. Report 64 (Critique AI): R4 — lead with what works: reported physical outcomes are the highest-rated theme (12, mean 4.92: 'It helped me lost 50 pound'; 'i'm in shape now because of this app') and social / confidence outcomes 4.75 ('you go from not talking to anyone to talking to everyone'), against 2.17 for the AI layer the name sells. Report 65 (Rabit): design is the durable asset — 106 (21.29%, mean 4.57): DES_CUTE 79 ('fofo/fofinho', hand-drawn icons) and DES_SIMPLE 58, 19.4% → 13.0% → 10.2% of eras, praised even inside 1★ and 2★ reviews; 'one of the few apps where UX was taken seriously. 5 stars for that alone' (uk). Report 67 (Habio): what survives among non-seeded reviews is the calm, soft visual design (PR_DESIGN 39, in every era, often from complainants: 'I love the look and feel of the app, it's calming') and the reflection journal — keep them (§8.11).

title: Offer both check-in tracking and auto-counting (no daily check-in) per item
statement: A counter that runs on its own until you declare a break is report 6's differentiator against every check-off tracker, and fits abstinence streaks best.

title: When an item can be tracked more than one way, make the user choose the mode at creation
statement: Report 6: users who landed in the auto-count mode by default read it as the app fabricating progress (1★), and users asked for a mode that already shipped. Report 48: a decade of setup confusion (118 at 2–3% every era) concentrates on choosing between Habit / Target / Average / Project and on ambiguous yes / no semantics for bad habits (12) — the mode choice needs teaching at creation. Report 49: advanced users given a beginner plan (13) — let users enter existing fitness so the plan starts at the right level.

title: Show the paywall at the moment of need, not on app open
statement: Surface the upgrade when the user tries the gated action (the third streak, a freeze); an upsell on every launch reads as 'begs me for money' and feeds the greed cluster. Report 13: the paywall fired 3–15 times in the first three minutes while the real purchase trigger was hitting the cap after engagement; the report's experiment: delay the first interstitial until habits are completed on three separate days. Report 25: move the paywall to after first value, not after the onboarding survey — the survey-then-paywall sequence averages 1.17. Report 36: the report recommends never showing the upsell before the first habit is created. Report 55: M2 — show the upsell at the moment a sixth habit is added, not on every launch. Report 60 (Mindway): the counter-case — a paywall shown at the moment of need is fine only if the need is real; here the 'need' is the third task of a routine, so the moment-of-need paywall is the wall itself (19 blocked at 1.63★).

title: Never let the paywall imply a capability the product lacks
statement: A buyer who paid for a feature that isn't there cancels and says 'there are free ones'; it turns a feature request into a refund cause.

title: Cache entitlements locally — never block a paid surface on a live server check
statement: Report 7: widgets that re-checked Pro against a network service showed 'Upgrade' to paying users for 15 months (100% payers, mean 2.25), 4× more often in markets with VPN/DNS filtering; render from the last-known-good receipt. Report 24: cannot log in / paid but no premium access 96 (mean 1.375, 78.1% 1★). Report 25: three independent reports in three storefronts (fr, fr, nl) that the app stopped working immediately after payment — specific enough to reproduce against the entitlement path. Report 28: 'I paid the 14.99 to unlock the full app 2 days ago and it's still saying I need to purchase it… Total scam'; carrots not delivered after 2–3 hours with restart and restore both failing. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): the clearest case — 'If I don't have internet access the app asks me to go premium, when I already bought the app. This is a headache. Can you fix this critical error!' (EC, 5★ despite the bug): a receipt check that requires the network re-paywalls exactly the offline moments (commute, flight, poor signal) when a habit app is used; I1: cache the receipt / entitlement locally and never re-paywall a verified purchaser because the network is unavailable — 'the single highest-severity non-burst finding in this report'.

title: Market the generic-tracker use case
statement: Report 7: users track medication, migraines, supplements for a pet, art-project days — any yes/no daily thing — at mean 4.91, while the listing only says 'build habits'. Report 60 (Mindway): outcomes named are hydration, workouts, tidying, stretching, getting out of bed and chores — a routine planner is used as a generic self-care tracker. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): use cases described — fitness / sport progress, hydration and step counts (unserved by a binary daily check), religious practice, daily task focus; no review describes breaking a bad habit despite the accountability subtitle.

title: Native iPad layout
statement: A stretched phone UI on iPad does more rating damage than a missing Watch app and is cheaper to fix — a layout, not a new product (report 7). Report 20: an iPad-native app never shipped (43 complaints, mean 3.33). Report 23: iPad layout not optimised 8 (0.11%). Report 24: no iPad app / lost progress on device change 257 (0.59%, mean 2.693) — progress loss on device change is the most-cited reason a multi-year user stops. Report 28: iPad / larger-screen support requested by 6 (mean 4.67); screen-fit / aspect-ratio defects 5. Report 31: native iPad layout with landscape named as the 4★ → 5★ condition ('I will gladly give 5 stars'); Malaysia 21% platform requests. Report 33: iPad layout with landscape shipped Apr 2019; widgets did not refresh on iPad for years. Report 34: 'purchased Premium version for my iPad as well' refers to the iPhone app on iPad; iPad / Mac / web requested by 8. Report 36: landscape / rotation (5) and a real iPad layout (4) requested in early 2022, fading later. Report 43: the listing claims iPad, Mac (M1+), Vision, Watch and TV. Report 46: landscape / wider view requested by 4 ('The rating will change when there's a landscape mode'). Report 47: iPad not supported — the app runs at phone size (11, 1.87%, 2019–2026: 'iPadサイズに対応しておらず、画面が小さくて見づらい'); requested in every era; an iPad layout is a stated purchase condition. Report 48: an iPad app was requested 2013–15 (9) and landscape iPad 2015–16 (8); iPad is now supported. Report 49: iPad layout reported broken (part of device incompatibility 15). Report 50: marking done 'somewhat better on iPad' than iPhone per one teardown. Report 52: iPad HD version, landscape and split view requested (380, 63.7% in 2018–20). Report 54: iPhone only — iPad / Mac requested (7, 4.57; CN 3 of 7). Report 55: iPad runs the stretched phone app (IPAD 30). Report 57: iPad-native layout requested by 21 (18 Korean) — cheaper than full sync. Report 64 (Critique AI): the app 'refuses to work on iPad' for a payer who also could not log in on a second device. Report 65 (Rabit): no iPad layout requested since Feb 2021; crashes on iPad iOS 12.5; reminders absent on iPad.

title: Surface existing features where users look
statement: Features hidden behind 'Advanced Options' or unexplained modes are rated as missing — including by payers who bought and then believed the feature absent; report 7's weekly goals, multi-habit widget and notifications. Report 19: the only constructive reviewer found the product's real asset — a web course library — by accident, because the app never linked to it; the thirteen who called the product 'just a checklist' may have been describing the 10% they were shown. Report 23: a hidden backup/restore path, and edit/delete/undo actions hidden behind gestures — 250 UI-confusion reviews (3.44%, mean 2.66, 31.6% 1★) resolve into three actions: deleting a task, editing a task, undoing a completion; a single visible Edit / Delete / Undo affordance plus in-app text would address most of them. Report 26: a calendar/statistics view shipped ~late 2024 and users still cannot find it ('the calendar could be more easily accessible, I currently have to search for it') — a cheap discoverability fix on built functionality. Report 27: streak length is not readable from the day list (a full interaction spec given); a goal end date and archiving are on the listing and a reviewer could not find them; a streak freeze is listed and zero reviewers mention it; the website link in Settings points at a dead domain — the only support path. Report 28: an in-app 'Restore purchases' and 'Contact support' entry point is missing — four purchase failures and two 'where do I get help' reviews, while the developer answers e-mail within hours. Report 30: edit / delete / pause exist and three reviewers in three countries could not find them ('how do you pause a habit? how do you edit? I've looked everywhere'), one rating 1★ — a discoverability defect, not a missing feature. Report 31: misunderstandings about how to edit or delete a habit, what 'untracked' means, what colours and X/O marks mean and how 'quit' goals count — a UX problem, not a gap. Report 33: misunderstandings rise with feature count — a time-of-day filter hid habits and produced a false bug report; how to reorder or delete; skip vs cancel vs fail; 'every day starts skipped' (a setting); where the timer is; how to connect the Watch. Report 34: 'No widgets!!' two months after widgets shipped, and a request for an easier way to mark yesterday answered by the existing long-press ('That solves 90% of the struggle'). Report 43: roughly a tenth of scheduling complaints ask for shapes the app already has (custom days 'Monday and Wednesday's', timed tasks, untimed tasks) and land as 1★ / 2★; a Mac app is requested although the listing claims Mac. Report 47: the start date before creation exists but is hidden behind blank picker options — the second-largest request in the corpus (21) is a discoverability fix. Report 56: 'a feature-discoverability problem, not a feature-absence problem' — reminders requested twice after shipping (buried in the habit editor; v2.3.2 added a bell icon on every row), back-dating hard to find, widget transparency in the store preview but not findable — 'Shipping a feature is not the same as retiring its request'. Report 57: an AI habit-suggestion feature shipped in 2025 and both reviewers who mention it cannot find it; a Shortcuts 'Check-in ID' exists undocumented. Report 59 (Tappsk): NEG_UI_CONFUSING 152 (1.00%, rising to 1.4% in the latest era) — cannot find how to delete a habit or set a reminder on a habit ('не могу понять как удалить ненужную привычку'). Report 65 (Rabit): CONF_UX 12 (2.41%, mean 3.50) cannot find a control or how to mark a habit done; the timer is hard to find.

title: Intra-day completion: tap N times to fill N/N
statement: When a habit's target is more than once a day, each tap should count toward it; one binary tick per day is report 8's #1 unmet need, the only complaint theme still rising, and a stated uninstall. Report 20: multiple check-ins per day (water, medication, teeth) was requested 54 times (mean 3.87) and named as table stakes against Streaks and Productive; never shipped. Report 23: multiple-per-day / partial increments (111, 1.53%) largely shipped in 2016; residual complaints are about partial-progress display. Report 26: multi-count per day (5 glasses of water, 10 pages) requested by 7. Report 27: multiple completions per day shipped ~Aug 2025 and is praised ('the multiple check-ins per day feature is very handy'). Report 29: 'As someone who takes medication twice a day it would be incredibly helpful to mark the same habit done twice a day'. Report 33: multiple completions per day / quantities (water ×8, pills ×3) was the largest 2017–19 request (53, 50 before Aug 2020) and shipping multi-check-in goals in Habitify X retired it (2.9% of E1 → 0.1% of E5). Report 36: multiple completions per day requested by 5. Report 41: countable goals with over-achievement and partial credit ('if a habit needs a count of seven… and you have only performed it four times, you get credit for that'). Report 42: multiple completions per day for water, meals and reps do not exist — 6 reviews (all US, 13.0% of US, mean 1.50), two refund-seeking payers: 'Track your food? Great - you can track it ONCE/day'; 'So you're going to eat or drink water just once a day?' — the marketing promises a counter, the product delivers a daily checkbox. Report 43: 0/2 and 0/4 per-day counters with hourly nagging exist and sell the app. Report 46: several completions per day requested by 12. Report 52: multiple check-ins per day (237 — water × 8, meds morning and evening) and multi-check habits that force a detail sheet even with one-tap enabled. Report 53: brush teeth twice, meditate in two sessions (CORE_MULTI 12). Report 55: the same habit several times a day (CORE_MULTI 5). Report 57: multiple check-ins per day requested from 2019 ('stamping three or four times a day, like for medication'), shipped as 'goal', capped at 5 ('I need 10'), then tier-gated — producing the three angriest change complaints (24 requests). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): within-day granularity is the largest coherent feature gap — 4 of 45 (8.89%) from four storefronts over eight months: count a habit N times a day and sum at day end, more than one reminder a day ('One reminder a day is not enough' for water and steps), a value per day ('walked 5k, then 7k'); two described use cases (water, steps) are currently unserviceable; P1 in the roadmap. Report 65 (Rabit): a times-per-day option that cannot be partially completed — 'tenho que tomar vitamina 2x ao dia, porém não consigo marcar caso eu tenho tomado apenas 1x. É tudo ou nada'; 'i'm not really sure what it is supposed to be used for' (S4).

title: Habits, focus timer and journal in one simple app
statement: Report 8's 3-in-1 bundle is load-bearing: none of the three parts draws a 1–2★, and users value not switching between three apps — as long as each part stays minimal. Report 49: a bundle of screen blocker ('a godsend… the typical screen time limit apple has… doesn't cut it' — no detractors), Pomodoro, workout and calorie trackers, journal, meditation and book summaries (22 + 23 praise) around the habit core. Report 50: all-in-one praised by 17 (4.94) — habits + tasks + schedule with time blocks + journal + mood + weight in one place.

title: Every promotional or onboarding modal must be dismissible on the smallest screen
statement: Report 8's full-screen 'add a widget' prompt had an unreachable close button on small iPhones and blocked the app for 20 months. Report 24: pop-ups and unskippable steps (182, mean 2.082) and unskippable completion celebrations; make animations skippable. Report 31: a 'Self-care Christmas' banner hid the bottom habit; a permanent 'Just for you' list cell slowed scrolling and tapping — never let a promotional element occupy a habit row or slow the list. Report 33: a full-screen offer on every open and a banner covering the third habit that cannot be closed (2023–26; upsell 1.7% of E5). Report 55: see [[C274]] — a pop-up whose X started a purchase. Report 64 (Critique AI): a paywall that reads as uncloseable — PAY_SOFTLOCK 39 (9.31%, mean 1.72) across 20 storefronts and 17 months ('no cancel button, no ignore button, no X button. NOTHING!'; 'I cannot press the don't pay now button even if I press it 20 times'; returns after relaunch) — reconciled by one German reviewer: the X 'is invisible, tiny and impossible to find'; two trapped users rated 4★ while asking for help; the rate fell 16.9% → 6.8% after launch but 7 reports remain in the latest quarter; F1: large, visible, reachable on first paint, verified on small screens and after force-relaunch. Report 64 (Critique AI): 'Doesnt work on smaller phones' and 'I can't scroll in the app, which means I can't choose the correct options' — defects that exclude rather than annoy (R7). Report 65 (Rabit): the onboarding questionnaire's advance button rendered below the visible screen (2023–2024) — 'a layout bug, not a logic bug, and trivially fixable' (F6); an ad close button under the status bar on iPhone 13.

title: Harden onboarding before January
statement: The New Year cohort is the largest of the year, writes reviews in its first days, and judges onboarding, not retention — every create-flow or first-day logging defect is amplified about 2× in January (report 8).

title: Let people use the product before they pay
statement: Users forgive a price; they do not forgive paying blind. Report 9's hard paywall before any experience produced 159 'let me look before you charge me' reviews at mean 1.79, and buyers who paid before seeing the product became the angriest cohort (mean 1.94). Report 12: a hard paywall with nothing evaluable produced a paywall corpus — 46.5% of 404 reviews complain about the gate, 172 reviewers left without ever seeing the product, and the theme never dropped below a third of reviews in any year. Report 17: seven reviewers rated an app they never saw ('Can't even look at the settings or examine how the app will handle cancelation'); confirmed payers averaged 3.63 against 1.14 for those blocked at the paywall — the strongest argument in a 38-review corpus for letting people in. Report 18: the reviews that converted best came from people who used the app free for a week or a month first; the reviews that generated refund demands came from people charged before they could evaluate. Report 19: only four non-payers appear in the corpus and all four refused for the same reason — no way to evaluate first; everyone else went through the paywall and then tried to reverse the transaction. Report 25: 'I could not evaluate the product' outweighs 'too expensive' — ~31 of 55 price objections are gate objections; every positive trial review describes having had enough product access to form a judgement; a survey-then-paywall sequence is the lowest-mean theme in the corpus (1.17) because it spends the highest-intent moment and then gates it. Report 26: an evaluation-window problem, not a pricing problem — 'You get about 5 days free to make one flower then you have to pay'; 'the flower stops growing once you reach 17%, which I finished in about 2 weeks'; a user writes the hypothesis: give one garden free 'and that would probably get me intrigued enough to get a subscription'; proposed tests: time-boxed full access, cap 8–10, or one garden to 100%. Report 30: 'nobody forms a habit portfolio of two — the cap converts evaluation into rejection'; the cap, not price, is the top upgrade barrier (15), and the substantive rating of everyone with something specific to say is 2.87. Report 31: 'Free is useless, paid is too expensive to try' — the evaluation argument is the plurality monetisation objection since 2016; 'Tried the 3 free habits and wanted more' was an E1 purchase trigger when the unlock was a $4–9 one-off. Report 33: 'Three habits, and three days, is simply too little'; the evaluation argument is the plurality of monetisation objections; 44 say 'would buy if…'. Report 34: 'two habits is too few to judge the app' is the plurality of 78 monetisation-friction reviews; a 2-habit tier converts believers and repels evaluators. Report 36: a 1-habit free tier 'you can't really test the app without paying'; roughly half of 121 friction reviews are willingness to pay the model cannot accept. Report 41: purchase decisions in hours on a 3-habit free tier ('I bought the lifetime after trying it for like 20 minutes'), while others say 'you can't get a proper demo out of this without having at least 8 or 10 habits'. Report 42: 'you can't get… a test to see whether it's actually worth paying'; a migrating HabitBull power user lost at the wall ('I couldn't move around or familiarize myself enough to justify paying to unlock integral features'); 'every tab I open to poke around is locked'; the 1★ band's 'never used the product' population (~20) needs a trial, the 'paid and regret it' population (13) needs the product to be worth it. Report 43: 'Why not give 2 weeks fully functional, then handicap it to 3?'; 'Would have more stars if I cd test out >3 goals — Prior to paying!' Report 46: 'By the time you discover that you can only track 3 habits with the free version, you've already spent 20 minutes or more setting it up' (16 votes); 'every tab I open to poke around is locked'-style evaluation failures; a 30-day full trial asked for. Report 48: 43 state an intention to pay that the current terms defeat (4.12) — 'I will pay for an app after I use it for a couple weeks and have grown to appreciate the app'; 38 payers describe long free use before paying. Report 50: three of four intent-to-pay reviewers use the free tier first, and two actual payers state the sequence (months free, then pro) — the path a cap cut interferes with. Report 53: 'I was asked to pay too soon, without really trying the app'; 'Let me try before upselling'. Report 54: the strongest conversion stories got enough free room to be convinced — two weeks, one week, a few minutes with the whole feature set visible — while the cap 'terminates evaluation rather than gating it'. Report 56: free-trial-then-charge patterns at competitors are explicitly rejected — 'No obnoxious free-trial trick. Actually free'; 'really free, no false promises'. Report 57: new users who hit the creation ad 'stop using the app before finding out if you like the functionality'. Report 59 (Tappsk): 40 purchasers bought within days because the app worked in the first days ('Поюзал один день и купил навсегда' — used it one day and bought forever; 'took premium the same day I downloaded it'). Report 60 (Mindway): 'the decision the corpus forces' — move the paywall behind first value: the value users report (structure 15, habit outcomes 12, wellbeing 9, mean 4.79) takes days to appear and the current design charges before any of it can happen (ad → questionnaire → 'asked for money right away'); the three reviewers who met the cost as optional averaged 4.33★, the thirteen who met it as a wall 1.69★ — 'how the cost is encountered, not the cost itself, determines the rating'; every one of the 13 confirmed payers wrote a negative review; E1: raise the free cap to a full day's routine (8–10 tasks) for a randomized cohort; E2: replace the count-based paywall with a time-based one — full app, 7 days, no card ('I wish it would of let me try it out first'). Report 64 (Critique AI): the purest case in the ledger — no free tier, 0 of 419 report free ongoing use; 166 (39.62%, mean 1.52) blocked at the paywall; 82.58% never got in (mean 2.35) against 3.87 for those who did (+1.52 stars); 95 (22.67%) propose a way in (free tier 66, trial 26, tiers 21, ads 12); strip out money and 126 reviews remain at 4.41; the 3★ band is 'I want to buy this and cannot' (PAY_PRICE 45.7%, PAY_SCAM zero) — 'If a free or cheaper tier ships, this band converts first'; M3: tracking + XP / leaderboard free, AI analysis, focus mode and coach paid; 'Nobody defends the price from outside the paywall — which is the whole argument for a free tier in one sentence'. Report 67 (Habio): the E2 objection was paying blind — 'I'd love an opportunity to try before I buy!'; MON_HARDWALL 47; the free era E1 averaged 3.03 with 53.42% praise against 1.73 once the wall arrived; §8.8: a real free tier or card-free trial, measuring chargebacks and refund requests rather than only conversion.

title: The paid product must deliver what the ads and onboarding demonstrate
statement: Report 9 showed an interactive guided-breathing coach in its ads and onboarding, then never offered it again — 'it's just a checklist' became the worst-rated major theme (99 reviews, mean 1.45), half of them from payers. Report 19: five reviewers paid for a personalised plan promised by a quiz and received a blank tracker plus four thin sister apps ('some useless little apps'); a Spanish-language Instagram ad delivered an English-only app; 'not as advertised' ran at 18.10%. Report 24: acquisition ads and a web questionnaire promise personalisation the plan does not deliver — 'the app asked very few questions and made very many assumptions before designing a plan for me'. Report 41: a buyer paid for the Home Screen widget shown in the listing screenshots while it was 'coming soon' (2★); another: 'no widgets… which was the entire reason I bought it. The preview looks nothing like the app this is a scam'. Report 42: a 'goal for the day' shown in marketing could not be found (1). Report 49: Solo Leveling ads promise an avatar, quests and penalties — 15 'not what the ad promised' (1.40) and 38 'just a checklist' (1.68) vs 38 who love the framing (4.87); an Instagram ad said 'get your free life reset plan today' (advertised free 37, 1.08) — 'the fix is in the ad, not the app'. Report 64 (Critique AI): '$50… expecting actual coaching' — 'all it does is organize workouts I had already organized myself'; 'Temu quality'; an AI that 'points out what's supposedly wrong with you without offering any solutions' (R3: give the AI something to say after the critique). Report 67 (Habio): U_AD_MISMATCH 195 (9.51%, mean 1.08) — Instagram ads showing a 'bionic' bold-first-letter reading tool for ADHD that does not exist (22: 'What a bait and switch!!'), a quiz promising a Myers-Briggs / ADHD profile or tailored plan ('Nothing like that exists in the app', 31), and ads that did not match the product (99); §8.5: withdraw creative for features that do not ship.

title: Respect Reduce Motion — no rapid flashing animation
statement: A self-care app's fast animation was reported as a seizure/vertigo risk (report 9, promoted as a safety finding despite one review).

title: Never ask for a rating before the user has used the app
statement: Report 9 put the rating prompt inside sign-up: users were asked for 5★ before seeing the app, the public rating ran 1.35 stars above written reviews, and Apple's guidelines forbid it. Report 12: an in-app instruction to rate 5★ during onboarding — 'It said I had to give them 5 starts so here I am' — was called out by 23 reviewers, two of whom named the exact 4.8 store aggregate; 14 of 77 five-star reviews contradict their own rating. Report 25: eight reviewers say the app asked for a review before they had used it, and one says it would not proceed without a review — if that gate existed, the 5★ share is not a satisfaction measurement for that period. Report 28: 'Every time I checked something off it would ask me to rate it' (5★, asking it to stop) — a prompt fired on the completion tap. Report 29: 'It asks for you to review it the moment you check one thing off' — ratings from people who have not yet used the app. Report 33: prompts 'three in 10 seconds' in 2017–18. Report 43: rating prompts 'every time I open this app' and 'every 2 minutes'. Report 46: 'It's asking whether I like the app just as I downloaded it!'; 'every other time I marked a habit as complete the app popped up a window asking me to rate it'. Report 50: see C094 — a prompt during the intro produces 1★ from users with no opinion. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'Хватит меня каждую секунду просить оставить отзыв' (stop asking me every second to leave a review, 1★) — cadence, not just timing. Report 60 (Mindway): 'Good but forcing me to rate😅🙄 / ITS FORCING MEE' (5★); 28 reviews (12.96%) say the reviewer has only just started ('I'm ready / I'm excited'; 'Just getting started, figuring it out!'; 'Lo voy descargando y ya me esta gustando') — 20 of the 128 5★; two 1★ with neutral text ('To soon to say'; 'Not sure about app yet') look like users rating the experience of being asked to rate; D6: stop harvesting ratings from users who have not used the app — a prompt after a routine completed on the fifth consecutive day would produce fewer, better, more durable reviews (E5). Report 64 (Critique AI): 'it got me to rate it before it charged me money so I gave it a 5 thinking that it was free because I am 13 and broke' — the likely mechanism behind a −2.09-star gap (written 2.589 on 419 vs public 4.68 on 18,785, ≥ 1.84 in every storefront), with 57 reviews (13.60%, mean 4.54) rated without product experience; research: does the prompt fire before the paywall — 'it changes how every dashboard in the business should be read'.

title: Never cap or paywall a support conversation mid-crisis
statement: Report 9's AI coach hit its free message cap while a user was 'almost having a collapse'; an emotional-support chat needs an uncapped crisis path and a handoff to real help.

title: A promised pre-charge trial reminder must actually arrive — in-app, with amount and date
statement: Report 10: 'you promised to remind me before charging' is the highest-intensity complaint in a 70,041-review corpus (billing-dispute family mean 1.97, 60% one-star, 17% of all payers); the reminder must be a blocking in-app card on next open, not only a push, and the exact amount and charge date must sit on the trial screen and permanently in Settings. For an ADHD audience the reminder is the feature, not a courtesy. Report 48: charged the full year at the start of a 7-day trial; a receipt shared by 'another active subscriber'. Report 50: no trial-expiry reminder before a ~$50 annual charge (AU) — fix F1 pairs it with the price mismatch. Report 59 (Tappsk): a confirmation e-mail with the renewal date is the report's first immediate fix (MON_AUTO_CHARGE 229, MON_CANCEL_TROUBLE 73). Report 67 (Habio): 'The day before my trial ended, they took the money and THEN emailed me and said my trial was up the following day'; MON_NO_RECEIPT 68 (3.32%); §8.3: a reminder 48 hours before conversion with the renewal amount in local currency and the plan length.

title: Automatic cloud backup on by default — never manual opt-in
statement: Report 10: progress stored on-device with a manual opt-in backup produced 551 data-loss reviews (9% of all 1★), a family rate that quadrupled in four years, and clinicians publicly withdrawing recommendations; 37 users did not know a backup was required until after the loss. Warn before any destructive path (delete for storage, phone change). Report 20: recovery from a developer-caused wipe was paywalled behind a manual premium iCloud backup; the recommendation is automatic daily local + iCloud snapshots with restore available to free users, and regression tests on the migration path. Report 23: Settings > Manage Data > Backups existed but was repeatedly discovered via support e-mail; several reviewers upgraded their rating on learning it existed — surface backups in the first-run tutorial, not a support reply. Report 27: iCloud sync exists ('seamless iCloud syncing'; the listing confirms) but is not legible — 'if my device gets reset all the data will be gone or I can recover it?'; a user will not reorder habits for fear of losing data; one churned after an update lost all progress; fix: a Settings line 'Backed up to iCloud · last synced <time>' plus an explicit restore path — a communication fix, not an engineering one. Report 29: optional iCloud backup, off by default and account-free, proposed against 9 data-loss reports and 3 sync requests — while one reviewer names 'I didn't even have to list my email' as the deciding factor. Report 34: a local-first no-account app praised for privacy loses data on reinstall and factory reset; optional iCloud sync would keep data off the developer's servers while fixing loss, multi-device use and exit. Report 41: a recoverable migration loss was recovered only by the developer by hand — the report asks for visible backup / restore with a 'last backed up' state. Report 42: no visible backup / restore; 'update → restart → history truncated' recurs across 2020–2026. Report 43: local-only storage with optional iCloud lost users four years of history in July 2026; the report's #1 fix is iCloud backup on by default with a visible restore path and a 'last backed up' time. Report 46: the report's #2 is a per-habit change history with one-tap 'undo last 7 days' and conflict resolution that never deletes a completed mark. Report 47: a free backup exists since Feb 2024 but the 2026 loss shows sync overwriting local history on update and recovery e-mails not arriving — backup is only as good as its restore path. Report 50: no backup or restore capability mentioned anywhere in 205 reviews after two data-loss reports.

merged_from.note: existing cards re-attached during consolidation

title: Compensation for lost data must match the loss — never a flat token
statement: Report 10: a flat 5,000-stone remedy offered to users who lost 20,000–200,000 stones, multi-year streaks and unrepeatable items was described as insulting and in bereavement language; restore inventory or history, not a token.

title: Never remove a feature people bought the app for — add alongside, do not replace
statement: Report 10: every major removal (Journeys → streak-based Self-Care Areas, automatic mood check-ins, exact-time goals, milestones, colour palettes) produced a dated backlash, explicit paid cancellations, and none were reversed; generic 'you removed a feature I used' grew 16× in four years. Report 18: the Sept 2024 split of the interleaved routine + to-do list into two tabs drew 32 protests at mean 4.25★ — the paying base — including subscribers who had bought a year because of the merged view days earlier; the weekly view and the Challenge feature were removed in the same release; nobody had asked for the split. Recommendation: restore it as a toggle, since a minority came to prefer the split. Report 23: the interactive widget lost at iOS 14 was partly an Apple platform change, but the five-year gap before restoration cost a top-three downgrade reason; a capability users bought for must be restored, not left behind. Report 24: the 'Make Me Fabulous' activity launcher was removed or hidden after a redesign and background music was removed — both named by long-tenure payers as renewal reasons. Report 25: an Apple Watch app reported 'suddenly removed' (Oct 2025) and Vision Pro support withdrawn — single reports, recorded not asserted. Report 27: the year-at-a-glance grid — the signature view the bundle ID is still named after (goalStreakCalendar) — was demoted behind a per-habit tap in 2025; its praise fell 16.7% → 0% and by late 2025 it appears only as a loss, even from a reviewer who still gave 5★ ('I loved it before the previous update'); the removed one-tap note export produced the corpus's only 2★ — 'one reviewer represents a workflow, not a preference'. Report 31: 'The app gets prettier. The actual functionality gets worse. Every time.' — removed monthly/yearly frequency (58), streak on the main list (52, partly restored then removed again), swipe between days (41); 'That is one of the biggest reasons I paid' (feature removed after paying, 21); a minority liked the redesigns. Report 33: removals came in release-shaped spikes — v2.0 charity points and data (2016), skip and Russian UI (2017), notes/skip to Premium (2019), Habitify X (2020), notes back-dating and editing (Dec 2024 – Jan 2025), compact/incremental/streak widgets (May 2025), passcode lock (2025) — regression 197 (5.00%, mean 2.51), 14.9% of E3; 2★ is the 'I used to love it' band (regression 15.1%, churn 12.2%); every removal needs a toggle or a migration. Report 34: CSV export, present for years, was disabled in 2026; the one-time purchase option vanished 'after updating the app'. Report 36: 'Antes: Excelente. Ahora: Pésima' — a 2★ after widgets went paid. Report 43: 'pause a habit' removed by the 2026 update. Report 46: an unrequested Dec 2022 completion animation cost a subscriber ('I'll not renew'). Report 48: the web app (2015 – ~2019) was discontinued and Windows users lost access — 17 still ask for it; widget interactivity was removed after shipping. Report 50: an update removed single-occurrence editing of recurring habits (see C073). Report 52: a ¥68 buyer asked for a refund after a Dec 2024 redesign removed to-do sorting.

title: Content and event releases need a crash gate across device generations
statement: Report 10: a monthly event's 'grow potion' animation crashed the app on load for a large cohort (120 crash reviews in Feb 2026, 4–6× baseline), destroying 600-day streaks and locking paid users out for weeks; reviewers blame the event cadence for shipping untested code. Report 31: 1.19.0 (launch crash), the May 2022 hang and 2.7.1/2.7.2 (count corruption) were all shipped to everyone. Report 52: release waves recur on old OS versions (v2.41 on iOS 13 biometric unlock; iOS 14.x launch crash for 20+ days) — F5: a release gate for old iOS and data migrations, staged rollout, crash-safe local store before schema changes; target no month with ≥20 crash reviews. Report 55: F4 — test every build against current and previous iOS versions and screen sizes; staged rollout; halt on a crash spike (no month with >10 crash reviews). Report 59 (Tappsk): the report's immediate fix is 'a release check on the oldest supported iOS and on the show-completed-tasks path before shipping; a fast hotfix path' — the 2021-10 crash hit only older iPhones and the 2023 crash only one setting path; the Turkish habit-reminder crash adds locale to the gate. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): I3 — a regression gate on tap / hit-testing before release plus a fast rollback path; 'nothing in this corpus suggests a process change prevented the next one' and one bad build cost ~0.32 stars on the whole written history.

title: Every guilt mechanic must be optional — streaks, repair prompts, countdowns
statement: Report 10: the app was praised specifically for not guilting users (476 reviews, mean 4.87); after streaks shipped mid-2024, 96 reviews say it now punishes the missed day the audience was promised it wouldn't, and repairing a streak costs currency. A single 'gentle mode' toggle is the corpus's own proposal. Report 18: an automatic streak 'shield' made the streak number feel fake ('I get complacent since the number won't disappear'), while an ADHD reviewer said a broken streak is the feature that makes them quit and asked to hide the UI; another sat in red all day because the routine could only be finished at night. Conclusion: streak, shield, light and cheer messages are per-user toggles, default shield off. Report 23: loss-framed reminder copy is a guilt mechanic users in four languages ask to switch off or reframe. Report 26: a 'no wither' / Zen mode (the garden does not decay) exists as a premium option; gentleness and no streaks are praised at mean 4.76 and the mental-health segment (32, mean 4.66 — 'this app helped me fix my severe depression') is the clearest argument against any harsher rule. Report 28: rabbit health/energy decay with guilt notifications ('YOUR BUNNY'S LOSING HEALTH COME AND DO HABITS TO FIX IT!') and a challenge-mode full reset penalise exactly the cautious beginner ('I have few habits because I'm starting a healthier lifestyle slowly'); a defender values the stakes — make decay a setting, separate it visibly from the data model. Report 33: an 'Are you sure the day is over?' confirmation on fail/skip with no off switch. Report 36: 7 ask for streaks / reps / loss-on-break (incl. a 45-vote review) while 11 praise the absence of streak shame — make streaks optional, with a 'don't skip twice' rule proposed. Report 41: 'the percentage focus and backseating of streaks made this a thing i actually use' — one streak-prominence request is treated as a minority against the differentiator. Report 46: the skip mark is why perfectionists stay — 'you don't want to break a streak, so you keep going' with 'no punishment other than a break in the color gradient'; rule 17: do not remove or harden the forgiving skip. Report 47: the streak resets to zero on a miss and is praised by 3 as motivating, while the grid's kept colour is the non-punitive part reviewers love; a missed-day marker (4 requests, 3 KR) should be optional. Report 49: an optional hard mode that resets to day 1 with penalty tasks on a miss is loved by a small, intense, entirely satisfied group (13, 4.77) — opt-in severity works; guilt-inducing tone as a default is criticised (13). Report 54: 12 (3.25%, 4.75) praise the deliberate absence of streaks — 'most likely because it does not track streaks (which my black and white brain reads as failure if I am not perfect)… These are skills. Skills can be learned. I am not broken'; 'I have adhd and using streaks has always resulted in beating myself up'; one downloaded because a review said there were no streaks; D6: claim it; §8.5: do not add streaks with penalties. Report 59 (Tappsk): a daily productivity score with a trend arrow demotivates a minority — NEG_SCORE 23 vs PR_SCORE 84: 'ОЧЕНЬ ДЕМОТИВИРУЕТ эта стрелочка которая показывает насколько я продуктивна' (this arrow showing how productive I am is VERY demotivating, 4★). Report 65 (Rabit): a missed habit kills the plant — 'Missing one scheduled habit completely kills a plant?!! … I don't mind a penalty but this is dark souls level'; 'are we supposed to lie?' — users accept the penalty when deserved and reject it when not, so plant death is 'the single riskiest design decision in the product'.

title: Credit for non-consecutive, cumulative progress alongside streaks
statement: Report 10: replacing cumulative Journeys with consecutive-streak Self-Care Areas was the lowest-rated change in the corpus (mean 2.76, 21 of 49 one-star); chronic-illness and ADHD users say a streak-only model is structurally incompatible with their lives. Ship cumulative credit next to streaks, not instead of them.

title: Launch-to-core-action path with no interstitials
statement: Report 10: 'overwhelm' is the largest UX complaint (1,046 reviews) — an app sold to people with executive-function difficulty accumulated six sequential screens (quote, mood prompt, event cutscene, visitor, chest, claim-confirm-claim) before the checklist. Report 24: an app sold as an ADHD focus aid is described as itself overstimulating ('This app literally GIVES me adhd') — cluttered/overwhelming 1,324 (3.05%, mean 3.068) and confusing navigation 1,507 (3.47%, mean 2.338), rising through the good eras too (1.90% → 4.26%); 46.1% of clutter requests come from 4–5★ users, so a low-stimulus home screen that opens on today's routine with coaching, Discover, Circles and cross-app promotion below the fold is a retention feature; checking off one habit takes 3–5 screens. Report 47: check-in takes 2–4 taps (long-press → record screen → done; a reviewer counts '記録したい項目を選択→＋→完了→＜') and one-tap logging has been requested since 2019 — too many taps 14 (2.38%, mean 2.86: '気軽にチェック入れたいのに何タップもアクションが多くて億劫になる'); the report's E4 is an optional one-tap mode with the memo screen skipped unless long-pressed. Report 48: 'open the app, click a check mark, exit' is what simplicity means to 817 reviewers — see [[C264]]. Report 65 (Rabit): BUG_ONBOARD 22 (mean 1.45, the lowest of any theme with n>10) — recommended installs that never got past the intro ('TODOS OS MEUS AMIGOS ME RECOMENDARAM'), twice as common outside Brazil, i.e. in the expansion audience.

title: Honour what onboarding asks — a declared limitation must change the suggestions
statement: Report 10: the onboarding asks about disability and then ignores the answer ('I have mobility issues, so I clicked that… ever since, the app has been suggesting that I do things that I've told it I can't do'); 597 accessibility reviews at mean 4.56. Report 24: a long onboarding questionnaire produces an identical plan for everyone — 'You will answer a ton of questions about your habits and goals and then the app will not take any of your answers into account'; 'I told it I drink water all day. The first habit I'm to build is drinking three glasses of water' (no-customisation 175, mean 2.097; forced first habit 124, mean 2.452, consistent across eleven years and six languages). Report 49: asthma, post-surgical injury, nerve damage and mobility limits cannot be entered and running stays the only cardio (10 + 20) — see [[C266]].

title: Values and identity screens are optional in both directions
statement: Report 10: 54 users deleted at a mandatory pet-pronoun step, 109 objected to Pride content, and 111 loyal users (mean 4.57) complained representation was missing; the only intervention the corpus supports is a skip option and a show/hide filter for themed cosmetics — optionality, not editorial change. Report 24: onboarding includes a 'letter from your future self' and a held-finger 'contract' signed with the fingerprint sensor, reached via a social ad and a web questionnaire.

title: Automated suggestions from user text must be safety-filtered; notifications must be crisis-aware
statement: Report 10: the goal-suggestion system parsed a journal entry about suicidal ideation into a goal to 'schedule time for suicide'; diagnosis quizzes returned severe results to children in a 4+ app; a 'you can do this' push arrived right after a text about suicide. Report 24: diet-culture / eating-disorder trigger complaints (61, mean 2.918) in a wellness routine app. Report 28: untargeted ad content inside a 4+ app used by self-declared 8–10-year-olds and by a teacher with students — 'ads for AI homework apps that will write papers for you… encouraging bad habits through these ads'.

title: Visible monthly plan — annual-default trials drive billing disputes
statement: Report 10: the 7-day trial defaults to an annual charge; 23 reviews ask for a monthly plan and several say they would have paid monthly; the annual default is the mechanism behind most of the 404 billing disputes. Report 25: the most specific repeated billing claim is that a 7-day trial renews into the annual plan when monthly was selected ('charged 25,000 pesos when I had chosen the monthly option'; 'You can't choose to be renewed to the 1 month subscription'); make trial→plan mapping explicit and let the user pick the post-trial plan. Report 31: a monthly billing plan was wanted (8) and one user had to switch to monthly to be able to cancel before a €100+ renewal. Report 33: a monthly plan missing in some storefronts or offered only on the web ('only … yearly and lifetime … I would have signed up for a month'; 'pagar 50-60€ como única opción?') — offer monthly in-app everywhere. Report 59 (Tappsk): the 7-day trial converts to the annual (999 ₽) by default; 111 of 306 trial mentions report an immediate charge and the annual sum is what makes the 1★ ('a year's money'). Report 64 (Critique AI): annual-upfront is an upgrade barrier and the billing-dispute class — three payers expected trial or monthly flexibility and got a full-year charge; 'Almeno dividessero il prezzo in mesi'; M5: a monthly or one-time SKU visible before the annual.

title: A random-rotation shop with paid re-rolls and unpurchasable catalogue items is a friction generator
statement: Report 10: goals yield 3–12 stones while items cost 500–900, the shop rotates randomly, and the item you want never appears — 196 complaints from engaged, currency-rich users, the ones most likely to subscribe. Let users buy what they can see.

title: Official community channels must tolerate criticism
statement: Report 10: the Facebook group, Discord and subreddit are described as heavily moderated and hostile to criticism across five years (211 reviews), with paying users 7× over-represented; suppression of criticism resurfaces in every later controversy.

title: Keep the therapeutic core in front of the game layer
statement: Report 10: as breathing, first aid and soundscapes moved behind menus and paywalls, tool mentions fell 15.6% → 2.7% and the core-benefit family 30% → 23%, while reviewers called the product 'a pay-to-play loot box checklist simulator'; the game is why people call it cute and motivating, but it must not be paid for by burying the layer people came for. Report 64 (Critique AI): a paying reviewer's verdict splits the product — the AI plan is not worth it, the coaching and challenges are.

title: Cosmetic and colour variety as the paid layer
statement: Report 10: buyers name extra colour options, seasonal items and a larger shop as the specific hook ('I started getting finch plus solely because I found the extra color options… very motivating'); restricting palettes later (Aug–Sep 2026) drew a backlash. Report 36: cosmetic gating (≈10 premium skins) is 'broadly accepted when it is the only gate' — 'So far the app is mostly free aside from cosmetics (understandable)' — and 3 of 34 payers bought for skins; selling skins separately on top of the membership reads as double-charging ('$15 for permission to buy a $10 skin'). Report 47: more colours unlocked by watching a video (2022) — the one rewarded-ad surface reviewers accepted. Report 52: themes sold separately (~¥6 each, 2018) then made free for members — a buyer was refunded.

title: Monthly seasonal event with a paid reward track
statement: Report 10: event completion is a stated purchase trigger, but events are also the named cause of the 2026 crash and data-loss clusters, FOMO complaints, and the sponsored-IP values breach.

title: Completion verification / anti-cheat
statement: Report 10: 158 users volunteer that they check boxes without doing the task and ask to be held accountable (mean 4.59); its sibling 'it's just a checklist' (111) is the churn thesis.

title: Configurable day boundary and hemisphere seasons
statement: Report 10: 146 reviews say the app assumes a conventional daytime schedule and northern-hemisphere seasons; night-shift workers and southern-hemisphere users ask for a movable day boundary. Report 18: a configurable day-end time was requested ~15 times across KR, JP and US, and the timezone stayed on Korean time for diaspora users from 2021 to 2024 (US daylight saving unhandled). Report 23: day-boundary / midnight reset requested (54, 0.74%, emerging, mean 4.02). Report 25: a day-start time setting exists for shift workers but is capped at 11:45. Report 26: a user-set day boundary requested alongside backfill (29); persistent across five years. Report 27: a Monday week-start setting asked twice in early 2024 (DE/AU) and never again. Report 31: a day-start offset for late sleepers and shift workers (capped at 5 am) was later removed; day-start / midnight rollover 18. Report 34: 'My day always ends after midnight' — a configurable day start, citing Habitica's setting. Report 41: custom day-start and week-start shipped May 2025 after being requested from 2021; night-shift day reset 5. Report 46 (counter-signal): none; the grid's day boundary is not raised. Report 49: the wake-time control permits only ~5–10am, excluding night-shift, graveyard and FIFO workers — 31 reviews at 3.42 (well above the corpus), 23 stating their shift, US +2.15pp, several saying they want the product while uninstalling; the daily recap closes the day at a fixed ~9pm (10) — 'the cheapest high-value fix in the report'; a partial fix turned a 4★ into 5★. Report 52: night owls' check-ins after midnight land on the next day — 50 text mentions ask to end the day at 2–4 am. Report 53: end the day at 1–5 am and handle time-zone travel (CORE_DAYSTART 9). Report 59 (Tappsk): NEG_DAY_BOUNDARY 19 — 'Как быть совам' (what about night owls, 1★); the report proposes a user-set day boundary alongside back-dating. Report 65 (Rabit): 'My day does not start or end at 12am… I track my water usage past midnight and it doesn't reset after I sleep??'.

title: Accessibility stack: VoiceOver, motion, sound and light sensitivity, text size
statement: Report 10: 597 accessibility reviews (0.85%, mean 4.56) from blind, mobility-limited, chronically ill, motion-, sound- and light-sensitive users; dark mode is argued as an accessibility need, not a preference ('Cute clothes for the bird were apparently shippable'). Report 23: accessibility / VoiceOver 19 (0.26%, mean 3.79). Report 24: accessibility (vision, font, VoiceOver) 129 (0.30%, mean 3.101). Report 26: a detailed, actionable VoiceOver defect report — images without alt text, focus loss, elements announced only as 'botão' — plus larger text and low-contrast reports; dynamic type was added and praised; promoted on inclusion/legal grounds at 5 reviews. Report 31: no VoiceOver support, small fonts/buttons (19) — ship VoiceOver labels, Dynamic Type and 44 pt targets. Report 33: memo input breaks under Japanese IME. Report 36: respect the silence switch and add a global audio toggle (2, one an uninstall). Report 41: the Mac app has no text zoom — 'text and icons are too small on my 27-inch display' (the only accessibility report). Report 42: premium pop-ups 'difficult to click out of' alongside a text-size accessibility complaint. Report 43: 'this app works with voiceover since I am a voiceover user' (the only screen-reader confirmation); 'The text is small, I can not see to read it!' Report 46: accessibility requests 8 (font size, VoiceOver, reading needs — 'unique reading needs' from a dyslexic 5★); a VoiceOver regression on iOS 15 (IT). Report 47: time-picker digits unreadable in dark mode (2); the skip key hidden by the keyboard (Jul 2025); the settings button hidden by long tab names (a payer). Report 48: accessibility 6 (3.50). Report 53: VoiceOver compatibility shipped on request (2022) for blind users. Report 54: a detailed VoiceOver report (many fields and buttons unreadable, DE, 1★, offering to re-review once fixed) and Dynamic Type text cut off — 'below the 1% bar, but flagged under the standing exception for accessibility, and cheap to fix'. Report 57: dark mode paywalled against photosensitivity. Report 60 (Mindway): time entry on a 24-hour clock only, no AM/PM option — 'This confuses me a lot'; F6: add AM/PM time entry, 'one review, one line of work, and it is the only reported input-level usability defect in the corpus' — respect the user's locale time format. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): an app that cannot be operated by tapping is an accessibility failure in effect — the June build; zero explicit accessibility requests otherwise.

title: Per-day / per-habit notes and journal text
statement: A note field on each check-in is pure upside and requested by happy users (reports 2, 3, 7); a single cramped line is the common complaint; charging for journal text while mood is free drew complaints (report 9). Report 20: notes per day was the single most-requested feature in the corpus (79, mean 3.66) and never shipped. Report 23: per-completion notes were requested from 2015 (43, 0.59%) and shipped ~Mar 2023; the residual ask is navigation between notes. Report 25: a notes / journal / mood field per day requested by 7 (mean 4.43). Report 26: a journal / gratitude note requested (~4). Report 27: daily memo prompts exist and their value is disputed ('simply yet engaging daily memo questions' vs 'the note taking doesn't really have a point to it'); a fuller daily log is wanted. Report 28: journal/notes per day and mood tracking used by 38 (4.63%, mean 4.29). Report 31: notes/journal per entry and timestamps (added Jan 2017) — 82 mentions (mean 3.52); 'last done / minutes ago' removed in 2022–23. Report 33: per-habit per-day notes / journal moved to Premium in Apr 2019 (free users lost 300 days of notes) and in Dec 2024 – Jan 2025 lost back-dating and editing (1,000+ gym days logged in memos). Report 34: notes per completed day are Premium (praised 11, mean 4.91); notes on missed days and opening a note from the calendar requested by 9 (a 'No Spend' habit). Report 36: notes on a habit requested by 3. Report 43: journal / per-day notes praised by 9 (mean 4.44) — but a journal prompt forced on every skip in the 2025 redesign drew a 1★ from a long-time payer. Report 46: journal / per-day notes shipped Dec 2023 (praised 12, mean 4.67) after 9 requests. Report 47: a per-day memo attached to each check-in is the diary feature Korean and Japanese reviewers name as the differentiator (memo + photo 32, 5.43%, mean 4.75); a note-length limit is asked by 3; one user stopped writing memos after the 2026 data loss. Report 48: per-entry notes praised by 21 (4.95), requested by 14; whether notes are free is disputed in-thread. Report 50: see [[C268]] — the journal is a primary reason to choose the app and its editor the worst-quality surface. Report 52: check-in notes are the largest unmet need (JRNL_WANT 668, 3.24%, very strong) and a praised micro-diary with 'on this day in past years' (234, 4.85). Report 54: notes per habit requested (3, 4.67). Report 56: per-habit description / notes requested by 3 — ship a short label first; journaling is a separate question. Report 57: notes allowed only on successful check-ins — 9 ask across six years and three languages to write why they failed ('I want to write down why I couldn't do it on the days I failed'). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a per-day value / note ('walked 5k, then 7k') requested by a 4★ reviewer. Report 64 (Critique AI): a notes space requested (ch, 5★). Report 65 (Rabit): a notes / description field per habit (REQ_DESC 2) and calendar notes on why a habit was missed (S7). Report 67 (Habio): the daily reflection journal is one of the two things the corpus says to keep.

title: Sub-tasks / sub-routines nested inside a habit or routine
statement: 'Shower routine' reused inside 'morning routine'; sub-habits are what heavy users ask for after categories (reports 1, 5, 7). Report 41: sub-tasks with time per step requested by 7, one blocking a purchase ('I need sub tasks with time for each'). Report 52: sub-tasks requested (62, weak).

title: Multiple profiles (me, kids, pet, work)
statement: Requested alongside folders in report 1 — separate people or contexts inside one app. Report 23: family/multi-person use inside one account is a stated reason for more task slots.

title: Updates must not break function or wipe progress
statement: 'Then Boom… updated! Now… the progress is gone' (report 4); a nine-week window of hard functional failures (report 8); an update broke chronological sorting across four countries in one week (report 9); near-daily forced updates are themselves a complaint (report 10). Report 18: a July 2026 update told a mid-term subscriber to buy a new plan; lag, solved by 2025, regressed sharply (1.83% → 5.38%) as routine modes, intensity levels and note/tracker features were added. Report 26: the 2022 'music cannot be turned off' defect (10 reviews, May–Nov 2022) was fixed and stayed fixed — a clean, closed defect; the later inverse (music won't play) is 3 reviews. Report 27: the 2025 update broke launch on iOS 26 and removed the one-tap note export, the day-tap record popup, the single-screen annual overview and backfill from the annual grid — the same update that shipped multi-check-ins and flexible frequency; 'feature removals in this app are more expensive than feature absences'. Report 28: a listing version ten months older than the newest reviews coincides with 2026 freezing, crashing and broken-login reports — 'verify the app on current iOS and ship an update'; the 2022 rabbit-off-screen, can't-clean-the-room and orange-screen bugs were fixed and stayed fixed. Report 31: v2 rebuild (Mar 2022) brought 10–30 s tap lag, a broken Watch app and removed past-entry editing (restored in 2.0.8); v3.0 (Jan 2023) brought a week-start bug and a custom-count +1 bug. Report 33: v2.0 (Nov 2016) wiped data and Premium; Habitify X broke the Watch; 'update made it worse' spiked 7.6% in 2020 and 5.8% in 2025. Report 43: regression after update 16 (2.51%) — 3 → 4 → 9 by era, eight of the nine recent inside Oct 2025 – Jul 2026; three updates in two days then 'I can no longer access the app… All the I spent created things are lost'. Report 46: 'The new IOS update has wiped all of my historical and tracking data' (GB, 1★, Sep 2022); a Sep 2020 'won't open after the update' cluster of six reviews in three days across five storefronts. Report 47: an update in August 2026 overwrote years of history (8 reviews in 3–20 Aug); an update in 2022 scrambled habit order (5); the back button vanished in Nov 2020; 'アプリ更新したら勝手にデータ上書きされて'. Report 48: paid subscription not recognised after an update (3); the 2015 v3.0 release lost data for 25 and duplicated trackers for 20. Report 52: an update that could not be downloaded or reinstalled produced 12 reviews on one day (31 Jul 2023); BUG_UPDATE 524 (2.54%, 3.26). Report 53: re-certify Watch app and widgets on every iOS release — iOS 11.3, iOS 13 and iOS 18/26 each broke a surface. Report 55: crash waves after the July 2017, 2018 and 2020 updates; fixes reported twice, the second after nine months. Report 56: a sync update deleted habits; defects clustered in the Jun–Jul build cycle. Report 57: 'an update broke it' is constant for seven years (update_regression 59, 7.57%) — a Sep 2020 release broke the note keyboard (21 reviews in three days, mostly still 5★) and a Jun 2020 release stopped launch (8); 'every update breaks something that worked. Please just leave it alone'. Report 59 (Tappsk): BUG_UPDATE 103 (2.83★) and the four release-clustered regressions ([[C031]]); the quietest release era (E4, 2022-03 → 2023-05) is also the best-rated (4.70★, praise 80.3%, defects 3.5%), and the regression era that followed the lowest since launch on crashes. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'Seems like each time when it updates the habits progress for the last week wipes. These happened two times already' (KZ, 2★, Aug 2026) and a total loss on launch ten months earlier — present before the June regression and still present after it was fixed; I4: treat habit history as migration-critical data with an integrity check on upgrade — 'in a streak product, destroyed history destroys the only thing the user has accumulated'. Report 65 (Rabit): plants purchased under Plus re-locked behind a padlock after an update; 14 reviewers attribute a regression to a specific release (BUG_UPDATE, mean 2.71).

title: Never let fear of losing history be the reason people pay
statement: Report 11: the only stated purchase motive was 'I had 3 years worth of history I didn't want to lose' on an app with no export or backup; when the entitlement then failed, the loyal long-tenure user became the 1★ 'scam' review. Sell durability (backup, export, long-history analytics) as a gain, never gate access to what the user already built. Report 33: a weekly check-in cap locked free users out of long streaks ('After 500 days I was pay-walled'). Report 34: 'forced to keep paying … if you don't want to lose all your history' — export disabled and a paid backup before delete, both 1★. Report 36: 'the most dangerous customer' is the multi-year free user who changed device or ran out of habits in 2026 — data in the app, no export and no sync, 'cannot leave cleanly and cannot continue without paying' (LOCKIN). Report 57: free-tier history cut to 30 days while backup is Premium — 'in the end I learned for the first time that without paid Premium, backup and recovery are impossible'.

title: One clear SKU shelf — every plan distinctly named, stating its period, and delivering exactly what its label says
statement: Report 11: three SKUs shared the identical display name 'Habits PRO Functions' at $1.99 / $6.99 / $8.99 and none named a period, while reviewers described 'annual', 'VIP' and 'lifetime' purchases — neither the user nor support could tell what had been bought. Report 12: ten SKUs including three 'Weekly Subscription' and two 'One-Time Payment' entries at different prices, visible on the store page. Report 19: charged ≠ agreed ($29.99 annual agreed, $59.99/month billed) when the plan bought was never named back to the buyer. Report 30: Monthly $5.99, Yearly $44.99, a second Yearly $29.99 and Lifetime $59.99 — 'Te dicen que es de por vida el plan y es solo para un año' ('Cuidado, engañan'), and the monthly option could not be bought ('it charges for a year'); five of the six reviewers who reached payment had a bad outcome. Collapse the shelf. Report 41: the Lifetime SKU was intermittently invisible — 'I can no longer see the lifetime plan which I would like to purchase!'; 'When activated trial there was a lifetime subscription option. Now don't see it'; 'bummed I missed out on the lifetime deal'; and a Chinese user found no purchase entry at all — 'the cheapest revenue recovery in the report'. Report 42: seven concurrent IAPs, five near-identically named at $39.99 / $59.99 — reviewers quote wildly different prices by year and storefront. Report 43: the purchase sheet does not say 'one time' — 5 reviewers (mean 4.20) could not tell whether $2.99 was monthly or once, three of them 5★ users trying to buy ('can't seem to figure out if the $2.99 is per month or a one time purchase.?') and one who wrote a 2★ believing it was monthly; the thing the sheet fails to state is the product's most-praised attribute. Report 46: three concurrent premium SKUs (ED Premium Monthly, Everyday Premium Year, ED Full Year Access) beside a lifetime; a web price cheaper than in-app ('only $12 a year on the website, more in the app'). Report 49: the UK's advertised £1.99–£2/month resolves to a £24.99–£29.99 annual charge at checkout (misleading checkout 8.86% of GB, +7.48pp) while 'price too high' runs below global — 'the checkout presentation, not the price level, is what is generating one-star reviews'; a monthly plan costing more for two months than the annual for twelve (15). Report 52: two one-time tiers (小太阳 / 大太阳) with no upgrade credit between them; tier confusion carries a ×5.11 payer lift. Report 54: a one-time purchase that 5 reviewers think is a subscription ('the one time fee for a whole year'; 'is the ¥68 membership a one-off lifetime buyout?'). Report 60 (Mindway): 'When purchasing, it implies the option of monthly billing, but auto drafts the whole year' (1★, 'It seems scammy'); the annual is chosen to escape the weekly ('paid the $40 annual to avoid $7/week') and then regretted — plan clarity at purchase is one of the five paid-user issues; F2 includes the monthly-vs-annual selection screen. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'What is the difference between the 34 and 59 paid subscription?' — a buyer had to publish a 5★ review to ask, because the paywall did not answer it; M2: differentiate the two tiers on the paywall itself.

merged_from.title: Every SKU delivers exactly what its label says — one clear shelf, a working monthly option, and 'lifetime' that is lifetime
merged_from.note: C245 (report 30: two yearly SKUs beside a 'Lifetime' produced 'lifetime delivered as annual'; the monthly plan could not be bought) and C177 (identically named / period-less SKUs) are the same rule about an unambiguous price shelf; entitlement delivery itself stays in C033

title: A quiet, adult, non-gamified tracker is a positioning some users actively seek
statement: Report 11: 'Functional, no frills and no infantilization. I tested half a dozen similar apps before finding this one'; 'I hate apps that demand set times'; 'without any imposed junk' — four of 33 reviewers chose the app for what it refuses to do, and three switched from gamified competitors. A live tension with the pet/mascot category norm. Report 27: two reviewers name the absence of gamification as the reason they chose the app — 'There's not pets to take care of, there's no flashy graphics or anything, and that is just perfect for me'; 'it removes a direct emphasis on urgency and/or self-competition' — and 52 praise minimalism; in a category converging on pets, gardens and streak anxiety, deliberate plainness is a defensible position that any future monetisation must not contradict. Report 28 (counter-evidence): the gamified pet loop is what works here — 'especially having adhd, this gamification works so well for my brain'; one reviewer chose it because it is less feature-heavy than Finch; the plain/gamified split is a positioning choice, not a rule. Report 29: 'Everything that you need, nothing that you don't' — 119 praise simplicity against 3 wanting rewards or more features; do not add features to the main flow. Report 30: 'понятный и удобный интерфейс. Без заморочек' — a minimalist tracker's one proven strength; the thesis works and the packaging fails. Report 31: the simple, colourful adult tracker is loved consistently in every era, and contrasted with Habit-Bull's 'roided-out CrossFit guy'. Report 34: 'Feels like it was made by Apple'; 'Native iOS gem'; 'The whole app just feels calm and clear' — calm native design praised by 156 at 4–5★, gamification requests (5) outnumbered by praise for its absence. Report 41: 'What you will not find here: being told which habit to do. Challenges against other people'; the report's do-not-add list — to-do list, journal, pet, plant, challenges, social feed, AI coach. Report 43: 'not all illustrated with pink & blue kittens and ribbons, have a psychologist's daily thought for the day baked in, nor is it incessantly asking me to note my feelings for the day'; 'you don't have to read a bunch of flowery, condescending you can do it! messages'. Report 46: 'habitica but without the stupid game mechanics'; no gamification praised (3, all 5★). Report 52: SOC_NOSOCIAL 120 (4.85, payer lift ×4.55; 100% mainland) — 'please never add social features, I just want to check in quietly by myself' (48 votes); 'no ads, no noise' praise rose in 2024–26 as reviewers compared the new ad experience. Report 54: 'Unlike some other apps which include too many unnecessary settings, this app has just what you need. No distractions, and no complications'. Report 56: users praise absence — 'no random pop ups—just put your habits in and track them'; 'track their habits without the faff'. Report 58: 'no visual noise'; 'straight to the point of habit tracking'.

title: Do not run a paid twin app beside the free app
statement: Report 11: a separate 'Lifetime Premium' binary collected one rating in six years, ran a version behind, undercut the in-app lifetime SKU by $5 and created a second entitlement surface that plausibly fed the 'lifetime subscription… suddenly cancelled' confusion.

title: No 'wait, don't go' exit discounts or countdown timers on the paywall
statement: Report 12: a lifetime offer at 17.99 that drops to 5.99 when the user tries to close, a '90% off' timer that still grants no access, and a 10× regional price jump were described as 'gross' and 'another major red flag'; 42 reviewers used the word 'scam'. The ladder is also visible to every prospect as ten SKUs on the store page. Report 13: 'Here's one star for you. You can buy the rest at a 49% discount' — the exit-intent discount tells every full-price buyer they overpaid. Report 19: customers charged $98.50/month and $99 were offered $5 and $49 lifetime plans on cancelling; all three left 1★ and one wrote 'That is probably the real value of the service' — a save-offer at 5% of the charged price converts a pricing objection into a fraud belief. Report 24: the cancellation flow offers progressively lower prices and reviewers publish it as a trick ('keep opting for cancel, you'll eventually get $5/month') — it converts some but establishes that the list price is not the real price. Report 31: countdowns that reset — 111 reviews (2.14%) — '72 hour countdown and reset back to 72 hrs'; 'like the DFS adverts, constantly on sale'; 'ran for months'; 'I'm pretty sure this type of fake sale is actually illegal'; fake urgency backfires in a self-improvement category. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'Предложение куда-то исчезло и желание купить пропало' (the offer vanished somewhere and so did the wish to buy, 2★); 'нажимаю на купит, а кнопка не активная' — time-boxed discounts that disappear lose the sale. Report 64 (Critique AI): an exit-intent 'one-time offer' after dismissing the first paywall — 80% / 75% off, '$2/month' — splits 5×1★ / 3×5★ (PAY_DISCOUNT 9, 2.15%, mean 2.44): it produced the only clean purchase-trigger record in 419 reviews and it reads as 'Preis 80% Rabatt, wenn man Zahlung abbricht. Unglaubwürdig.'; a second paywall 8 (1.91%, mean 1.25); M7: at minimum show the billed total on the discounted offer.

title: If the app is paid-only, say so in the subtitle and first screenshot
statement: Report 12: the description already said 'purchase is required to access any content' but the price label read Free — 162 reviewers (40%) wrote a 1★ review having never seen the product. A discovery and framing failure fixable at the top of the funnel. Report 25: ~7 reviewers ask for the app to be paid up front instead of 'fake-free' — an honest paid listing is preferred to a free download that gates at habit four. Report 36: 'It's not free. You can't do more than 1 habit without paying'; 'Si c'est payant mettez le là c'est caché après avoir téléchargé' — DISCLOSE 6, mean 1.67. Report 43: 'If it's a paid app then say so. You can only add 3 items before you have to upgrade' (1★); 16 'deceptive free' reviews (mean 1.25), zero after Oct 2021. Report 46: 'free forever' on the listing and website with a 3-habit tier is the angriest cluster (27, mean 1.85 — 'Potential but FREE FOREVER description is misleading'; 'IS NOT A FREE APP, it just has a free try-it-and-see mode'; 'not a one [screenshot] shows what the free version looks like'); the report's #5: remove 'free forever' and add a screenshot of the free tier. Report 50: a listing that says 5 free habits while users get 3; journal-app sync 'as advertised' that does not work; templates the listing 'promises' — fix F7. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'Пишите сразу, что ПО платное, а не встроенные покупки' — reviewers want the paid nature stated in the listing, not hidden as 'in-app purchases'. Report 60 (Mindway): 'Put the price next to your product in the App Store' — a paywalled app advertised as a free planner produced five misleading-advert reviews and five scam accusations, every one 1★.

title: A pre-use hard paywall makes every purchase non-evidence-based and non-durable
statement: Report 12: no reviewer in 404 said they paid because of a feature they had seen working; purchases were made to evaluate, under an exit discount, or on the strength of the intro — and 0 of 80 self-identified payers rated 5★. What the gate protects must be able to survive inspection: 13 buyers said it was a worse version of Apple Calendar. Report 25: an onboarding questionnaire followed by an immediate paywall — 'I did the whole survey and at the end I had to pay'; 'first 10 minutes of test… then it turns out you need a subscription' — every such reviewer left 1–2★ (mean 1.17). Report 49: a hard paywall before any use — 43.67% of the corpus attacks how it is sold; buyers convert on a 2am impulse, the Solo Leveling frame or a low point, and payers then average 1.92. Report 60 (Mindway): the pre-value paywall follows a mandatory onboarding questionnaire — 'it was really strange like answering a questionnaire. Then it asked for money right away' (1★); 'Stop playing games and get to plan'; 19 blocked plus 3 interrupted (8.80% + 1.39%) are the largest upgrade barrier. Report 64 (Critique AI): only three first-person purchase accounts in 419 — a $2/month exit discount, 75% off annual, and creator trust; 'No reviewer in this corpus says they paid because of a specific feature' — 'sold on price anchoring and creator trust, not on value demonstration'; 13 self-stated payers average 1.85, 12 of 13 report a defect or shortfall, 1 of 13 unreservedly satisfied. Report 67 (Habio): the purchase path is ad → quiz → small paid trial ('€5.49 seemed like a reasonable amount to see if the app could fulfil on the promises') → immediate add-on → auto-renewal; 995 reviewers say money left their account (mean 1.05) and only 35 describe a deliberate purchase (mean 1.23); very few buy because of the product.

title: A pre-planned, structured day is the outcome ADHD and autistic users praise
statement: Report 12: 'I lose track of time, forget to do things, and never have a plan, but that girl made sure I DID have a plan' — the one narrow, consistent praised outcome (22 reviews, mean 4.95) is being told what the day looks like. Report 25: an app titled 'Routine / Planner for ADHD' models whether a habit happened, not when — per-habit clock time with a notification at that time is the biggest unshipped feature (29, mean 3.41, 17 of them 4–5★; 9.0% of the 4★ band), clustering with one-off tasks (10), every-N-minutes reminders (4), an hour-by-hour agenda view (4) and long-term goals (7); buyers who expected time structure found a checklist ('Just a to-do list app'; 'I get to see all the things I haven't done and feel bad' — a £29.99 purchaser).
