Whoever ships routine scheduling rather than routine checking takes the ADHD-planner positioning. Report 43: a red / yellow / green time-window timeline and multi-step timers are what ADHD users name — 'when I don't have the brain power to think it just tells me what to do next'; an adult child with autism's morning routine on timers. Report 59 (Tappsk): the one-screen day plan with habits on top is what forgetful and ADHD reviewers credit ('keeps me together with my bad ADHD'). Report 60 (Mindway): organisation and structure is the most-cited benefit (15, 6.94%, mean 4.80, 13 at 5★): 'I used to be a mess, today I'm organised' (IL); 'Now I have a regular plan' (TR); 'You plan what you're gonna do at the next day'; the ADHD reviewers credit exactly this ('helps me stay on task instead of getting distracted').

title: Gendered branding narrows the audience; a neutral name is already tested
statement: Report 12: four reviewers objected to a girls-only brand ('I don't think a todo app should be targeted at one certain gender'); the developer ships a gender-neutral name in es/mx, the two highest-rated storefronts in the sample — an existing A/B result to measure. Report 55: a launch-screen photo of a woman hiker (DES_SPLASH 20, 2016–2022) — 'I purchased premium. I am uninstalling due to lack of dev response to the main photo of the girl'; an issue in a NoFap context; some ask only to turn it off. Report 64 (Critique AI): 'the quiz questions are clearly directed toward men, and didn't have a nothing option' (au, 3★, one review) — consistent with the male-coded framing throughout ('looksmax', physique, 'made me more into a man').

title: Aesthetic and a polished onboarding convert; they do not retain
statement: Report 12: 17 reviewers praised the design and 11 of them rated 1–2★; nine 5★ reviews praised the narrated intro before using the product; 'The intro before you purchase seems to have more thought put into it than the actual app itself.' See also report 9's warm shell over a thin product. Report 26: Eden converts on beauty and on the absence of a subscription, fast, often before the user has evaluated the functionality — which explains both high purchase velocity and payers rating a full point below the corpus (3.56 vs 4.570): 'I bought this one a little too soon I think'. Report 49: the questionnaire and personalised 'analysis' convert the segment it fits, but fit, disciplined reviewers told they have '40% more bad habits than the average person your age' read the assessment as a sales device (13). Report 52: the look converts within days — 'Downloaded, five minutes later bought premium'; 'within 24 hrs of the trial I bought lifetime' — while cuteness praise fell 18.5% (2017) → 2.9% (2026) and calm / clean held. Report 60 (Mindway): design praise sits beside price rejection in the same sentences — 'Es ist eigentlich sehr schön gemacht und gestaltet aber einfach zu teuer'; 'It is a good app well designed but cost abit of money' — P_DESIGN has a mean of 3.00; one dissent finds the cute styling 'too bubbly… better off to be more neutral and simple', and the report says do not redesign on that one complaint. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): praise_ui_design 6 (13.33%, 4.17★) sits beside the cap-driven uninstall — 'Really clean, minimal UI and super easy to use' then 'so I ended up uninstalling'. Report 64 (Critique AI): the onboarding analysis works as a hook — a reviewer praises the personalised analysis then refuses to pay (PERSONALIZE 5, mean 4.40); a physique scan and a projected score are the free teaser before the wall.

title: Never revoke what earlier buyers paid for when the model changes
statement: Report 13: in Aug 2017 a $3.99 one-time purchase became a subscription, unannounced in the release notes, and prior buyers were downgraded to free ('my purchase was worthless'); the mean fell 1.79 stars in nine months and no month since has been above 4.0. Subscriptions later silently expired after updates. Grandfather, always. Report 17: an abandoned one-time-purchase app relaunched as a subscription with no grandfathering, no discount and the old app left broken split one loyal base into delighted returners (4.46) and betrayed buyers (1.17); the reviewer listed the three remedies himself — grandfather, discount, or leave the old app working — none was done. Report 20: the cleanest natural experiment in the set — on 27 Jan 2021 a pay-what-you-want one-time purchase became a $39.99/year subscription, every prior buyer's entitlement was revoked and the free tier capped at 3; daily review volume went 2 → 61 → 135 at means of 1.15–1.36, 615 reviews (15.19%) describe losing a purchase, and the mean never recovered in five years (4.56 before, 1.62 after). The Feb 2021 patch was three weeks late, offered one free year instead of permanent restoration, was never announced and did not hold — revocation reports recur to Jan 2026. 'I bought your app precisely because it wasn't a subscription.' Report 23 (receiving side): an entire cohort arrived at a one-time-purchase competitor after another app revoked already-purchased premium features. Report 26: the late-2022 move from a $5–7 / €6.99 one-time unlock to $25 lifetime / $19.99 yr / $4.99 mo withdrew the unlock earlier buyers had paid for — 'the premium version I bought was taken away from me… I consider that a breach of contract' (7 in Sept–Oct 2022, recurring in 2024–25); losing what they bought is the top paid-user complaint (16.7% of explicit payers). Report 31: 189 legacy one-time / lifetime buyers (mean 1.38) found their purchase shown as 'Done Basic' after an update, reinstall or new phone, beginning at the Dec 2020 ownership change and spiking Apr 2023 — support 'told me they wouldn't honour my previous purchase', offered a free trial, or removed 'grandfathered access'; one wrote the top 'Done app review' article and then a 1★; validate receipts for every historical SKU and grandfather them automatically — worth more than any feature. Report 33: a lifetime purchase is a bet on continuity — hostile lifetime reviews are about removals, not price ('I paid for the lifetime subscription because the old app was exactly what I wanted. It never occurred to me that they would update it and actually remove things … I wish I had got the monthly subscription so I could cancel'); the 2019 switch converted a £9.99 buyer from two days earlier to one year; a lifetime model obliges the developer to migrate, not delete. Report 34: lifetime holders' only negatives are continuity — the one-time option gone after an update (Nov 2025) and a lifetime licence that 'wont be working anymore' (Jun 2026, 'False claim', 2★); 'a lifetime model obliges the developer to honour and migrate, not withdraw'. Report 42: retroactive paywalling of an installed base — 'forcing subscription, disabling buttons'; 'everything has become paid'. Report 43: a Chinese payer had to re-buy after a system reinstall (1★); 'How do I restore purchase' (1★). Report 46 (fear of it): 'Among apps that charge ¥30 for lifetime, this one wants ¥328 — I really don't dare buy it, in case it disappears'; five Chinese reviews hesitate for fear the app will 跑路. Report 48: the corpus's defining event — a paid app converted on 19 Jan 2015 to a $4.99/month subscription with a mandatory account; nine months at 2.21★ with 68.2% 1–2★ (February 1.66★, 83.9%), 92 'broken bargain' reviews (paid-then-subscription 60, forced account 25, grandfather promise broken 14 — 'Rent what you've paid for'); reversed in October 2015 (free unlimited tier) and the mean jumped to 4.62 — 'The recovery is as clear as the crash'; the theme is extinct after 2016 but still 10.7% of all one-stars. Report 52: in 2020 buyers were told their lifetime purchase is now annual; PAY_REGRESS 75 at 2.15; M1: grandfather every past entitlement explicitly ('you bought X in 2019; you keep X') — 'Honouring old purchases costs almost nothing and is the single strongest trust signal in these reviews'. Report 53: one-time buyers were pushed into a subscription — 'the VIP I bought outright has turned into a subscription? Charging twice is unreasonable' (cn, 2023); 'I had previously PAID to have full access… now they're forcing a yearly subscription' (ca, 2025); 10 in Feb–May 2026 under a new 'AppLife' plan ('all of a sudden I can't use the additional habits I created… without purchasing a $14.99 upgrade'); PAY_REGRESS 16, mean 1.50, payer lift 5.53. Report 55: 'I specifically paid for the app because it was a one-off rather than subscription, so I actually feel I should now get my money back'; 'they offered life time… the people who bought the lifetime pass are no more able to use it' (PAY_REGRESS 9, 1.33, lift 12.27). Report 57: 'I paid for the premium and now it asks for subscription??! DO NOT BUY IT' (HK, 1★, Jul 2026) — §8.2: an explicit, published grandfathering policy; 'One public DO NOT BUY IT on the storefront costs more than the subscription it was protesting'. Report 59 (Tappsk): lifetime buyers are the ones asked to pay again — BUG_PURCHASE 45 and MON_PAID_TWICE 28 of the 430 lifetime reviews; 57 lifetime reviews are 1–2★; the 2021-01 update is the largest cluster and the rest spread to 2026: 'Покупала версию «Навсегда», спустя год написали, что пора опять оплатить «навсегда» ещё раз' (bought Forever; a year later told it was time to pay forever again); 'Купила навсегда, а получается не навсегда'.

title: No paid acquisition into an auto-converting trial in frictionless-payment markets
statement: Report 13: a Douyin campaign drove Chinese installs into a 7-day trial that opened a ¥208/yr subscription with password-free payment and no authentication step; China became 73% one-star and 51% of all involuntary-charge reviews. Where the payment rail has no friction, the app must add an explicit confirmation step. Report 67 (Habio): paid Instagram / Facebook acquisition into a web quiz and a $1 auto-converting trial across 81 storefronts; volume tripled in the web-funnel era (572 reviews, mean 1.17, scam language 51.4%).

title: The app must open offline — never block launch on a network call
statement: Report 13: a blocking in-app 'update in progress' migration bricked the app on launch in three waves (Nov 2019, Oct 2020 at 5.9% of that month's reviews, Sep 2025 → Aug 2026), destroyed data on reinstall ('lost almost 3 years of habit tracking') and locked out paying subscribers; 'Will not launch without internet'. Report 14: 'works fully offline' was one of two named reasons a reviewer chose this app over rivals already tried. Report 16: 'why in the world does ticking a box require connectivity!' — 9 reviews, zero 5★; a remote worker without internet for days could not use the app. Report 25: one reviewer names iCloud sync as the stuck state on first run ('shows synchronising with iCloud and nothing happens') — a first-run data path, not rendering; add a skip-setup / continue-offline path. Report 28: offline use is reported as paid and then removed; 6 complain about an internet requirement (mean 3.83). Report 46: free users cannot check off a habit offline ('ticking off habits while offline are locked behind a paywall', 7, mean 2.14) — the mechanism behind China's 'offline mode while online' cluster (16 of 17 Chinese, Sep 2019 – Apr 2020, consistent with the backend being unreachable from the mainland); the report's #14 allows offline check-off in the free tier. Report 47: a crash loop after logging in to the free backup (6, Feb 2024 – May 2025) with log-out as the only workaround; a white screen when typing a habit name (13, 2020–24). Report 53: in mainland China the launch screen hangs for seconds to 10+ minutes from build 2.8.0 (Dec 2022) through Aug 2026 — BUG_LAUNCH 30 of cn's 273 (10.99%); 'with a network connection it won't open; it only works offline' points at a blocking network call (analytics, paywall or ad SDK slow or blocked in China); F5: test cold start with no network and with blocked endpoints.

title: Public review replies answer the specific complaint — never canned, never argue price, never press a reviewer to change the rating
statement: Report 13: copy-paste replies restating Apple's cancellation instructions under reviews had a mean of 1.40 with zero 5★, and multiple reviewers edited their rating downward afterwards ('If you're just going to copy-paste an answer again, don't leave one at all'). Report 25: 'the developer preferred to argue about what I could see on my end' — an argumentative support reply ended a trial. Report 31: a support reply 'full of emojis' offered a free trial instead of honouring a purchase; a public developer response was edited after the fact. [Merged from C260: Report 46: 6 reviews (0.28%, mean 1.33, all 2021 or later, five in 2024–26) say a public developer reply was rude or defensive — 'snarky remarks about working for free and making an overpriced app isn't the way to do it'; 'developer takes any criticism with such a nasty attitude'; 'After reading developer's response I am degrading rating to 1 star from 2… 5/5 rating for app but 0/5 for your behaviour' (13298363427) — and 2 say the developer pressed them to change their review ('the developer keeps contacting me to pressure me into changing my review', 11709301622). Every one of these reviews went from 'too expensive' to 'and the developer is hostile', a reputational cost no pricing change recovers, while 53 reviews (mean 4.94) praise the same developer's private support. The report's zero-cost fix: thank, state the free tier and lifetime option factually, never argue value, never ask for a rating change.] Report 60 (Mindway): five explicit warn-offs ('Don't waste your money'; 'Don't ever download this app'; 'Don't download if you need for a routine'), all 1★, remain visible on the listing at the point of decision — an upgrade barrier the report counts alongside billing trust damage. Report 67 (Habio): a templated public developer reply under reviews is mentioned by 19 reviewers; §8.6: no identical public replies.

merged_from.title: Never argue price in a public review reply, and never ask a reviewer to change their rating
merged_from.note: C260 (report 46: rude or price-defending public replies and pressure to change a rating) and C189 (reports 13, 25, 31, 43: copy-paste and argumentative replies) are one rule about how a developer responds in public; both lower ratings after the reply

title: No weekly billing tier
statement: Report 13: weekly billing introduced in 2024 ($3.99, €6, R$29.90, ₽499 per week) drew the corpus's most hostile pricing language — 'insane', 'immoral', 'Per week! I didn't even test it' — and price complaints rose to 26.7% of 2025 reviews. Report 60 (Mindway): weekly pricing reads as expensive — $7/week and €8/week both cited with outrage ('8€/WOCHE… Frech'), and the annual is chosen to escape the weekly; E3: offer a cheap one-time purchase or a low monthly tier alongside the weekly — nobody objects to paying something (M_COST_NOTED 3 at 4.33★).

title: Never shrink a tier someone already holds — a paid tier's limits, or free capacity a user has already filled
statement: Report 16: Pro was capped at 3 habits, then 6, for 29 months; a cap on the paid tier has no monetisation function (there is no higher tier to drive to) and two of three buyers who paid specifically to escape the free cap hit the next one and rated 3★ — 'A paid user pays $40/year just to create only 6 habits simultaneously?' Report 48: 23 users who built history on 10 or 7 free trackers found the cap shrunk under them (mean 2.22) — retroactive reduction lands on the longest-tenured users; fix #2: never reduce existing users' free capacity. Report 50: grandfather existing free users at 5 — the two cap-cut reviews describe loss, not a low starting cap; experiment: grandfather-vs-migrate. (Consolidation after report 50: the title was widened from 'Never cap the tier someone has already paid for' because the Report 48 and Report 50 evidence is free users losing capacity they had already filled — grandfathering is the fix in both.) Report 59 (Tappsk): the 2021-01 cut shrank free capacity users had already filled — habits removed from the free tier for existing users and a 20-task cap on lists people were using; 2021-01 was the busiest month of the corpus (372 reviews) and 2021-03 the lowest-rated (4.19★). Report 65 (Rabit): capping the free tier after years of generous use drove the E1/E2 cohort out — a user since 2020 uninstalled in 2023 ('antes era mejor'), another had recommended it to about 30 people ('ate eles se importarem mais em ganhar dinheiro que ajudar os outros'); COMP_WORSE 11 (mean 2.09), all Dec 2022 or later — 'The competitive position was not lost to a competitor's feature. It was given away'.

merged_from.old_title: Never cap the tier someone has already paid for
merged_from.note: reports 48 and 50 attached retroactive free-cap reductions (10 → 7 → 3; 5 → 3) to this point; the evidence is about taking back capacity already in use, paid or free — cap size itself stays in C007, slot reuse in C219

title: A trial must end in a usable free tier, not a cliff
statement: Report 16: a well-liked no-card 28-day trial that dropped to a one-habit tier read as a bait-and-switch — 'it encourages people to start habits and continue them for three weeks and then hits you with a steep bill' — and was the fastest-growing negative (2.4% → 7.2%). Taper, warn earlier and in-app, or keep the streak read-only.

title: When a trial or subscription ends, the user lands on a usable free tier with read-only history — never a cliff
statement: Report 16: a cancelled payer could not edit, view or even complete the one habit the free tier allows — 'It's my habit for walking my dog, who is recently deceased… I guess the app is bricked for me now.' A lapsed subscriber with read-only history is a resubscription candidate; one whose data is hostage is a permanent loss. Report 16 (trial side): a well-liked no-card 28-day trial that dropped to a one-habit tier read as a bait-and-switch — 'it encourages people to start habits and continue them for three weeks and then hits you with a steep bill' — and was the fastest-growing negative (2.4% → 7.2%). Taper, warn earlier and in-app, or keep the streak read-only. Report 60 (Mindway): with a free tier of 1–3 tasks there is no usable free tier to land on — a lapsed or refused subscriber has nowhere to go but the wall.

merged_from.title: A trial must end in a usable free tier, not a cliff
merged_from.note: C192 (trial ends in a cliff) and C193 (lapsed subscriber's data held hostage) describe one transition rule from two entry points

title: Do not paywall content the user already bought elsewhere
statement: Report 16: the daily lessons and articles restate the Atomic Habits book; paywalling them was the packaging decision reviewers found hardest to forgive ('I already read the book which only cost me $15 one time') and praise for the content fell 6.8% → 1.2% once it went behind the wall. Content free, slots paid was the corpus's proposal.

title: Premium pricing on a trust-based personal brand spends the brand
statement: Report 16: $120/yr on the official Atomic Habits app produced the lowest-rated theme in the corpus — personal attacks on James Clear ('How to ruin your brand overnight'; 'changed my view of James') — plus 69 'cash grab / greedy / predatory' reviews with zero 5★; the only negative theme still growing in 2026. Report 24: Duke University / Dan Ariely / behavioural-science framing (736, mean 3.865; 1.77% of 5★) is thrown back the moment trust breaks — 'they use behavioural science to help you make positive change, but also to get you to subscribe'; 'discredited for falsifying results… I no longer trust this app'; a credibility asset raises the expected standard of conduct.

title: A subscription is a promise of continued delivery — back it with a visible cadence
statement: Report 17: an app relaunched on a subscription went 3.5 years without a release while still charging; four of its last six reviews were about abandonment and the one paying 3★ stated the deal plainly — 'If we can get iPad and watch apps along with more regular debugging, I will keep paying. Otherwise, I am switching to Blocos.' Subscribers believe they are funding development; when it stops, the subscription has no story, and a 'lifetime' tier sold against a dormant build compounds the grievance. Report 20: an annual subscription was charged for seven years against a product that shipped nothing new; the 4★ band told the developer exactly what would make it a 5 and almost none of it was built. Report 24: repetitive coaching content (103, mean 2.660) in a content subscription. Report 31: 'a subscription for a checklist is unjustifiable' — the subscription came with removals, lag and no visible new delivery. Report 41: a German reviewer chose the subscription over lifetime deliberately — 'I want the app to still work in 3 years'. Report 55: 'It's not like a yoga or meditation app, which is constantly adding new videos/content, so why a yearly fee?!?' — an annual fee reads as a promise of ongoing development, and reviewers measured the app by its update log; M3: price the subscription only on features that work. Report 57: 2★ reviews concentrate the oldest users hit by silent tier changes (long_tenure_user 10.3% vs 2.95%). Report 59 (Tappsk): stagnation is the dominant criticism of the latest era — 'nothing changes' (NEG_DEV_PROMISE 1.1%) alongside subscriptions still being sold. Report 60 (Mindway): benefit claims (habit outcome, motivation, wellbeing) peak in the burst period and vanish to zero in the 14-review tail while paywall complaints rise to 28.57% — 'the corpus's least comfortable pattern' for a subscription product.

title: Shift the whole day's schedule at once (global schedule shift)
statement: Report 17: 'there is no other app that allows you to easily globally shift a schedule, rather than moving all tasks individually… invaluable for my erratic work and sleep schedule… jet lag' — named as the one capability no competitor matches, and absent from the store listing. Single source, high value.

title: Edit one instance of a repeating block without changing the series; a slipped block pushes the ones after it
statement: Report 17: two independent 4★ users — 'I can only change ALL workout blocks in the sequence for today and everyday going forward'; adding ten minutes to a block made the next one overlap 'rather than being pushed to 7:16am'. A time-blocking app whose blocks cannot absorb a real day's slippage fails when most needed; 'If these two features are added it is definitely 5⭐️.'

title: System calendar integration — see appointments inside the plan
statement: Report 17: calendar integration existed in the predecessor, was removed at relaunch ('I loved seeing my appointments, too'), and four years later is the single feature keeping the most recent payer from switching to a competitor. Reports 12 and 13 also carry calendar-integration requests. Report 41: calendar view / calendar integration requested by 7. Report 50: Apple / Google Calendar integration requested by 3 (4.67). Report 52: calendar integration requested (41, weak).

title: Never meter the completion action — a free cap may limit habits, never check-offs
statement: Report 18: the free tier advertised 10 habits but ticking a habit consumed a 14-per-week memo quota (two check-offs a day), so tapping 'complete' produced a purchase sheet; 139 reviews (6.79%, mean 2.32★, 19.6% of all 1★) and five years of 'stops working on day 3/5/6/10'. A habit tracker that refuses to record a completion in the first week demonstrates that it does not work, to a user deciding whether it works — 'I was 90% ready to buy… I just lost all feeling for it and deleted it.' Report 25: from Nov 2025 editing an existing habit — including the ones onboarding created — was reported as paid; five 1–2★ reviews, zero before that date; 'never gate editing of habits the onboarding created'. Report 33: a free-tier cap of ~15 check-ins per week (Oct 2020 → 2024) drew 29 reviews at mean 2.00 — the worst-rated monetisation mechanism, 4.2% of E3 — and punished the most engaged free users ('three habits is reasonable. The problem … I can't check into those habits more than 15 times a week'; 'limiting the number of check ins per week ruins the whole point').

title: A user-set partial-completion threshold — a 'good day' below 100%
statement: Report 18: a traffic-light day status that turns green at a user-chosen ~60–80% is the most-articulated praise in a 2,048-review corpus (92 reviews at 4.24★; explicit partial-completion praise at 4.80★): 'with percentage apps you aim for 100 and suffer; here you switch to "green is good enough"'; 'a 60% check feels like 100% achievement'; 'I never feel guilted or pressured'. Rest / postpone / skip options sit alongside it. Some users want it harder (a must-do habit that gates the light, a 90% threshold) — so the threshold is a setting, not a constant. Report 23: a 6-of-8 day rendered as ✗ is named as demotivating and the reason people keep a second app; render a partial ring, not a failure mark. Report 26: partial completion earns nothing (all-or-nothing garden growth, 20 reviews, mean 2.80); ship partial credit as a setting, with full completion still rewarded more — the existing 'no wither' option is the precedent. Report 41: a daily completion percentage ring with partial credit is the quiet differentiator (40, mean 4.67) — 'as someone who suffers from perfectionism and binary thinking… you're never thinking about the cliff edge of losing a streak… made this a thing i actually use and bought over the hundreds of habit apps i browsed'; 'a meh day means about 70%— C work, but a better baseline'; two want weighted habits, one dislikes 'out of 100%'.

title: A light social layer that is explicitly not a social network
statement: Report 18: seeing other users' routines, copying them and sending cheer messages was praised by 66 reviewers (3.22%, mean 4.45★) precisely because 'it isn't like SNS'; a teacher chose the app over rivals because its social features are lighter, and following a friend was described as a shared exchange diary. Very strong only in Korea (3.69%); emerging elsewhere. Report 24: Circles — an in-app feed with comments and writing prompts — runs at mean 3.897 (0.85%), neither a driver nor a grievance. Report 52: a minority asks for accountability buddies (74, weak) against a larger 'never add social' group (120). Report 58: following friends requested once alongside cross-device use. Report 64 (Critique AI): a community feed is 'priceless' to one payer, 'a probably fake community page' to another, and over-moderated to a third (R5: loosen comment moderation); only paying reviewers describe it.

title: Onboarding lets the user author their own routine first — suggested plans, surveys and pledges are optional
statement: Report 18: the lowest-rated theme (34 reviews, mean 2.03★) was an onboarding that ran a long survey, built the routine for the user, assumed a 9-to-5 weekday life, demanded a signed pledge and then showed the paywall — 'I wanted to create my own routine not have you suggest one for me. Hence the name of your app. MY routine not your routine'; 'an app that wants to turn you into a very ordinary machine'. Shift workers, night workers and parents were excluded before they reached the product. Report 24: the forced first habit ('drink water', gated three days, then breakfast) is the concrete example inside every larger personalisation complaint; the fix is an 'I already do this' branch, keeping the default. Report 25: an onboarding questionnaire suggests starter habits (free) — and from Nov 2025 those starter habits could not be edited without paying. Report 26: onboarding offers preset-only habits and custom habits could not be created (8 verified, mean 2.50). Report 49: cannot add own tasks 80 and cannot edit the generated programme 70 are the top themes of the 3★ and 4★ bands (9.43% / 15.09% among payers) — 'the design is excellent, the idea is right, and I cannot make it fit my life'; custom tasks shipped mid-2025 cut 'cannot add' 10.2% → 1.0%; still needed: week-by-week edits, swapping running, entering existing fitness. Report 60 (Mindway): a mandatory onboarding questionnaire followed immediately by the paywall ('answering a questionnaire. Then it asked for money right away'; 'Stop playing games and get to plan') and preset packs the user must delete rather than a routine they author; one reviewer asks for '3 complete day schedules' to pick from so 'adding and subtracting would not be so overwhelming'. Report 67 (Habio): preset routines only — 'What if I want the routine to include a workout but not meditation?'; REQ_CUSTOM_ROUTINE 18 and NEG_NO_CUSTOM_HABIT 9, 'the most consistent product request from people who got past the paywall'; forced intentions / rewards / reflections steps (7).

title: Never destroy user work at the paywall
statement: Report 18: two users each spent an hour building routines, were asked to pay to save them, and lost the work anyway. Work the user has already done is never the hostage of a purchase sheet — save it, then ask. (The labelling half of the original point — 'reviewers cannot tell what they are buying' — lives on C110 and C218, to which the same cards are attached.) Report 53: reviewers over the free limit hit the paywall when editing an existing habit.

merged_from.old_title: Never destroy user work at the paywall; label paid features before they are used
merged_from.note: the original title bundled 'label paid features before use', which duplicates C110 (legible free/paid boundary) and C218 (listing truth); narrowed to the one rule no other point carries

title: Aggregated, searchable journal / diary across days
statement: Report 18: people wrote daily reflections for years and could read them back only one date at a time; diary/memo aggregation, a calendar of entries and search was the highest-rated request theme in the corpus (22 reviews, mean 4.68★) and the reason a lifetime buyer switched to a competitor. Report 53: a list of all notes, and notes on the calendar (47-vote jp review).

title: Swappable day templates / routine modes for irregular schedules
statement: Report 18: shift-work / variable-day routine profiles were a meaningful request (31, 4.03★) from 2022; 'routine modes' shipped Dec 2025 as Pro and won back a churned subscriber ('神✨'; a nurse: 'rain in a drought') but shipped buggy — switching a mode rewrote past days, modes applied forward-only, edits did not persist, and the feature was buried in Settings.

title: Let users hide surfaces they don't use — tabs, social, recommendations, streaks
statement: Report 18: 'UI complexity / can't find things' was the largest negative theme by count (149, 7.28%) and high-priority in all three eligible storefronts (KR 6.75%, JP 10.76%, US 8.33%), rising as features accumulated; an ADHD reviewer asked to hide social, recommendations, to-do, diary and streaks; another asked the developer explicitly not to add more. Report 24: retained users ask for a 'just my routine' mode — coaching, community, discovery and cross-app promotion below the fold or hidden. Report 33: hide friends, challenges and journal until enabled — 'simple mode' defaults. Report 36: daily motivational messages loved by 13 (all 5★) and disliked by 4 ('strangely negative — talking about destruction or a kind of wasteland'; 'Wish I could disable those') — make them switchable, don't rewrite them. Report 43: the report's #2 fix is a settings toggle for the skip-journal popup and calendar header introduced in the redesign — 'should have option to TURN OFF'. Report 52: the 2026 'habit ball' collection could not be hidden.

title: Photo / media / URL attached to a habit, memo or diary entry
statement: Report 18: ~25 reviews across KR and JP asked to attach a photo, media or link to a habit, memo or diary entry. Report 47: a photo attached to each check-in ('motivation photos' per habit) is a purchase trigger and part of the named differentiator; attaching a photo crashed the app in January 2021 (10 reviews in 16 days); photo multi-select shipped within a week of the request. Report 52: photos in check-in logs and notes are 'the most repeated single ask' within the largest request theme — 'please add photos to check-ins!! I really want photos!!!' (2017 → 2025). Report 57: photo attachment shipped but capped at 3 even with Premium (9 request more). Report 59 (Tappsk): U_ATTACH_REQ 223 (1.47%) — REQ_PHOTO 124, REQ_NOTES 106 ('ГДЕ ПРИКРЕПИТЬ ФОТО' — WHERE DO I ATTACH A PHOTO); one of the requests that never stops across eight years.

title: No sign-up wall before first use
statement: Report 18: 'sign-up / login required or broken' was a very strong signal (70, 3.42%, mean 3.13★); a sign-up wall before any trial was a ranked purchase barrier, and Japan's form demanded e-mail, phone and real name before the product was visible. Distinct from having an account system: the account should be offered when there is something to protect. Report 27: 'no account required' is praised as a feature (4, mean 5.00 — 'so many habit apps are expensive and require an account'; 'All this without asking for my personal details') and the listing's no-data-collection label is part of the positioning; a required account 'rules out ad-funded or data-funded models'. Report 29: 'the fact I didn't even have to list my email sold me' — do not require an account; adding one for billing has its own cost. Report 41: 'No account or login is needed' is a reason to choose the app; one payer cancelled rather than enable iCloud. Report 48: 39 reviews (1.64) objected to a forced account on a local tracker in 2015–18; the complaint ended when iCloud sync replaced the account. Report 50: sign-in required before first use, Apple or Google only (see C035). Report 55: a registration screen first; F6 — never block first use. Report 56: 'I tried a couple of them on the App Store and hated them immediately. They usually ask 20 questions just to get started'; 'no sign-in wall' named as why it stuck. Report 58: §8.5 do not require an account to start.

title: Bill App Store users through the App Store — never route them to an off-store subscription the app cannot show or cancel
statement: Report 19: the app was the front door to a web-billed subscription that did not appear in Apple's subscription list, carried non-refundable website terms, and could be cancelled only by email; 18 of 105 reviewers (17.14%) described the consequence, 19 were charged after cancelling, 19 were charged with no subscription they recognised, and 60 distinct reviews flowed from a customer who could not see or stop their own plan. If a web funnel must exist, the app shows the active plan, price, next charge date and a working cancel button. Report 24 (43,469 reviews): the largest theme in the corpus — 5,791 core billing disputes (13.32%, mean 1.110, 94.2% 1★; 52.4% of all 1★; 38% of 2024–26) — follows mechanically from selling the subscription through a web checkout (Chargebee; 'Fabulous SAS' on statements): it is invisible in Apple Subscriptions, cancelling in the App Store does nothing, Apple cannot refund it, and the user is routed to a 250-character web form with no phone; 212 escalated to their bank, the BBB, the FTC or a lawyer. The failure is dated — quarterly rate 5.4% (2023Q1) → 12.0% (Q4) → 33.1% (2024Q4) → ~50% from 2025Q2 — and an earlier 2018–19 episode was fixed in one month (Dec 2019: 12.7% → 2.6%, mean 2.884 → 4.206), so it is recoverable. Reviews that mention money average 2.006; those that do not, 4.356. Report 33: web purchases through Paddle did not unlock the iPhone (18 days; 6+ weeks) and had no in-app cancel; refunds were routed to Apple and then refused ('denied a refund due to the company's arrangement with Apple'). Report 59 (Tappsk): the one case where off-store billing was forced (App Store payments blocked for Russian users from 2022-03) shows the cost: the direct-card route is praised by those who wanted to pay (54 of 74 payment-route reviews are 5★) but produces charges after deletion and a subscription the phone cannot show or cancel ('После отмены подписки приложение каждый раз пытается списать с карты средства' — after cancelling, the app keeps trying to charge the card) — if an off-store route is unavoidable, it needs in-app cancellation and bounded retries ([[C232]]). Report 67 (Habio): a web quiz funnel from Instagram / Facebook ads sold subscriptions billed off-store — MON_OFFSTORE 137 (6.68%) 'not displayed in the AppStore and the receipt comes directly from Habio'; 'even after you delete the app you will still be charged $50 every 180 days unless you redownload the app and cancel through there'; MON_WEB_FUNNEL 30 paid on the website before installing; the listing still says payment is 'charged to iTunes Account' and cancellable in Account Settings; web purchases were not linked to app accounts so buyers could not restore ('couldn't find any purchase history'); U_CANCEL_TRAP 597 (29.11%, mean 1.03); off-store complaints 13.81% of the 2023-07 → 2024-02 era.

title: No second, separately-cancelled add-on subscription
statement: Report 19: an e-book/PDF plan at $17–$45/month was enrolled on top of the programme subscription with its own cancellation path; 11 of 105 (10.48%) across five storefronts described it, and two reviewers on two continents reported the same asymmetry — the main plan cancels, the add-on does not. Collapse add-ons into the main plan or delete them. Report 24: 324 reviews (0.75%, mean 1.398) describe being enrolled in a multi-app bundle (Clarify, Shape, Sphere…) during onboarding through near-identical full-screen offers whose decline is a small corner 'skip'; the $39.99 + $29.99 same-day pair is the signature in hundreds of 2024–26 reviews, each subscription must be cancelled separately, and 338 report a charge with no consent at all (mean 1.047, the lowest in the corpus). Bundle complaints went 0.30% → 0.06% → 0.17% → 2.62% across eras.

title: No conditional refunds — no proof-of-use requirement, and an advertised guarantee is honoured on request
statement: Report 19: refunds were refused for 25 of 105 (23.81%); a 'prove 14 consecutive days of use' condition (6), a 30-day money-back guarantee that was advertised and then denied (3 — all three bought because of it), and retention bots answering refund requests (5) turned refusal into fraud allegations, chargebacks and an FTC report. A guarantee you will not honour is a fraud allegation you have pre-purchased; the refund is cheaper than the dispute. Report 24: refund refusals (968, 2.23%, mean 1.070) quote near-verbatim T&C clauses across years and markets — 'the set-up fee for the trial period is non-refundable' and 'unless cancelled at least 24 hours before the renewal date'; 227 reviewers hold an e-mail or screenshot confirming cancellation and were charged anyway. When a refund is actually reached it works and reviewers upgrade in place (1★ → 4★), so the failure is reaching it. Report 30: 'quise cancelar suscripción… no puedo recuperar el dinero' — a refund dead end for an accidental subscription. Report 33: refunds routed to Apple, then refused — a child's 598 RMB refused twice; 45 refund reviews (mean 2.16), 13 from Korea. Report 43: a refund refused inside the EU 14-day withdrawal period (DE, 1★). Report 48: refund requests 23 at mean 1.04★ — the lowest-mean theme in the corpus with n > 10. Report 49: a marketed '66-day money-back guarantee' cited 13 times (1.85) with undisclosed conditions (66 logged days at ≥ 50% completion — 'Very misleading'), met conditions and no refund, a confirmed PayPal transfer that never arrived, 'nowhere to be found'; 21 of 36 refund requests refused or ignored (1.14) — 'a marketing promise generating one-star reviews at a higher rate than having no promise would'. Report 54: every refund request (5, all 1★) was caused by a failed entitlement, not dissatisfaction with the feature set. Report 55: refund requests 19 (1.11), 17 from payers, 9 from the UK. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_REFUND 159 (1.05%, 1.94★) — refunds reported granted ('Все вернули! Оперативно') and refused ('техподдержка не видит причины возврата' — support sees no reason for a refund; 'I was rejected to refund of 20$ annual subscription'). Report 60 (Mindway): four refund requests, all 1★, all US, all after an annual charge — refused ('NO EXCEPTIONS OF A REFUND'), no route found, 'this needs to be reported', 'I wish I could get my money back'. Report 64 (Critique AI): a parent bought for a 12-year-old found it too advanced and asked for a refund in a review; 'would not let me have my money back' after a 'cancel anytime' promise. Report 67 (Habio): MON_REFUND_DENIED 242 (11.80%, mean 1.01); an advertised money-back guarantee cited as not honoured by 42 (2.05%) — 'Money back policy requires that you use the product for 21 days consecutively!'; 10 invoke the EU 14-day withdrawal right; refunds granted in 10 (mean 2.80), 3 of them via the bank or PayPal rather than the developer.

title: If you position on ADHD or executive-function help, cancellation must be the easiest flow in the product
statement: Report 19: 13 of 105 (12.38%) accused the product of targeting people with ADHD because they will forget to cancel — 'preying on ADHDers they know may not remember to cancel'; friction a neurotypical user calls annoying this audience calls predatory, because the marketing itself asserts they cannot complete multi-step tasks. The ADHD positioning and a retention funnel are incompatible; six reviewers escalated to banks, card networks and the FTC. Report 24: an app whose subtitle is 'ADHD Help' has ADHD users as its angriest segment (933, mean 2.747, 54.2% 1–2★) and 201 of them (mean 1.159) say the cancellation design exploits the condition — 'they know because of your poor executive function that you won't take the extra effort to find the cancel button'; the segment grew 30× across eras (0.20% → 6.01%) as the marketing worked, and the outcome got worse. Either build for the condition or stop claiming it. Report 25: the same segment that rates the product highest (ADHD, mean 4.44) writes the most cutting paywall criticism — pop-ups 'hyper désagréable et malvenu pour des TDAH'; 'profit off of your disability'. Report 60 (Mindway): an ADHD-positioned routine planner whose subscription four users could not cancel and whose paid trial billed within hours — the positioning makes the billing failures a betrayal of the audience it names. Report 67 (Habio): ads pitching ADHD help and a 'bionic reading' tool; USE_ADHD 97 (4.73%, mean 1.25 — below even the non-seeded 1.31), 35.05% refund denied, 23.71% describe dark patterns: 'en sachant pertinemment à quel point le TDAH est difficile à vivre au quotidien notamment vis à vis de la gestion financière'; 'they're using your own ADHD against you' (UK, where ADHD is 14.47% of reviews).

title: A bare checklist or task-slot paywall cannot carry a premium price — it is compared to Reminders, Notes, alarms and paper, free on every phone, and loses
statement: Report 19: 13 of 105 (12.38%) said the phone's alarm, Notes, calendar, paper or Excel did the same job for free ('If you can set an alarm on your phone you don't need this app'); at $45–$99 that ceiling read as theft rather than expense and produced 96 one-star reviews. A product charging above a few dollars must deliver what a checklist structurally cannot — real personalisation, coaching content, human accountability, or data the user could not assemble. Report 23: 68 one-star reviews (0.94%) make the coherent case 'this is a checklist, iOS Reminders does it free, and it cost me money' — a positioning failure: the listing sold a to-do list rather than streak psychology plus HealthKit automation; Apple Reminders is the low-end competitor (9 mentions, mean 3.67). Report 25: among people who hit the paywall the comparison set is Apple Reminders, Health, Notes and a paper notebook (nine reviews explicitly) — a free tier must beat Reminders, not beat Streaks; ~7 reviewers would rather the app were honestly paid up front than 'fake-free'. Report 27 (the other side): a free, minimal, account-less tracker wins the category comparison outright — 13 reviewers explicitly rejected rivals over price ('Don't get streaks for $6. 👎 Get this!'; 'way better than those paid apps'), and switched-from-competitor rose 0% → 16.7% across eras without the app changing; as the category monetises harder, the free position sharpens by market drift. Report 29: 52 comparison shoppers (14.21%) arrived after rejecting paywalled trackers ('downloaded 20 habit tracking apps and none was satisfactory'; 'premium this, subscription that… here it's just free, like properly FREE') — the app 'wins a bake-off it never enters', so competitors' pricing drives its installs. Report 30: every reviewer calling the app 'too basic' also objects to paying — 'a value complaint wearing a feature costume'; do not add features in response. Report 31: 'How is this app worth $499.99?'; '$90/pY for what?' — simplicity is quoted both as the reason to use the app and the reason a subscription is unjustified. Report 60 (Mindway): the same verdict from buyers — 10 (4.63%, mean 1.50), five of them confirmed payers, say the paid product is 'nothing more than preloaded to-do lists'; 'just a suggestion list'; 'basically just a load of lists and reminders'; 'I cannot believe I spent $40 to use this app for one day' — and six non-buyers price it against Reminders, Notes, Calendar and paper ([[C277]]). (Consolidation after report 60: C277 was created by the report 60 merge and folded in here the same pass — the report's D2 'sell the outcome, not the task slots' is the constructive half of this rule.) [Merged from C277: Report 60 (Mindway, 216 reviews): price objections are relative, not absolute — 13 reviewers (6.02%, mean 1.69, no 4★ or 5★ among them) reject the price by comparing it to a substitute they already own, and 6 (2.78%) name it: Apple Reminders, Notes, Calendar, a paper planner — '8€/WOCHE für einen Tagesplaner, den man sich auch selbst im Kalender bauen kann. Frech.' (€8 a week for a day planner you could build in your calendar. Cheeky.); 'einfach zu teuer dafür dass ich das auch gratis in meinen Notizen machen kann'; 'paper planner is cheaper than this LOL'; 'Just use your remind app it's the same thing'. The report's reading: 'the competitive set Mindway is being priced against is not other habit apps — it is the free tools already on the phone', and a count-based paywall ('you have used your 2 free tasks') invites exactly that comparison because task slots are what those tools give away, whereas guided routines, progress history and a self-care library are not comparable to Reminders — 'the corpus shows Mindway losing a fight it chose' (D2: sell the outcome, not the task slots). Related: [[C214]] (a bare checklist cannot carry a premium price), [[C133]] (gate on capability, not quantity), [[C004]] (price against subscription competitors).] Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'Asked for a payment in simple app like this' (MN, 1★) — an objection to paying for simplicity, the flip side of the app's own positioning; one of only two flat price objections in 45 reviews. Report 64 (Critique AI): 'I don't think any one is gonna pay 40$ just to check off a list'; 'I lost 40 dollars on something I could've just done on the notes app'.

merged_from.title: Price the paid tier against what the phone already gives away — a paywall that sells task slots, reminders or a checklist is compared to Apple Reminders, Notes and paper, and loses
merged_from.note: C277 (report 60: price objections are relative — 13 reviewers compare a $7/week task-slot paywall to Reminders, Notes, Calendar and paper; 'the competitive set is the free tools already on the phone') restates C214 (reports 19, 23, 25, 27, 29, 30, 31, 34, 42, 46: the phone's alarm, Notes, calendar, paper or Excel do the same job free, so a checklist priced above them reads as theft); one pricing rule, so the newer point is folded in and the title widened to name the paywall shape that triggers the comparison

title: Support reply time must be shorter than any cancellation deadline it serves
statement: Report 19: a 24-hour pre-renewal cancellation cut-off was served by a support queue that replied in 48 hours — 'They said cancel within 24 hours before and they take more than 48 hrs to get back to you' — an unsatisfiable deadline by construction; support otherwise ran silent, circular, or hostile ('a rude lecture via email about how I signed up on purpose') for 17 of 105. Report 24: support unresponsive or automated-only in 947 reviews (2.18%, mean 1.528); the specific obstacle named 17 times is a web contact form with a 250-character limit and no telephone number. Report 49: reviewers emailed for days about refunds, were told the app is not eligible for an App Store refund, then hit a 404 on App Support. Report 59 (Tappsk): payment-route questions were answered 'within 10–20 minutes' in 2022 and earned 5★; billing e-mails that go unanswered earn 1★ — the same company, different channels. Report 60 (Mindway): five of thirteen payers used a 1★ review as their support channel; 'I am getting no help and stopping the subscription' — a support route that is slower than the review prompt turns billing tickets into permanent 1★ reviews. Report 67 (Habio): 19 reviews quote a published support response time of up to four business days against a three-day trial — 'How convenient when they offer a 3-day trial'; MON_TRIAL_SHORT 9; §8.3: make the trial longer than support's own response time; §8.6: first human reply within 24 hours.

title: A forgiving long-run measure — cumulative or decaying credit that a missed day does not zero — alongside streaks
statement: Report 20: a non-streak percentage that drops when a day is missed rather than zeroing — 'missing one day and breaking my streak tends to send me into a spiral where I give up'; described as logarithmic and 'much closer to psychological reality'. The product's one genuine differentiator (38 explicit, the highest-affection language in a 4,048-review corpus; unclaimed by any competitor), broken by a 2021 rewrite when the score stopped decaying and never restored — 'Please bring that algorithm back!' Users who asked for a streak counter asked for it alongside, never instead of, the strength score. Distinct from C201 (a day-level partial-completion threshold): this is the long-run measure. Report 10: replacing cumulative Journeys with consecutive-streak Self-Care Areas was the lowest-rated change in a 70,041-review corpus (mean 2.76, 21 of 49 one-star); chronic-illness and ADHD users say a streak-only model is structurally incompatible with their lives. Ship the forgiving measure next to streaks, not instead of them. Report 24: paying users name 'missing a day is not punished' among the things they value most. Report 25: a paying user describes the day view as 'all the things I haven't done' and feeling bad — the un-forgiving frame is a churn reason. Report 26: the garden only grows if every habit is checked that day — 'If I miss only one out of 6 of my habits, nothing happens. Behaviourally this means people will say it's not worth trying'; 'doing 90% should be rewarded'; 'No room for off days… I'm human' (20 verified, mean 2.80) — while 25 (mean 4.76) praise the app for being gentle and streak-free; partial credit as a setting reconciles the two. Report 28: decay that resets 'ALL of your progress' after a bad week is read as data loss; a gentler or optional decay with a visible backup state would separate punishment from bugs. Report 41: the non-binary percentage ring rather than streaks is why a perfectionist bought. Report 54: 'the evidence of consistency and the punishment for breaking it are separable, and this user base wants the first without the second' — colour-density calendars, per-habit completion counts and monthly totals, not a streak counter with a reset (D4, 48 reviewers). Report 57: 'This is the only habit-building app that didn't make me feel like a failure for missing a day'; a detailed proposal asks for a skipped / failed distinction to keep it that way. Report 58: 'an effective habit tracker that did not discourage me when I missed a day'. Report 65 (Rabit): streak-only scoring is 'too all-or-nothing' — a completion-% score alongside the streak requested by a payer (S7).

merged_from.title: Credit for non-consecutive, cumulative progress alongside streaks
merged_from.note: C158 (report 10: cumulative credit next to streaks) and C216 (report 20: a decaying strength score instead of resets) are the same product principle stated by two corpora

title: An unexplained metric reads as broken — explain the score on-screen
statement: Report 20: a weekly habit completed once showed 4%, not 100%, and users could not work out why; the developer's answer (~91 repetitions to reach 100%) read as arbitrary. A documentation failure, not a maths failure — one explainer screen and an optional 'this period' toggle was the cheapest satisfaction win in the corpus (20 classified, undercounted). Report 59 (Tappsk): 'не очень понятно что значит 115' (not clear what 115 means) — the productivity score is unexplained on screen. Report 60 (Mindway): 'It's just a basic to do list' — the absence of any metric at all (no completion %, no consistency view) is read as the product being unfinished. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'you see a sea of dots without being able to distinguish month, week and day' (IT, 1★) — the dot / heat-map grid others paid for carries no time axis, and a 4★ asks for the options to be explained: 'the UI is legible to people who already understand it'; P8: a visible month / week / day framing as a design test; P7: one-line hints on first use.

title: Store listing and paywall copy stay true — disclose limits, and never advertise a feature you removed, lack, or don't integrate
statement: Report 20: the listing said 'Unlimited amount of habits. You don't need to pay a penny' for at least two years after the free tier was capped at 3; 24 reviews (mean 1.21 — the lowest of any theme) called it false advertising by name. Zero engineering cost, unmade for over two years. Report 18's screenshots advertised a timer a buyer could not find. Report 6 / 19: a buyer who paid for a feature that isn't there cancels and says 'there are free ones' — it turns a feature request into a refund cause. Report 2: sibling apps implied an integration that did not exist; the purchases it drove ended in 1★. Report 25: the App Store listing showed Apple Watch support that could not be installed. Report 26: the German store listing carried a typo — 'Eden-Gewohnheitstrinker' (habit drinker) for 'Gewohnheitstracker'. Report 28: a listing that says 'habit tracker' for a product that is a pet game produces 'it's not what it says it is' 2★ reviews. Report 29: a privacy label saying 'analytics and diagnostics' while the app asks to route third-party traffic through the user's IP — the store disclosure must cover what the app actually does. Report 30: the listing still says 'Track up to 2 habits' after the cap became 3, the advertised streak/interactive widget is not the shipped widget, and one reviewer says the IAP was not visible at the decision point — correct the listing to remove expectation-mismatch 1★. Report 23: reviewers said the task cap was not disclosed in the description and asked for refunds on that basis; the 68 'it's just a checklist' 1★ reviews are an expectation failure the listing could pre-empt. Report 30: the listing still said 2 free habits after the cap became 3. Report 31: 57 say the price was hidden or the listing implied 'free' ('needs an in-app purchases mark'; 'online ads … said it was under $10 one time'); 50 describe an intro price renewing much higher only 'in the small print' (9.99€ → 100.99€; £5.99 → £51.99, 'just hoping someone doesn't cancel'). Report 33: 'you finally mention that habits are limited … after they've created it'; 34 price-hidden / misleading 'free' reviews. Report 34: users who searched for free apps met a 2-habit wall — 'only to find out AFTER downloading the app that there is a fee'; 'I just wish it was said earlier (for example, here)'. Report 36: a store screenshot showing a habit named 'Run 15 minutes' made a buyer expect a built-in timer (2★). Report 41: Spanish and Portuguese are on the listing while reviewers in ES / CL / BR report them missing (2024–2026). Report 42: the listing names 36 languages including Hebrew and Ukrainian which the app does not deliver — 'They present it as if it's in Hebrew. In practice there's no option for a Hebrew interface' (IL, 1★); 'Preview on AppStore was on Ukrainian, I don't like that it's on russian' (three of Ukraine's eight reviews) — a factual misstatement, not a backlog item; a 'goal for the day' advertised and absent. Report 43: 'Not a free app. The whole app is an in app purchase'; 'Bait and switch. After 3 they make you pay' — 14 of 16 such reviews US, none after Oct 2021. Report 46: 'Every picture shows a bunch of colorful habit trackers, not a one shows what the free version looks like' — a screenshot of the actual 3-habit free view is the fix. Report 47: the Japanese listing (12 Sep 2026) says the free version offers 'unlimited task registration' while reviewers from Dec 2024 to Mar 2026 report a free cap of 6 ('6 habitudes gratuites'); two say the paid nature was not disclosed — state the cap and trial length on the listing and at the paywall. Report 48: the listing states 3 free trackers while reviewers report 10 / 8 / 7 / 6 / 5 / 4 / 3 / 2 / 1 across eras; 48 hit an undisclosed wall after setup (1.65★) — disclose the limit on the listing and at first run. Report 49: 'Free with In-App Purchases' and an ad saying 'get your free life reset plan today' front a product with no free use — advertised as free 37 (1.08), tripling after the trial launched. Report 50: search summaries of the listing state a 5-habit free cap, 1 reminder per habit and 3 journal notes per day while five 2026 reviewers in four storefronts get 3 habits and nobody mentions the other caps — 'Either way this is a disclosure problem'. Report 53: the listing claimed Family Sharing that in-app purchases don't support (M5: remove it). Report 54: three reviewer-reported listing-versus-product disagreements — 'Advanced Statistics' that is a calendar, a €2.50 subscription on the listing the app did not sell (a reader who 'would book that immediately'), and a listing that said 5 free habits when the app gave 3. Report 56: a store preview shows a widget-transparency setting the user cannot find in the app. Report 57: 'I bought Premium and nothing differs from before — I can't use the features shown in the screenshots'; Family Sharing advertised but not delivered. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_DISCLOSURE 80 (1.95★) and MON_PAYWALL_SURPRISE 64 (1.70★) — 'Пишите сразу, что ПО платное, а не встроенные покупки' (say up front that the software is paid, not 'in-app purchases'); 50 + 44 of the 674 1★; the listing does not state the caps and the report's experiment is to state them. Report 60 (Mindway): M_MISLEADING_ADVERT 5 (all 1★: 'Click bait'; 'Not set up as advertised'; 'is it free? No. So Change to paid.'; 'it said it was free') and both ad-sourced reviewers at 1★ — F4: state the subscription price and the free-tier limit in the App Store listing and in the first ad frame, which 'removes the click bait / it said it was free class of review entirely'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a Health integration a reviewer believed was advertised does not work — 'either make it work, or remove the claim'. Report 67 (Habio): the listing claims App Store billing, 'optional subscription', 'designed in collaboration with mental health professionals' and sharing with friends, while reviewers describe off-store billing, a hard paywall ('Optional subscription was a lie') and no sharing; an old pinned 'it has a free version' review misled later installers.

merged_from.note: C138 (paywall implies a capability the product lacks) and C218 (listing advertises a removed feature) are the same rule on two surfaces

merged_from.title: Never imply cross-app integration you don't have
merged_from.note: C087 (implied cross-app integration) is a third surface of the same rule

merged_from.title: Disclose product limits in the listing — an undisclosed cap or scope becomes a refund request
merged_from.note: C224 (report 23: an undisclosed task cap became refund requests) is the omission side of C218 (the listing advertising what the product does not do) — one listing-truth rule

title: A free cap must be concurrent, never lifetime — deleting a habit frees a slot
statement: Report 20: the 3-habit free cap behaved as a lifetime cap — users who deleted a habit to make room could not add a replacement and the add button routed to the paywall; this turned a pricing decision into a functional dead end and was the mechanic that converted annoyance into uninstalls. Report 31: a minority reported 2 or 4–5 free slots after deleting and re-adding, which the free tier did not always allow. Report 36: archived / completed habits counted against the cap — 'when I went to archive one of my completed habits and tried to make a new one it wouldn't let me … seems like kind of a ripoff'. Report 48: users who deleted a tracker to make room found the slot gone (23, mean 2.22, 'the most damaging variant') — fix #2: restore slots freed by deletion. Report 50: 'unlimited for the first few days' then 'keep only three habits' — the cap applied retroactively to habits already created.

title: Never take a paying user's reason to buy away — the widget sold the upgrade and never worked
statement: Report 20: the widget was by a wide margin the most-named purchase trigger and the feature that most often didn't work — 182 reviews (mean 1.94), 113 from confirmed payers (12.4% of all payers), reported broken for five years with an in-app FAQ offering 'restart your phone'; even when present it was a Today-view widget while screenshots implied Home Screen. Ship it properly or remove it from the paywall copy and refund on request.

title: A receipt with a working product link after every charge, and a renewal reminder before it
statement: Report 19: reviewers could find no record of what they bought — 'no confirmation email anywhere'; support's answer 'we sent you an EMAIL notification' conceded that one e-mail with the fine print in a footer link was the whole safeguard, and 'the ONE SINGLE EMAIL they sent confirming my purchase with no actual link' left an ADHD buyer unable to find the product at all. Every charge produces a receipt that names the plan, the amount, the next charge date and links to the product; every renewal is preceded by a reminder. Related: C152 (the trial-end reminder) and C177 (SKU names). Report 24: 197 reviews (mean 1.168, 0% 5★) say the renewal came with no notice — the cheapest item on the report's list; 1,412 edited reviews are largely downgrades added after a later charge. Report 26: renewal with no advance notice (2) inside the lowest-rated theme. Report 31: show the renewal price before purchase — 50 renewal shocks (mean 1.44). Report 59 (Tappsk): 'списали деньги за приложение, которого у меня нет' (money taken for an app I no longer have) — without a receipt naming the product, a renewal on a deleted app reads as fraud. Report 65 (Rabit): renewed after months of non-use with no warning — 'Achei que agiram de má fé… Espero que repensem o formato de receita'. Report 67 (Habio): the charge appeared under the company name, not the app — 'Tuve que investigar que aplicaciones tenía GOTOTOP LTD para saber que me estaban cobrando'; no receipt or reminder before the charge in 68 reviews.

title: A hard habit cap is a defensible design position only with an opt-in pressure valve — the default never changes
statement: Report 23: a paid one-time tracker capped at 6 → 12 → 24 tasks drew the largest request in twelve years (620, 8.53%) in every market and every year; each raise cut the complaint rate roughly in half (8.76% → 5.06%; 11.90% → 6.16%) and bought about three years before it rebounded, and it never fell below ~6%. Against it 118 (1.62%) defend the cap as the reason the app works, and nobody in the 620 asks for the default to change — they ask for the ceiling to move. The cap is a durable position and a permanent 6–12% complaint tax; ship extra capacity off by default behind a setting that states the rationale. Report 24 (the same principle from the coaching side): the product's real moat is a refusal — it declines to let users add more habits; small-steps pacing is the highest-rated theme of any size in 43,469 reviews (1,817, mean 4.692, 2.0% 1★; 'I stacked everything I wanted to change and failed miserably; this time I followed the program'), and the same constraint produces the four complaint shapes ('I already do this' 124, 'it ignored my answers' 175, 'too slow' 168, 'doesn't fit my week' 31). The corpus asks for one branch — declare a habit already-held and start at habit two — not for the constraint to go. Report 25: 19 reviewers (mean 4.32) defend a 3-habit free cap on principle ('helps me to only keep track of what is the most important to me') while 138 object — and the objectors name the number they would accept, median 8–10. Report 26 (the reward side): the cap is 3→5→6 habits plus a growth ceiling; users who love the constraint-free gentleness still say five slots cannot hold a routine, and propose their own valve — one full garden free. Report 46: 66 reviewers (3.03%, mean 4.92) defend a 3-habit cap on habit-science grounds ('shouldn't be tracking more than three in the first place'; 'the limit is beneficial since it kept me from piling expectations onto myself') while the counter-offer is 4–7 — the defensible cap is disclosed and framed as focus. Report 47: a user proposes buying slots — 'タブ数だけ買わせてください' ('let me buy just the number of tabs I need', 4★, 2025); the report's E2 is a per-slot purchase for free users at the cap. Report 48: the pressure valve reviewers propose is a cheap, narrow tier that only unlocks trackers — pay once for capacity, subscribe for sync / reports (58 one-time requesters, $10–$20); 15 ask to raise the free cap. Report 49: 40 want a free tier, ads or donations instead of a hard paywall (several volunteering heavy advertising); an Indian reviewer proposes 3–5 free habits with premium above — a report experiment. Report 59 (Tappsk): the cap held at 2 habits for five years generates a steady 4.4–5.1% objection per era with no sign of decay; three is the number reviewers repeatedly propose as enough to evaluate. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a fixed cap of 3, unchanged over 17 months, produces a steady trickle of cap reviews from otherwise satisfied users; the report's alternative to a raise is a time-limited 4th habit — a pressure valve rather than a moved wall.

title: Undo / un-complete is a visible button — never a gesture-only path
statement: Report 23: the only undo for an accidental completion was a shake gesture available immediately after the action; 77 reviews (1.06%, mean 3.38) across 12 storefronts called it unacceptable, several found the only workaround was resetting all history, and some deleted the app over it. Keep the gesture, add a button and a long-press-to-uncomplete path. Report 43: the Done and Info buttons sat adjacent for four years and swipes were mis-read ('I was constantly marking things as done when I really wanted to mark them as skipped… so I deleted it'; 'Tap targets for your most common actions… are tiny'); undo an accidental Done requested. Report 48: can't edit / delete a log 32 (3.22). Report 52: 'tap again to undo' was removed (2021) and a mistaken tap can only be marked 'failed'.

title: Disclose product limits in the listing — an undisclosed cap or scope becomes a refund request
statement: Report 23: reviewers said the task cap was not disclosed in the App Store description and asked for refunds on that basis; the 68 'no value / it's just a checklist' 1★ reviews (0.94%) and most of the 123 price objections are expectation failures the listing could pre-empt.

title: A one-off free promotion (App of the Week, partner promo) acquires durable users
statement: Report 23: a Starbucks 'Pick of the Week' promo in 2015–16 drew 13 reviews at mean 4.62, and one of those users was still active in July 2025 — ten-year retention from a free promo on a paid-up-front app. Report 34 (counter-case): a ~29 Jun 2023 free-lifetime giveaway brought 27 short 5★ reviews in three days and a wave of non-English users asking for a language the app did not have; no durable-retention evidence. Report 41: two early users were given the full version free at the 2020 launch and rated 5★. Report 50: two 5★ reviewers ask for a referral / discount programme ('rewards for recommending the app to friends… in the form of discounts') while 37 evangelise it — S3: build one.

title: App-icon badge count of outstanding habits, with an active-hours window
statement: Report 23: a badge count of tasks still open today, limited to an active-hours window, is named by many reviewers as the core motivator of a paid one-time tracker. Report 41: app badge counter broken / absent (3). Report 43: 20 reminders per day named as a cap. Report 55: a badge countdown of outstanding habits motivates some and can't be removed for others.

title: A 'graduated' state — keep tracking a mastered habit without it occupying an active slot
statement: Report 23: the single most persuasive argument for more capacity, made repeatedly, is that people want to keep tracking a habit that has become automatic while starting a new one; a mastered/graduated state that keeps history but frees the slot answers it without raising the cap. Report 48: end dates and archiving requested by 23 (4.09). Report 50: archive completed habits requested (2) — a completed short-term goal cluttering the screen. Report 53: archive without losing history (274-vote review).

title: Text fields must handle IME composition — Hangul and CJK input
statement: Report 23: the task-title field mangled Hangul (typing 약 stored 야ㄱ), reported four separate times over five years and never fixed, producing 1★–4★ reviews from otherwise-satisfied Korean users in the storefront with the worst refund rate. Report 28: CJK font fallback rendered Japanese glyphs for Chinese text and silently truncated habit names; a localisation update once turned every 'r' into a black square — audit font fallback and string handling whenever a language ships. Report 30: the onboarding name field rejected Arabic input — 'it won't accept any name' — 2 of 3 Saudi reviews, both 1★; a hard block at first launch for an entire locale. Report 57: a Sep 2020 update stopped the note keyboard appearing (21 of 22 reviews in three days).

title: A deliberate completion gesture — press-and-hold with haptic and sound, not a bare tap
statement: Report 23: press-and-hold completion is described as physically satisfying and as accident-proofing, attested inside the two largest positive themes; some criticise it. Copying 'tap to complete' loses something real; pair any tap model with a visible undo. Report 36: 'very satisfying to hold down a button … and get actual physical feedback from my phone … Much nicer than just tapping a complete button on a reminder list'. Report 47 (counter-evidence): a long-press that opens a record screen before 'done' is counted as too many taps by 14 (mean 2.86) — a deliberate gesture must complete the check-in, not open a form. Report 48 (counter-evidence): a redesign that made every log a double click cost ten reviews in three months from loyal payers — see [[C264]].

title: Sync merges an append-only, timestamped event log — never last-writer-wins state replacement
statement: Report 23: after a 2022 migration to direct iCloud sync, complaint-framed sync went from 1.42% of 2015–17 reviews to 7.60% of post-2022 reviews (mean 2.90) and data loss from 0.33% to 4.62% of the era; failure modes were a device overwriting newer state with older state, deleted tasks resurrecting, Watch completions never reaching the phone, and completions un-completing seconds later. A customer review spells out the correct architecture: immutable timestamped events applied in order. Report 48: duplicate entries 32 (2.31), 20 of them in the 2015 sync rewrite. Report 50: to-do entries lost and unrecoverable for a Premium user (Apr 2026).

title: Audit the funnel per market and per channel — storefronts diverge on billing and funnel stage, not on the product, and written reviews are a complaint channel that under-rates it against public ratings
statement: Report 24: Latin-American and Gulf storefronts (Brazil 4.266, Mexico 4.381, Peru 4.511, Ecuador 4.593; bill_core 2.35–6.42%) carry the same product that rates 2.1–2.6 in the US/UK/AU/CA during 2024–26 at 42–52% billing disputes; Brazil stays at 4.002 through the worst era. Language-neutral ratings rule out a classifier artefact. Whatever is different in how the product is sold there is the model — and rich English-language markets were the worst, not the best. Report 25: Argentina (mean 2.95, monetisation friction 40%, billing 10%) and the Spanish-language block (blocker 36% more common, paywall register markedly more hostile) vs Great Britain (mean 4.06, zero blocker, zero confusing-UX) — the same product, different market experience; check Argentine pricing display and trial mechanics. Report 26: Germany (63.6% 5★, 19.83% friction), France (20.37%), Australia (18.52%) and Canada (cap 10.09%) vs Russia (85.3% 5★, 7.34% friction) and Vietnam (86.8%, 5.15%) on the same product — though Russia's low friction may be a payment-availability effect: if users cannot reach the paywall, low friction is not satisfaction. Report 28: China (n=12) has zero ad complaints while its three critical reviews are all localisation — if ad inventory does not serve there, CN is a natural control for the ad-free product. Report 30: Russia is the product's real market (only continuous 13-month stream, most purchase attempts, most nuanced feedback, substantive mean 3.20) and where the payment flow is visibly breaking; Spanish-language organic reviews (AR/MX/UY, 0/6 templated, mean 2.33) are the harshest in the corpus while ES/CL are 16/24 templated at 4.75. Report 31: Australia shows the monetisation and integrity story without the crash wave (friction 43.5%, entitlement 14.0%, billing 19.7%, launch 9.3%); Canada is the worst large storefront (2.10, 57.7% 1★); Brazil and Mexico are wave-dominated (launch 28.6% / 28.1%, upsell only 2.2% / 3.5%); Switzerland was offered 10 CHF and charged 59 CHF; Hong Kong and India show 26.7% / 17.1% entitlement failure. Report 33: storefronts differ sharply — cn blocked (57.8%), de subscription-averse (price 14.7%, subscription 9.2%), kr the account-deletion centre (5.5%), jp highest payer share (16.0%) and Watch / update complaints, ru Mac/web 10.1%, vn happiest (4.61). Report 42: Brazil (41.8% cap complaints, 9 of 12 lag reports), the US (all six multi-count complaints, near-zero cap), Russia (5 of 7 crashes, 4 of 6 data losses, no payment rail) and Japan (both reviews 1★ on price) each fail differently on the same product. Report 43: 18 of 20 crash reports are US (4.40% vs 0.87%) — more likely a reporting-behaviour artefact than a device fact, unresolvable from reviews. Report 46: the same product is loved and disputed differently per storefront — Germany 3.95 with every monetisation theme 2–4× global, Russia 4.43 calling the price fair, China objecting to the payment shape not the cap, India negotiating, Turkey regional price, Spain the harshest cap objection (mean 2.00) beside Catalan praise. Report 47: Japan (mean 3.54) carries almost all the monetisation shock and the payers; Korea (4.33) requests and forgives (6 of 13 KR crash reviews still 5★); the same product rates 3.70 in JP + KR and 4.25 elsewhere. Report 48: 'Praise is remarkably uniform; grievance is local' — simplicity and flexibility land within a few points everywhere while price sensitivity clusters in CA / AU / DE / CN and localization in RU / CN; China splits sharpest (crash 12.33%, localization 12.33%, simplicity at 5.00★). Report 50: the cap change is invisible in the US (all four US cap statements say 5) and concentrated in Turkey, Australia and Mexico (four of Mexico's five reviews in 18–24 Aug 2026) — hypothesis: it lands hardest where the subscription is expensive relative to local purchasing power. Report 53: Spanish- and Portuguese-language storefronts carry 34.1% monetisation friction against 21.3% globally; Germany's top theme is price (18.00%); Taiwan's is reliability (37.5%) with only 8.9% friction. Report 54: payer and cap-complaint rates are identical in the high-volume group and globally (11.9%), so those are product properties, while price objection (CN 16.7%), restore failure (non-US) and outcome language (US 24.4%) are market-specific. Report 57: the same product shows three market problems — Korea (tenured base worn down by regressions), the US (top-of-funnel lost to a 30-second ad; ads and uninstalls 15.15%), Japan (would convert at ¥2,000, converts at zero at ¥4,500). Report 59 (Tappsk): monetisation pain is geographic and product love is not — without the Russian storefront praise (76.8%), ease and the free-limit objection are unchanged while billing falls 3.2% → 1.4% and payment access 0.7% → 0.0%; billing 3.7% in Russian-speaking storefronts vs 1.0% in English-speaking; high-star reviews hide support tickets (CONTRA_RATING 155: 102 are 4–5★ reviews whose text reports a crash, charge or refund request — 'Возможно ли вернуть деньги после списания', 5★), so star-filtered monitoring misses refund requests. Report 60 (Mindway): the US vs rest-of-world split is a funnel-stage split — the US has bought and been disappointed (under-built 7.92% vs 1.74%, billing 9.90% vs 0.87%), the rest of the world has been stopped at the door (paywall cap 11.30% vs 5.94%); whether the billing rate improved after 2024 or the US share of reviews simply fell (85.3% → 26.8%) cannot be separated from review text (Q3). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 45 written reviews vs 536 public ratings (8.40%), written mean 3.111 vs public 4.52 — 'the written corpus is a complaint channel, not a satisfaction measure'; per storefront the gap runs to −3.56 (UA: 39 ratings at 4.56 vs two 1★ reviews) and Ireland's one 1★ review is its entire public rating; Argentina is the one storefront where the June burst shows in the public number (3.82). (Consolidation after report 62: the title was widened from 'Audit the sales funnel per market — the same product can rate 4.3 in one storefront and 2.1 in another on billing alone' to cover the channel dimension the batch added; the original storefront finding stays in the statement.) Report 64 (Critique AI): written vs public gap −1.84 to −2.92 in every storefront with ≥ 5 reviews (US 180 @ 2.66 vs 9,557 @ 4.73); high-spend ('rich') markets carry the friction (2.53, 47.9% 1★) against volume markets (2.91, 34.3%) — the paywall binds where the creator's audience is; the US argues the amount (price 30.0% > hardwall 29.4%) and is where people get in (22.2% vs 11.5%), while GB argues the wall's existence (40.0% vs 20.0%); the app ranks worst in the US (48th) where 43% of written reviews come from.
